articles.title: Ukraine accuses Elon Musk’s SpaceX of throttling Starlink terminals
articles.body:
Musk says US military controls Starlink’s limits after Ukraine outcry
Officials say ability to block Russian drones restricted as Kyiv reels from second night of ballistic missile attacks.
Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of throttling Starlink satellite services, disrupting its ability to carry out military operations and leaving Kyiv vulnerable to deadly attacks.
An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that without warning, services had been limited for terminals travelling over 100mph overnight on Wednesday – effectively limiting Ukraine’s ability to launch drones, which use satellite internet to pilot the craft.
Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, which operates Starlink and its military version, Starshield, has since claimed on X that the United States government and military control all Starshield speeds.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [President of the United States],” wrote Musk, a major US defence contractor and former top adviser to US President Donald Trump, after receiving criticism for the disruptions.
The White House has not confirmed or denied Musk’s assertion. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Writing on Telegram, Ukrainian defence technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said Ukraine was “deprived of one of the few chances to defend itself from Shahed drones”.
He added that frontline logistics and long-distance missions were also disrupted.
Asked about the restriction on the military version of Starlink, Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan Uncensored it was “a big mistake” that “will bring a lot of human losses”.
US Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a member of the armed services and foreign relations committees, wrote on X: “These restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starshield must stop immediately. Lives are at stake.
“The Pentagon is also required to notify Congress if it pauses or downgrades intelligence sharing with Ukraine. If that happens, Secretary of War [Pete Hegseth] must provide that immediately.”
The suggestion that Musk’s company had throttled Starlink services drew the ire of Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv’s behalf.
“Hey Elon Musk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” wrote Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister. “As your European customers, we are watching you.”
The “big man” gibe refers to a public dispute on social media between Musk, Sikorski and United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio in 2025, when the SpaceX boss told Sikorski to “be quiet, small man” on his X platform.
Starlink is a sensitive topic between Sikorski and Musk. The two previously clashed over the technology after the trillionaire said Ukraine’s “entire frontline could collapse” if he switched off Starlink.
Following the dispute in 2025, Musk said “no matter how much I disagree with the Ukraine policy, Starlink will never turn off its terminals.”
At the time he added, “We would never do such a thing or use it as a bargaining chip.”
‘Cannot be a coincidence’
The slowdown comes after Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv for the second night in a row, killing at least nine people and damaging electricity and heating infrastructure. Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not receive its usual warnings from Western allies for a second day, without specifying which partners.
Sources have told Reuters and other media that the US has threatened to cut off intelligence for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine, pressing Kyiv to suspend attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Trump said on Tuesday the US has not stopped sharing intelligence.
Beskrestnov warned that the slowdown “cannot be a coincidence” after Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel – despite international sanctions to isolate Moscow.
Speaking to AFP, another Ukrainian official accused Washington of throttling Starlink and helping Russia.
On Saturday, Trump suggested Zelenskyy had not done enough to end the war with Russia, blaming him for high diesel prices in the US.
Last week, Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel under pressure to curb fuel prices that have soared since the US war with Iran began as the midterms rapidly approach. He told Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries and urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskyy.
“It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” Zelenskyy said in the interview with Morgan.
The Ukrainian leader explained he was fine with Trump being in the middle between Ukraine and Russia, but “if you are in the middle, you have to stay in the middle.”

articles.title: Ukrainian drones are hitting Russia’s biggest data centers. Why are they so vulnerable — and can anything protect them?
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones are hitting Russia’s biggest data centers. Why are they so vulnerable — and can anything protect them?
After strikes on Yandex’s data centers, pro-war channels accused the company of inaction and even sabotage. Elements of critical infrastructure turned out to be completely unprotected against drone attacks. Now similar accusations will likely be directed at Sberbank: the bank’s largest data center in the Saratov region was attacked overnight on October 14. All these facilities were an obvious target for Ukraine’s military, if only because Russian forces are actively striking similar targets in Ukraine. Of course, the inadequate protection of the data centers has nothing to do with malicious intent or negligence on the part of Yandex and Sberbank’s management. It is known that, even before the strikes, authorities and the military discussed measures to defend such facilities with businesses. And judging by video of the attacks, at least in Yandex’s case some defense — probably in the form of mobile fire teams or automatic turrets — did exist: drones were fired at with small arms. This shows that Russia still lacks the resources to build a multilayered anti-drone air defense system anywhere except Moscow. And site-level defenses at individual factories, warehouses, and data centers cannot repel massed strikes.
First, a reminder of which facilities Ukraine’s military struck
Ukrainian strikes hit three of Yandex’s six largest data centers, also known as data processing centers, between October 7 and 11. None were located in the Moscow region, the area most heavily protected by Russian air defenses.
- The data center in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, which also housed two of Yandex’s three supercomputers, stopped operating entirely. Judging by satellite images from the Planet Labs, the wing of the building housing the data center had burned down completely.
- Data centers in Vladimir, one of two in the city, and in Kaluga sustained significant damage.
A Ukrainian strike hit Sberbank’s Mega Data Center in Balakovo, in the Saratov region, overnight on October 14. Construction began in 2021, when Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Chernyshenko promised the facility would become the largest in Russia.
When Yandex and Sberbank built these facilities before the full-scale war, they had no reason to design the buildings to withstand drones carrying warheads with dozens of kilograms of explosives. HAKA Moscow, the company that built one of Yandex’s data centers in Vladimir in 2016–2017, said its main objectives were:
- speed of construction;
- the ability to expand the facility;
- and, importantly, reducing the need for active cooling of the equipment, which increased the facility’s energy efficiency.
Reinforced concrete slabs — a material characteristic of Soviet industrial construction — were not used to build the building’s frame.
So what went wrong with the defenses at these data centers?
All buildings of this kind — built with modern technology out of metal structures — are vulnerable to drones carrying relatively small warheads. By contrast, defense and civilian enterprises built during the Soviet era, such as thermal power plants, are difficult targets for these drones.
The full-scale war has confirmed this. When striking targets in Ukraine, Russian forces prefer to hit reinforced concrete buildings with ballistic and cruise missiles, which carry warheads weighing hundreds of kilograms and can penetrate obstacles because of their high kinetic energy.
Likewise, Ukraine’s military, which has not yet received large numbers of missiles with a range of more than 300 kilometers (186 miles), prefers relatively “soft” but economically important targets: oil refineries, warehouses, and now data centers. Ukraine tries to strike Soviet-era industrial facilities with missiles such as the Flamingo cruise missile, but it does not yet have enough of them to achieve an effect of strategic scale.
Ukraine’s army has also used drones to damage facilities that are strategically important to Russia and its military. In most cases, though, foreign companies built the buildings housing these facilities using metal structures.
Optical Fiber Systems JSC in Saransk, Russia’s only major fiber-optic producer, was built turnkey by a Finnish company in the late 2000s. The plant was important to the Russian military because fiber optics are used, among other things, to make fiber-optic-guided drones for the front line. In 2025, Ukrainian drone strikes effectively destroyed the building and its equipment. Rebuilding it will take several years, Russian authorities reported. Other successful attacks on workshops built from metal structures have also been recorded.
Hi, I’m Yulia.
I’m an editor at Meduza, and for almost five years now, I haven’t been sleeping well for one reason: I’m worried about my colleagues in Russia.
I’m often woken up by messages from our freelance reporters inside the country. They sometimes work late at night or early in the morning, and they message me at all hours. I never silence my phone at night in case of an emergency. Every notification jolts me awake. Half-asleep, my first thought is always the same: they’re texting me because the police have come to search their home. In Russia, you can go to prison for working with Meduza. Sometimes I have nightmares about my reporters being interrogated by the FSB. Some of those nightmares have come true.
Meduza’s reporters risk their freedom to tell the world what’s happening inside Russia. They believe their work can help make a better future possible, and they refuse to leave. Please donate so they can keep reporting.
Beyond the vulnerability of the buildings themselves, Yandex and Sberbank also erred in choosing where to build. By the fifth year of the full-scale war, facilities in and around Moscow had gained a major competitive advantage: the military and Russian authorities have clearly chosen to allocate air defense resources to protect the capital, just as Ukraine’s leadership has done for Kyiv.
Traditional short-range air defense systems, the Tor and Pantsir families, remain the backbone of Russia’s drone defenses, and there clearly are not enough of them to protect the country’s entire territory. Concentrating these systems around Moscow, however, has made hitting targets in the capital difficult.
Difficult, but solvable: massing drones in a single wave sometimes lets Ukraine’s military break through the defenses around Moscow and reach particularly important targets, such as the Moscow oil refinery. Many attacks fail, however: videos and photos of drones shot down around Moscow circulate often, with no verified evidence that targets inside the city were struck.
Most of Russia’s key internet infrastructure nodes are located in Moscow and St. Petersburg. M9 (MSK-IX), the most important node, houses the infrastructure for the root DNS servers and sits in the southwest of the capital. During a drone attack on August 18, a fire broke out for unknown reasons at the CHPP-20 power plant, which supplies M9 with electricity, causing problems for thousands of websites. However, the data center itself was not damaged at the time.
How could these fragile targets be defended, in theory?
Methods of protection fall into two categories: passive and active. Passive measures include building physical protective structures around a facility or, where possible, dispersing production.
Building protective structures requires large capital investments with no guarantee the method will work. Russia also used to require government authorization to build these structures, but a 2026 law repealed that rule.
The problem is that not all structures are effective. Expensive protective structures, naturally, have a better chance of working. The same cannot be said for the ordinary anti-drone nets used at the front to counter small drones: they are not very effective against fixed-wing drones carrying warheads of dozens of kilograms.
This fall, Russian oil refineries and oil depots began installing sturdier metal nets of various designs. There is still no data on how much this protection helps. A video showing nets being installed at the Moscow oil refinery was published September 21, while the most recent attack — which again damaged unnamed equipment at the plant — had occurred the day before. The video was probably filmed before that strike, so doubts remain about how effective the netting is. There is also a risk that these barriers could be breached by repeated strikes on the same spot.
Previous experience has also failed to prove the method’s effectiveness. Bashneft, for example, began installing metal nets around its primary oil-refining units in the spring of 2024, yet drone strikes knocked the company’s plants out of operation in 2026.
That doesn’t mean more expensive, complex structures won’t offer protection. These experiments — sturdy metal cages and nets — are being conducted in Gulf states, though they, too, have not yet been tested in combat. Iran and its allies, the Houthis, have not recently used drones for strikes on land, preferring missile attacks instead. Russian companies, however, have already begun building these “fences” at their refineries.
Reliable passive drone defense might force an adversary to use more expensive munitions — missiles above all — to hit targets. Russian enterprises are already trying to build more reliable defenses that could also stop missiles in theory. At some power plants, for instance, construction has begun on structures resembling reinforced concrete sarcophagi.
Ukraine has chosen a second path of passive defense: dispersing potential targets. Fire Point, a manufacturer of drones, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles, has said more than 20 camouflaged production sites are working on its ballistic missile project. This approach naturally reduces production efficiency, if it doesn’t rule out mass-producing complex products altogether.
Ukraine is helped by its ability to move some production outside the country. In Russia, the equivalent might be relocating sensitive facilities en masse to the Far East, but a shortage of production factors there, labor among them, and complicated logistics stand in the way.
Active defense — air defense and electronic warfare assets — also has its drawbacks. Russia’s model relies on a network of traditional short-range air defense systems backed by mobile fire teams equipped with man-portable air-defense missile systems, small arms, anti-aircraft artillery, interceptor drones, and mobile radars. Covering the entire territory from the Ukrainian border to targets deep inside the country is impossible: Russia’s Aerospace Forces and Ground Forces had 129 Tor-M½ systems and just over 50 Pantsir systems at the start of the year, according to the Military Balance 2026 reference guide. Even mounting them on towers and tall buildings, a widely used practice, does not allow them to detect, track, and hit a low-flying drone at a range of more than 15 kilometers (9 miles).
Saturating the defenses with hundreds or thousands of mobile fire teams, each capable of hitting targets within hundreds of meters or, at most, a few kilometers of itself, is also impossible: the Russian military lacks the personnel for it. The Kremlin has tried to solve the problem by calling up reservists through the Combat Army Reserve of the Country program, created in 2021, under which participants receive small payments and attend annual military training while keeping their regular jobs. Russia, however, appears to have not found enough reservists.
Russia has not yet built a layered system of sensors and interceptor drones similar to Ukraine’s, though individual elements, such as mobile groups with interceptors, have been deployed. Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov promised in the spring that the system would be ready by November. Work is underway: new regional structures are being created, and the outlines of a defense are taking shape.
Even so, Ukraine’s layered defense isn’t perfect: Russian forces have managed to temporarily neutralize it by quickly shifting to producing thousands of faster jet-powered drones and miniature cruise missiles. Neither Ukraine’s interceptor drones nor the sensors supporting them are designed for these targets, so Ukraine’s military now has to build a new system and new production lines to counter the Russian drones. Both the jet-powered drones and the tools to counter them have turned out to be far more expensive than the previous generation of equipment.
As a result, Russia’s anti-drone air defense still tends toward protecting individual sites, but there are so many potential targets that protecting all of them is impossible. And where this protection does exist, attackers can overwhelm it by saturating the defenses with a mass of drones.
The Kremlin is trying to get the owners of these facilities to pay for their own drone defenses. A decree now allows the state to temporarily take over management of enterprises that fail to provide their own protection. Beyond passive protection measures, though, enterprises have few tools available for defense. Companies are allowed to “rent” air defense systems from the Defense Ministry, for instance. However, many large companies are trying to build their own radar and interceptor-drone systems. This effort is hindered, among other things, by aviation regulations, which there are now proposals to amend urgently.
A separate problem for private air defense is the inability to use explosive warheads on interceptors. Despite some successes, it is unlikely that fixed-wing drones can be reliably shot down using only the kinetic energy of a small, low-speed interceptor, though manufacturers claim otherwise.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: China’s drone modem pipeline: How mesh technology helps Russian UAVs penetrate deep into Ukraine
articles.body:
The Insider's correspondent in Ukraine examined a mesh modem — one made by China’s Xingkai Tech — that was found in a Russian Gerbera drone. Then, posing as a Russian military supplier, they obtained evidence that the Chinese company is knowingly willing to sell its modems to the Russian drone factory in Alabuga. Several banks, including DBS Bank, China Merchants Bank, and Ping An Bank, are actively facilitating these sales. Mesh networks are the most practical technology for controlling Russia’s long-range drones over Ukraine. They allow operators to control drones manually and send commands in flight, exploiting gaps in Ukrainian air defenses. According to The Insider’s estimates, Xingkai Tech accounts for about half the market for high-power mesh modems used in Gerbera and Geran drones, making its supplies critical to Russian military manufacturers.
In February 2026, the Russian military lost access to the Starlink terminals it had previously used to facilitate attacks on Ukraine. As a workaround, it has since turned to the use of Geran and Gerbera drones equipped with Chinese-made mesh modems.
A typical attack involving Geran and Gerbera drones works as follows: some drones flying near the border connect to Russian or Belarusian signal repeaters and relay signals to drones operating deeper inside Ukraine. Each relay node is equipped with a powerful mesh modem.
Gerbera drones are becoming increasingly important. They are significantly cheaper than Gerans and have a similar radar signature, allowing them to serve as decoys for Ukrainian air defenses.
In 2024 Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR) reported finding Xingkai Tech modems in Gerbera drones. Later, the use of these modems and the role of Gerberas in combat operations in 2026 were discussed on a major pro-Russian website. However, there was no evidence that Xingkai Tech was knowingly and openly supplying modems directly to the Russian Alabuga plant where the drones are assembled.
In an earlier investigation, The Insider found that Chinese company Shenzhen Xingkai Technology, also known as Xingkai Tech, had issued an invoice for 30 mesh modems destined for Vladivostok as part of a supply chain supporting Russian drones.
In 2026, The Insider examined a mesh modem obtained privately in Ukraine that had been found in an upgraded Gerbera drone fitted with a vertical stabilizer. This variant first appeared this past summer.
An investigator from the Nordsint project then posed as a Russian military supplier based in Alabuga, where Geran and Gerbera drones are manufactured. Xingkai Tech confirmed that the model was available and that Xingkai Technology was its sole manufacturer. The journalist also obtained an invoice for 500 mesh modems that were identical to the one examined in Ukraine — a shipment worth approximately $2.87 million.
How the modems are sold
Posing as a Russian military supplier, The Insider and Nordsint contacted Xingkai Technology through its official WeChat account to request a quote for modems “similar” to the one shown in a photograph from Ukraine. The undercover investigators made clear that the end user needed exactly the same version, with an identical casing.
A company employee who introduced himself as “Jack Jiang” (his actual name is Jiang Qin (蒋钦), and he is the director and owner of the company) confirmed that Xingkai Technology manufactured the modems; he even provided the investigators with the XK F-359 user manual. Some sources, including the Ukrainian military intelligence agency’s War and Sanctions portal, had previously misidentified the device as a separate but similar model, the XK F-358.
To make sure the end user would receive an identical device, the investigators asked Jiang to take photographs and video of the modem at the production facility. He complied.
The modem examined by The Insider in Ukraine proved identical to the device described in the manual and shown in the warehouse video. It differed only slightly from the models featured in Xingkai Technology’s online catalog. Jiang explained that other versions of the F-359 had different casings but retained the same internal layout.
The Insider and Nordsint then ordered 500 modems for delivery to Alabuga, home to a factory that produces most of Russia’s long-range drones. Jiang responded with an invoice for 19.5 million yuan, offering the “client” two payment options: U.S. dollars to Xingkai Tech’s account at DBS Bank in Hong Kong, or yuan to Jiang’s personal account at Ping An Bank in China.
Jiang also confirmed that identical modems were available through Shenzhen Sinosun Technology (although Xingkai Tech itself manufactured the devices). In their correspondence, Nordsint explicitly stated that the end user was a military production facility. Xingkai Tech’s director raised no objections.
Nordsint explicitly stated that the end user was a military production facility. Xingkai Tech’s director raised no objections
In another message, Jiang asked whether his Russian customer had “won” the “project,” apparently referring to a tender.
After being asked to “update the address,” Xingkai Tech issued a slightly revised invoice. This time, the company spelled “Alabuga” in Latin characters, making it harder to claim later that it had been unaware of the end user’s identity.
The Chinese bank account listed on the revised invoice was in the name of Huang Qiuping, who may also use the name Fanny Huang (she is listed under that name as a contact in the mesh modem’s user manual). According to Tesari records, Huang Qiuping left her management position at Xingkai Tech in 2025.
The revised invoice directed payments to an account at the Hongling branch of the China Merchants Bank in Shenzhen.
The key component of a mesh modem is a field-programmable gate array (FPGA). It enables the modem to make decisions about network topology and optimize communications. This “intelligent” component configures the mesh network linking a swarm of drones.
The Xingkai Tech director who corresponded with an undercover Nordsint investigator said the company uses the XC7Z020-2CLG4001 FPGA made by U.S.-based company AMD. When asked to provide an AMD licensing agreement (ostensibly to meet Russian bureaucratic requirements), Jiang refused, saying Xingkai Tech obtains its FPGAs through an intermediary.
The Insider contacted AMD, which provided the following statement:
“Xingkai Technology is not an AMD customer or authorized partner, and AMD has not sold products to the company. AMD complies with all applicable U.S. export control and sanctions laws and strictly prohibits the export or reexport of AMD products to Russia in violation of those requirements.”
What this little box can do
The XK F-359 modem can maintain line-of-sight communications over distances of 100–300 km. This means that an attack on Kyiv theoretically may require just a couple of Gerbera or Shahed drones acting as relay stations to provide a stable radio link for the entire attacking drone group, allowing the drones to receive updated commands in flight and maneuver to evade air defenses. The technology is also crucial for providing live video feeds from operator-controlled drones equipped with cameras and guidance systems, such as those recently reported by Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov.
Mesh modems can autonomously establish and manage network topology in real time.
The XK F-359 manual states:
“The network operates on a single frequency and uses multi-hop relaying. Each node can move rapidly and freely, while the network topology can change and update rapidly without disrupting data transmission. The network is easy to deploy, flexible to use, and simple to operate and maintain. It provides reliable, timely, efficient and secure integrated IP services, including voice, broadband data, high-definition video, visual command and dispatch, and other multimedia services in challenging conditions, such as rapid movement and the absence of a direct line of sight.”
In other words, the mesh network reconfigures itself automatically, freeing drone operators from having to manage it manually and allowing them to focus on military tasks.
Notably, the manual’s opening line lists military and police operations among the intended applications of mesh technology:
“Broadband self-organizing networks can be widely used in the military, public security agencies, armed police, fire services, civil defense, electric power, the oil industry, mining, transportation, water management, forestry, radio and television, medicine, maritime and aviation communications, and other fields.”
Given these capabilities, the Xingkai Tech XK F-359 is almost ideally suited to Gerbera and Geran drones.
The specific XK F-359 variant documented by The Insider in Ukraine does not appear in Xingkai Technology’s public catalogs. The manual for this version became available only after The Insider established direct contact with the company.
Some online sources, meanwhile, identified Shenzhen Sinosun Technology as the modem’s manufacturer. The company’s website features a photograph of an identical modem, sometimes found among drone wreckage bearing the HX-50 label. When asked about this, Jack Jiang of Xingkai Technology confirmed that his company was the modem’s sole manufacturer.
Who bought them in Russia
The Insider examined Russian customs data and found that Xingkai Technology had shipped its products to Russia, declaring them simply as “antennas” and “remote control equipment.”
One Russian recipient was Atlant-Engineering, a trading company that does not manufacture drones. The company is owned by the family of Rafik Zagrutdinov, a mid-level official in the Moscow city government. Another recipient was LT Global Forwarding.
Both companies filed declarations of conformity, apparently for Xingkai Technology equipment; however, for reasons unknown, Quanzhou Yunzhuo Technology was listed as the manufacturer.
What’s new with the Gerberas
Gerbera drones were initially inexpensive decoys, as their radar signature resembled that of older Geran models without turbojet engines.
Later, Gerberas were fitted with warheads and began carrying out reconnaissance missions. During the summer of 2026, upgraded versions began to appear, distinguished primarily by a vertical stabilizer. Some variants were also equipped with cameras.
Gerberas have been shot down in European countries. Recently, one such drone flew into Lithuanian airspace.
The Insider analyzed a sample of 30 listings for parts from downed Russian drones on Ukraine’s largest online auction site for war trophies. At least nine lots featured easily recognizable Xingkai Tech mesh modems. One listing offered 10 modems at once. Identical Xingkai Tech mesh modems have also been found in Banderol loitering munitions (drone missiles).
Equipping a drone — even one that once served as a decoy — with a modern mesh modem turns it into a weapon capable of threatening Europe. Recently, the Spanish publication El Mundo reported that the CIA had warned European countries that Gerberas could be launched against Europe from vessels belonging to Russia’s “shadow fleet.”
Many of Xingkai Tech’s drone components are available on the popular Russian online marketplace Wildberries.
The Insider contacted the press offices of DBS, Ping An, and China Merchants Bank, and also reached out to DBS by phone. None of the three banks responded.
Another mesh modem
The Insider identified another mesh modem widely used in Shahed drones that had not previously been publicly identified. Comparing listings on Reibert with the manufacturer’s website, it established that the modem is made by China’s Xi'an Sihou Network Technology Co., Ltd.
Xi'an Sihou Network Technology is another major player in the market for captured equipment sold at auction. It accounts for roughly half of the listings for captured mesh modems examined by The Insider. The company’s owner and director is Li Li.
Geran drones, along with Banderol loitering munitions, have become Russia’s main weapons in its campaign of terror against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, as well as in attacks on railway locomotives. The survival of Ukraine’s civilian population through the coming winter will depend largely on whether the West can use sanctions and diplomacy to quickly halt large-scale sales of mesh modems to Russia.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses US of helping Russia as Starlink restrictions disrupt drone attacks
articles.body:
Senior Ukrainian officials accused the United States on Wednesday of imposing restrictions on Kyiv's ability to use the Starlink satellite network, owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, for military operations in its defense against Russia's invasion. The satellite communications network is critical to the Ukrainian military, and officials in Kyiv now report restrictions on its use at high speeds, disrupting drone attacks against Russian forces, among other operations.
Musk and his company have not commented on the allegations, which come amid intense pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Musk, on Kyiv to halt its attacks on oil facilities deep inside Russia. According to reports, Trump has even threatened to suspend intelligence assistance or weapons deliveries to Ukraine.
Musk allowed Ukrainian forces to use Starlink's internet satellites in the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, the communications and navigation capabilities they provide have become critical on the battlefield.
Starlink is also considered more resistant to electronic jamming, making it useful for drone attacks carried out by Kyiv, particularly in Russian-held areas of eastern and southern Ukraine. According to Reuters, Ukrainian drones do not use Starlink when entering Russian territory, relying instead on other communications systems.
But senior Ukrainian officials now say restrictions on military use of Starlink are severely hampering Ukrainian operations, particularly along the front lines. The New York Times reported that officials in Kyiv were stunned by the restrictions.
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky, said Wednesday morning that no advance warning was given before the restrictions were imposed, disrupting several "missions."
According to Beskrestnov, the restrictions cut off access to the military version of the service at speeds exceeding 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph). He added that Starlink is also crucial to air defense systems Kyiv is using to intercept the fast jet-powered drones Russia has begun deploying in attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent months. These faster drones are more difficult to intercept.
Beskrestnov suggested the move was deliberate. "It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," he said.
Ukraine's military said the restrictions had also caused disconnections during drone flights at lower speeds of 110 to 120 kilometers per hour (68 to 75 mph).
"The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," said the 7th Rapid Response Corps, a Ukrainian air force unit operating in the country's southeast.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry also told Reuters that the restrictions significantly complicate logistics and the operation of several types of drones.
The Starlink restrictions come alongside allegations made in recent days by Zelensky and his aides that Kyiv had, on several occasions, failed to receive advance warnings from Western allies about Russian missile attacks.
Western intelligence is also critical to Kyiv's preparations for such attacks, and no warnings were issued in the Ukrainian capital on either of the past two nights when Russian missiles were launched toward the city.
According to the Ukrainian air force, Russia launched another 39 ballistic and cruise missiles overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, along with 128 drones. Only four missiles and 115 drones were intercepted.
At least four people were killed and about 20 others wounded in the overnight attack on Kyiv. Two other civilians were killed in the Dnipropetrovsk region and a third was killed in the Zaporizhzhia region.
"A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners," Zelensky said Wednesday morning.
A U.S. official told Agence France-Presse that Washington "has not changed its policy on intel-sharing" with Ukraine. However, a senior official in Kyiv told the news agency that the United States had threatened to suspend intelligence assistance unless Ukraine stopped attacking Russian oil refineries.
According to the Ukrainian official, Washington had in fact failed to warn Kyiv about ballistic missile launches on two occasions.
"And on top of that they've throttled Starlink speeds," the Ukrainian official said on condition of anonymity. "It's obvious they [the United States] are helping Russia for some reason."
Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries, arguing that they have caused a surge in global diesel prices. Experts, however, say the war in Iran is the main reason for the increase, which is hurting Republicans' chances of retaining control of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections.
After stunning Kyiv and its European allies by lifting sanctions on Russia late last week to allow it to export diesel to global markets, Trump also announced an "energy ceasefire" on Sunday, supposedly with the agreement of both sides. In reality, however, no such agreement had been reached.
Zelensky revealed Tuesday that Ukraine had indeed suspended its attacks on Russian oil facilities for two days, but said Russia had continued attacking energy facilities in Ukraine throughout that period.
He said the latest overnight strikes also targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, particularly in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions, leaving 600,000 people without electricity.
"We ask America and everyone in the world who does not close their eyes to reality to react and react harshly. Russia missed the opportunity for de-escalation and clearly chose to continue its insane war of destruction," Zelenskyy said following the overnight Russian attack.
Zelenskyy called on Trump to renew pressure on Moscow, invoking the approach of former Republican President Ronald Reagan. "Peace can only come through strength, and we ask America to remember this principle of Reagan's," he said.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Operation Vivaldi liberates another 101 square kilometers in Donetsk Oblast
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Operation Vivaldi liberates another 101 square kilometers in Donetsk Oblast
Key developments on Oct. 14:
- Ukraine retakes another 101 square kilometers in Donetsk Oblast's Lyman sector, Third Army Corps says
- Zelensky arrives in UK as London vows to speed up anti-drone missile deliveries for Ukraine
- 'Ostentatious disrespect' — Zelensky says Russia defied Trump's energy ceasefire with latest missile strike
- Germany puts Ukrainian on trial over Nord Stream sabotage
- SBU detains 18-year-old suspected FSB agent in Kyiv over attempt to activate 148 Starlink terminals for Russia
Ukraine's Third Army Corps, together with its attached units, has retaken another 101 square kilometers during the fourth stage of Operation Vivaldi on the Lyman sector in Donetsk Oblast, the corps announced on Oct. 14.
Ukraine liberated the villages of Zelena Dolyna, Lypove, and Kolodiazi, while Russia lost about 3,000 of its soldiers in the fourth stage of the operation, the corps reported on Telegram.
"The enemy was unable to cut the key logistics artery of our group in the Donbas. We thwarted the offensive of the group 'Zapad' and forced it to transfer part of the units of the 1st Tank Army, which weakened the pressure on Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi," corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said.
In total, Operation Vivaldi saw the liberation and return of 16 settlements and 277 square kilometers (106 square miles) to Ukraine, the corps said. "Four seasons of 'Vivaldi' are over, but the music continues."
On Sept. 15, Biletskyi confirmed that Ukrainian forces under the command of the 3rd Army Corps were conducting a series of counterattacks north of the front-line city of Lyman in Donetsk Oblast.
The operation dealt "a heavy blow to the combat capabilities of Russia's 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies," Biletskyi said then, adding that Ukrainian drone strikes had pushed Russian supply hubs across the state border.
The fight for the heart of the so-called Donbas fortress belt — Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka — is crucial going into the winter months, when Russia will look to maximize its foothold in urban areas to prepare for a 2027 offensive campaign.
read also
Zelensky arrives in UK as London vows to speed up anti-drone missile deliveries for Ukraine
President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in the U.K. on Oct. 14 to meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III, as London pledges missiles to help Ukraine counter Russia's jet-powered drones.
The visit comes at a tense moment for Ukraine, with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration pressuring Kyiv to halt strikes against Russian oil refineries and threatening to cut off intelligence sharing and arms shipments.
Ahead of Zelensky's visit, Burnham vowed that the U.K.'s support for Ukraine remains "rock-solid."
The Ukrainian president was first welcomed by King Charles at Buckingham Palace before meeting Burnham.
"I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience. It is important for me to have the opportunity to personally thank him for his unwavering support for Ukraine," Zelensky said on X.
The British prime minister then welcomed Zelensky at 10 Downing Street in the company of a military ceremonial guard, the first such honor granted to a foreign leader, according to the BBC.
The British government has announced an air defense missile package worth 45 million pounds (around $60 million) for Ukraine, as the country faces an intensifying onslaught of Russian missiles and drones.
"The U.K. will accelerate deliveries of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), which have proven extremely effective against jet-powered drones that are being used to strike far beyond the front lines in Ukraine, including Kyiv and beyond," the British government said in a press release on Oct. 13.
Russia has been increasingly deploying jet-powered drones that are faster and more difficult to intercept than older Shahed models, posing a new threat as Ukraine braces for massive strikes against energy infrastructure in winter.
Of the 45-million-pound package, the U.K. will expedite the delivery of 10 million pounds ($13 million) worth of LMMs to meet the most urgent winter needs.
"I’m announcing that we're accelerating the delivery of British-made air defenses for (Ukraine)," Burnham told the press while meeting Zelensky. The British leader also said he would seek to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the U.S.
Burnham's office said earlier that he had instructed his cabinet to prepare additional military and financial assistance packages for Ukraine, as well as fresh sanctions against Russia.
The U.K. further reiterated that it stands by its plans to ban maritime services for Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.
London said last year it would implement the phased ban over 2026 "in lockstep with our European partners."
The EU plans to ban Russian LNG imports by January 2027 but has failed to agree on a full ban on maritime services, with Greece securing a carve-out for Russian LNG exports to non-EU countries.
read also
'Ostentatious disrespect' — Zelensky says Russia defied Trump's energy ceasefire with latest missile strike
Russia demonstrated its disregard for U.S. President Donald Trump's proposed energy ceasefire by launching drones and missiles against Ukraine's power grid overnight, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 14.
Moscow's forces deployed 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones against energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv, Zelensky said, calling it "ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
At least three people were killed, and another 22 were injured as a result of the Russian strike that hit a residential building in the Desnianskyi district and power plants elsewhere in the city, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Russia has ramped up aerial strikes against Ukrainian energy sites as winter nears, despite Trump's unexpected and unilateral announcement on Oct. 11 that both Kyiv and Moscow agreed to halt attacks against each other's energy infrastructure.
Even as Kyiv said it had halted attacks against Russian oil refineries since Trump's ceasefire announcement, Trump declined to blame the Kremlin for breaking the truce when asked by a reporter on Oct. 13.
"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale," Zelensky noted, adding that at least 600,000 people are without power and reporting damage to 26 power facilities, as well as four oil and gas sites.
"Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," the Ukrainian leader added.
The comments come as Washington piles on pressure on Kyiv to halt its aerial campaign against Russian refineries, which he linked to rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by experts.
The Kyiv Independent has previously learned that the Trump administration threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials with cutting intelligence sharing and arms sales unless it stopped attacking Russian refineries.
While Ukrainian and U.S. sources told the Kyiv Independent earlier this week that Washington has not yet stopped intelligence support, questions about the early warning provided by partners are mounting as strikes now hit Kyiv even before the alarm sounds.
Presidential Advisor Serhii "Flash" Beskretnov and Serhii Sternenko, an activist and former advisor to ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, claimed on Oct. 14 that Elon Musk's SpaceX has limited the speed of Starlink terminals in Ukraine, causing disruption to "a number of critical missions."
"The American President has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor," Zelensky noted, urging Washington to impose sanctions on Russia under late Senator Lindsey Graham's sanctions bill and calling for additional supplies of Patriot interceptors.
read also
Germany puts Ukrainian on trial over Nord Stream sabotage
Ukrainian citizen Serhii Kuznetsov went to trial in Hamburg on Oct. 14 on suspicion of involvement in the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines.
A series of explosions rocked the controversial Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines in September 2022, destroying three out of four key gas pipelines linking Russia and Germany via the Baltic Sea.
Kuznetsov, a former soldier, was accused of leading the sabotage group, involving six other people. German investigators claim that he commanded the yacht "Andromeda," from which a team of divers allegedly carried out the attack against the pipelines.
On the first day of the trial, prosecutors accused Kuznetsov of being an accomplice to war crimes by committing an attack against civilian infrastructure.
Kuznetsov and Kyiv have denied any involvement in the sabotage.
The trial — the first held in connection with the Nord Stream sabotage — is expected to run until February.
Kuznietsov was arrested in August 2025 near the Italian town of Rimini under a European arrest warrant before being extradited to Germany.
Another Ukrainian suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravliov, was detained in Croatia in August 2026 and awaits extradition. Zhuravliov was first detained in Poland in September 2025, but a Polish court refused to extradite him to Germany and instead released him a month later.
The Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never became operational, had long been a flashpoint in European energy politics.
Even before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, critics said it deepened Germany's dependence on Russian gas and undermined European energy security.
read also
SBU detains 18-year-old suspected FSB agent in Kyiv over attempt to activate 148 Starlink terminals for Russia
Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) has detained an 18-year-old man in Kyiv suspected of working for Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). According to investigators, he attempted to register 148 Starlink terminals for use by Russian forces.
The SBU reported that the terminals were intended to support the planning of Russian military operations in the Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. Ukrainian security officers say they prevented the devices from being activated.
According to the investigation, the suspect is a former student at a Kyiv college, where he trained to become a welder. After completing his studies, he began looking for ways to earn quick money through Telegram channels.
He was allegedly contacted by an FSB officer who offered him money in exchange for cooperation.
Within days of being recruited, the suspect registered 15 Starlink terminals using the passport details of relatives and acquaintances. He then prepared personal information belonging to other individuals to register another 133 devices.
SBU officers detained the suspect near a post office, where he allegedly planned to activate another batch of terminals.
The 15 previously registered Starlink terminals, whose details had already been sent to his Russian handler via a messaging app, were also blocked.
The suspect remains in custody without the possibility of bail. If convicted, he faces life imprisonment and confiscation of property.
The case adds to a growing number of incidents in which Russia allegedly recruits Ukrainians to carry out assignments on Moscow's behalf, including a recent case on Oct. 12, when Ukrainian authorities detained a 19-year-old suspected of plotting a bomb attack on a bus carrying soldiers in Rivne.
According to the SBU, the suspect had also been recruited through Telegram channels offering quick money.
On Oct. 6, the SBU reported arresting a suspected collaborator in Kyiv who allegedly helped Russia establish repeater stations for its drones and gather intelligence on targets in the capital.
In August, the SBU detained a suspected Russian agent in Kharkiv Oblast who allegedly registered 27 Starlink terminals for Russian forces.

articles.title: Ukrainian officers warn Starlink slowdown ‘comparable to a nuclear strike against us’
articles.body:
Ukrainian frontline soldiers are alarmed that Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service is reportedly being restricted on fast-moving military platforms, warning of severe operational consequences.
“This is comparable to a nuclear strike against us. All operations are on hold. This will cost many of us our lives,” an experienced Ukrainian officer told POLITICO and the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.
The officer commands a medium-range drone strike unit in southeastern Ukraine. The unit relies heavily on Starlink for the operation and navigation of its American-made Hornet drones, used to strike targets at a range of up to 150 kilometers.
Advertisement
“Since last night, all Starlink and Starshield terminals used by our forces have been subject to a speed limit of 100 kilometers per hour,” the officer said.
POLITICO talked to three frontline soldiers, who all spoke on condition of being granted anonymity, as well as a Ukrainian defense ministry spokesperson and the EU's top defense official.
The reported restrictions have revived a question Ukrainian commanders have worried about for years: how much of the country’s battlefield communications can rely on a service controlled by a U.S. company.
Ukrainian soldiers say the restrictions have halted some medium-range drone strikes over Ukraine, disrupting attacks on Russian logistics and leaving frontline Ukrainian troops with less support. The scale of the disruption — and whether it was deliberate — remains unclear.
In a comment on X, Musk said: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," referring to the Starshield division of Starlink that is used for military purposes.
"Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX," he added. "Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."
Advertisement
Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's former defense minister who has good contacts in Silicon Valley, said late Wednesday: "Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored. Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense."
The White House and the Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The restrictions have brought “all medium-range strike operations to a complete halt,” the officer said, including those using mesh-based systems. These rely on a single Starlink-equipped UAV to receive and relay signals to other drones connected through a mesh network, allowing them to strike targets deep inside Russian-held territory or in areas heavily protected by Russian electronic warfare systems.
Such targets include the Donetsk region, the strategically important Novorossiya highway linking Russia to Crimea, the Crimean Peninsula itself, the Kerch area and the Black Sea.
“We can no longer fight effectively to support our infantry on the battlefield. We can no longer strike multiple-launch rocket systems, North Korean-supplied heavy self-propelled artillery positioned deep behind enemy lines, ammunition depots, command centers and other targets,” the officer said.
"The Ukrainian frontline is very much dependent on Starlink-operated mid-strike drones," Iryna Terekh, CEO of Ukrainian missile-maker Fire Point told POLITICO.
Advertisement
Ukraine's devastating campaign
For months, Ukrainian medium-range strike drones have inflicted significant damage on Russian logistics in frontline regions. They have disrupted the supply of fuel, ammunition and other military equipment, slowing Russia's advance.
Members of a special operations unit pilot a reconnaissance drone in the Kharkiv region on Feb. 27, 2026. | Chris McGrath/Getty Images
The officer said he feared that the Starlink restrictions will give Russian troops a critical opportunity to strengthen their positions.
“Starting today, the enemy will build up its logistics routes to Crimea to reinforce its forces there,” he warned.
Two other Ukrainian frontline soldiers operating ground robots and conventional first-person-view drones in the Donbas confirmed to POLITICO that Starlink services for Ukrainian units were abruptly restricted on Wednesday.
“On the night of October 14, without prior notice to the Defense Forces, SpaceX unilaterally restricted the operation of Starshield terminals while in motion,” a Ukrainian defense ministry official told reporters in Kyiv.
The official added that the problems occur at speeds varying from 72 kph to 161 kph, "depending on the specific vehicle and unit."
Advertisement
The slowdown in Starlink terminals comes as U.S. President Donald Trump exerts fierce pressure on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries. That follows his deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to release diesel onto global markets — part of Trump’s effort to reduce fuel prices ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said in a Facebook post.
Asked about the rising American pressure on Ukraine, EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said at a POLITICO event on Wednesday: "Political development sometimes makes strange influence. Elections are coming."
“We are quite dependent on American space capabilities,” Kubilius acknowledged. “The answer to that situation is to develop our own capabilities.”
The Starlink slowdown was condemned by one of Ukraine’s key European allies.
“Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you,” wrote Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski.
Advertisement
Ukraine depends on Starlink
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Starlink has become central to Kyiv's war effort. In the spring of 2022, Ukrainian defenders trapped in the besieged city of Mariupol used satellites operated by SpaceX to send messages to the outside world. Ukrainian units relied on the system to coordinate operations during the fierce urban fighting around Bakhmut in 2023.
To this day, soldiers use Starlink to rapidly adjust artillery fire and navigate naval drones during attacks on Russia's Black Sea Fleet. Ukraine's former army chief, Valerii Zaluzhnyi, once praised the terminals for their "extraordinary utility."
That reliance always carried risk. In the early months of the war, Starlink reportedly shut off terminals that were going to be used in a naval attack on the Russian fleet.
But SpaceX has also acted to favor Ukraine. In February, SpaceX shut down access to Starlink terminals being used illegally by Russia, causing immediate chaos. Ukraine then ramped its own use of the terminals.
Kyiv's armed forces began widely equipping medium-range strike drones with Starlink terminals. Without them, operations would become considerably more complex. The military would, for example, have to calculate terrain elevations and antenna availability itself and install additional communications equipment.
"Starlink allows you not to have to deal with radio physics," a Ukrainian officer with the call sign Jura said in August. "Starlink allows operators to maintain a live video connection with a drone until shortly before impact."
Advertisement
Starlink can also provide so-called "synthetic GPS coordinates," which can help drones navigate when conventional GPS signals are jammed.
A Ukrainian serviceman assembles a drone ahead of a combat mission in the Kharkiv region on May 22, 2026. | Diego Fedele/Getty Images
But Ukrainian officers feared that decisions made in Washington or in the executive offices of American companies could suddenly weaken Ukraine.
"Many of my colleagues and I myself are very nervous about the question of how we would operate without Starlink," Jura said. "We have discussed this question several times among our officers: 'What if Elon Musk or someone at SpaceX switches it off?'"
As Trump has ramped up pressure on Kyiv in recent weeks, Ukrainian officers reported growing problems with Starlink.
One Ukrainian drone pilot, who operates medium-range strike drones, reported severe connectivity problems on Sept. 11 and 12, as well as further disruptions on Sept. 17. He said soldiers from several Ukrainian units had experienced similar problems.
The incidents occurred shortly after U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had concluded visits to Kyiv and Moscow. "After few days, the normal work with Starlink come back. But I believe that was the signal," the pilot said.
Advertisement
He argued that Russian jamming equipment could not plausibly have produced such geographically consistent disruptions across multiple sectors of the front.
"So that was, I guess, administered from some office," he said. POLITICO could not independently establish whether the disruptions resulted from deliberate restrictions imposed by the American satellite provider or another technical cause.
The incidents have reinforced concerns among Ukrainian military personnel about their dependence on American-controlled technology.
"The reason is politics and the American option to 'switch off' or critically decrease” U.S. systems, the pilot said.
Veronika Melkozerova reported from Kyiv.Daniella Cheslow and Audrey Decker contributed reporting.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1694: Starlink cap cripples Ukrainian drone missions as Musk says Trump, not SpaceX, ordered the cut
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Ukraine blocks Russia from outflanking its fortress cities in Donbas, retaking 277 square kilometers and hitting 8,000 Russian troops. “Four seasons of ‘Vivaldi’ are complete. But the music continues. Until we meet again!” the Third Army Corps noted.
Intelligence and technology
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government”: Musk says Trump, not SpaceX, is behind cut hitting Ukraine. The ordinary Starlink on drones is capped at about 160 km/h, too slow for some missions, so faster flight needs the military StarShield version.
“Trump and Musk must be held accountable”: US senator warns Starlink network failing over Ukraine could cripple its shield against Russian missiles and drones. Ukraine’s air defense leans on Musk’s Starlink.
“Trump was looking for any opportunity to undermine our defense capabilities,” top Ukrainian volunteer, who supplied 291,502 FPV drones to front, says of sudden Starlink limit. Ukraine had stopped hitting Russian oil refineries as Trump asked, yet the Starlink limit still landed.
NATO country that pays for Kyiv’s Starlink warns Musk as his cap breaks Ukraine’s drone missions: “As your European customers, we are watching you”. “Are you playing politics with your products again?”, Poland’s foreign minister challenges Musk
Planned capacity of 12,000 interceptors a year, under 100 seconds to target: US firm pitches a low-cost drone killer. The fastest model cruises at 540 km/h, which may be enough to catch Russia’s jet Gerans, a defense news outlet suggests..
Ukraine-NATO AI built to forecast Russia’s front-line drone attacks from past data and weather is ready to plug into the army. Drone types, areas, time windows: the model was tested on real data. A second tool ranks artillery plans and is now in trials.
New Starlink restrictions disrupt Ukrainian drone missions. Kyiv adviser says move is tied to “political situation”. SpaceX may have imposed the restrictions at the Trump administration’s request, activist Serhii Sternenko suggested.
Ukrainian OSINT channel: Russia turned a bare field into a Geran-5 launch site in a month—and drones are already arriving. Eight launcher spots, 32 drone-prep pads, and a layout the channel likens to Tsymbulova, a Russian drone base Ukraine keeps striking.
Ukraine sent a spiked tank and a Bradley into Russian drone fire. The spikes held, and Ukraine’s own drones got them home. Armored vehicles aren't dead on arrival anymore on the drone-patrolled battlefield. Friendly drones can escort them to the fight.
International
“He thinks Ukraine is a weak link and that it needs to be squeezed into giving in”: diplomat on why Trump pressures Kyiv, not Moscow. Trump is using aid and intelligence as levers over Kyiv.
“It finances an economy geared toward total war”—Ukraine’s third president on the Russian diesel Washington just cleared. Viktor Yushchenko invokes the Budapest Memorandum and Pearl Harbor days after the US waived sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russia attacked Ukrainian retailer Epicentr’s warehouse 10 times in one day, destroying about 85% of goods, company says. The Khmelnytskyi hub had been effectively Epicentr’s only surviving large warehouse complex, after Russia destroyed its two largest logistics complexes in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast.
1,125 Kyiv residents injured in Russian attacks since the start of 2026, more than a third of them in five weeks from late August, Kyiv health chief says. Kyiv emergency medical teams have responded to 1,920 calls related to Russian attacks since the start of the year, according to the city’s health department head.
Ukraine warns of “a new type of humanitarian crisis” as Russia aims at its biggest cities. Even border and frontline oblasts are further along on resilience plans than the capital, Zelenskyy says.
Russia bombs Sloviansk’s warming center as the day’s attacks wound four Red Cross workers. The 250-kg bomb injured eight people and damaged five apartment blocks, and the wounded workers belonged to a Red Cross branch that had relocated from Lyman for safety
Three days after Washington announced an energy ceasefire, Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid. Zelenskyy says Russia has never shown America such disrespect. At least 600,000 people lost power, and four died in Kyiv.
New developments
Russia-linked bot networks kept their weekly rhythm after drone strikes on three Yandex data centers—disinformation monitor LetsData. One network that spread fake Die Welt sites now pushes a fake Ukrinform site about mobilization in Ukraine, its analysts found.
Read our earlier daily review here.

- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1692: Trump suspends Russian diesel sanctions, while EU blacklists record 1,569 arms suppliers
- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1691: Ukraine opens arms exports to 18 makers as defense output hits $55 billion

articles.title: ‘Blatant Disrespect Toward America’: Zelensky Slams Russia’s Strike on Ukraine’s Energy Sector
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky urged US President Donald Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia after a massive overnight Russian attack on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure left at least 600,000 people without electricity.
In a Telegram post on Wednesday, Oct. 14, Zelensky said Russia had launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions against energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv region, and Kharkiv.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He described the ballistic strike on Ukraine’s energy sector as deliberate and said its scale demonstrated Russia’s disregard for Washington’s calls for a ceasefire.
“Russia does not view the US President’s statements as strong,” Zelensky said, calling on the US and others to respond firmly to Moscow’s actions.
He urged Trump to impose “STRONG sanctions” on Russia, referring to legislation introduced by US Senator Lindsey Graham that Zelensky said provided the necessary tools to increase pressure on Moscow. He also called for additional interceptor missiles for Ukraine’s Patriot air defense systems.
“Peace can only be achieved through strength,” Zelensky said, invoking a principle associated with former US President Ronald Reagan.
The president added that further power outages were possible as Ukrainian crews worked to repair the damage. According to him, the attack damaged facilities and equipment at 26 sites in Ukraine’s electric power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector. He also reported casualties and injuries but did not provide figures.
Russian Overnight Strikes Target Kyiv CHP Plants and Kill Civilians Across Ukraine
Air defenses intercept 119 targets
According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russia began the combined attack at 6 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 13, launching 167 aerial weapons, including 39 missiles and 128 attack drones of various types.
The missiles included Iskander-M, North Korean KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx types. The drones included Shahed-type weapons, among them 77 jet-powered drones, as well as Banderol, Dan-T, Gerbera, Italmas, and Parodiya-type drones.
Ukraine’s Air Force said aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare systems, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups were involved in repelling the attack.
As of 9 a.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 14, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 119 targets: four missiles and 115 drones. The intercepted drones included 59 jet-powered ones.
The Air Force reported missile and drone impacts at 22 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight locations. Some Russian missiles failed to reach their intended targets.
Ukraine again reports missing missile warnings, White House offers no explanation
Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv’s CHP-4 power plant and a nine-story residential building late on Tuesday, Oct. 13, killing at least three people and injuring 21, including an eight-year-old child, Ukrainian officials reported.
The attack hit the capital at around 10:40 p.m., sparking fires across several districts. In the Desnianskyi district, a fire spread across apartments on the first through eighth floors before firefighters extinguished it.
Rescuers recovered two bodies from the building and evacuated 16 residents, while other strikes caused fires and casualties in the Holosiivskyi, Dniprovskyi, Darnytskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi districts.
Zelensky said CHP-4 was a main target and that Ukraine had received no advance warning from Western partners about the incoming ballistic missiles for the second consecutive night.
The Ukrainian Air Force confirmed that no warning had come through the usual channels, while presidential adviser Dmytro Lytvyn said military and intelligence services were investigating the missing notifications.
Notably, President Donald Trump said Washington continues to share intelligence with Ukraine, rejecting suggestions that the US had halted cooperation.
However, his administration has yet to explain why Ukraine received no early missile warnings for two consecutive nights.
Asked by Fox News correspondent whether the US had stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv, newly appointed White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Tuesday, Oct. 13: “I’ll have to get back to you on that.”
You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter

articles.title: SpaceX limits Starlink operations in Ukraine, disrupting military ops., missile defense capability
articles.body:
SpaceX has placed a limit on some Starlink services in Ukraine, stopping the operation of its military-grade version for vehicles moving above 100 miles per hour (160 km/h), disrupting combat missions, Presidential Adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said on Wednesday.
“Our defense forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions,” he wrote on Telegram, adding: “It is clear that this action is not coincidental and is related to the current political situation.”
A Ukrainian official told The Jerusalem Post that Starlink internet speeds in Ukraine dropped further on Wednesday evening, to 60–80 km/h.
Ukrainian officials fear the move was made at Trump's request
Ukraine’s security services detected disruptions to Starlink terminals across the country overnight on Tuesday night, a source familiar with the matter confirmed to the Post. Ukrainian officials fear the move by the company, owned by Elon Musk, may have been made at the request of US President Donald Trump.
Starlink terminals are one of the key tools enabling Ukrainians to maintain internet access amid Russia’s invasion. The disruptions reportedly interfered with several critical operations.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a social media post that Ukraine had not received an alert about incoming Russian strikes. “This is already the second time this has happened,” Zelensky wrote.
“During the first wave of drone and missile strikes, no warning was received, but an alert was issued during the second wave,” a source familiar with the matter added in a statement to the Post.
Trump himself claimed on Tuesday that the United States had not halted intelligence-sharing cooperation with Ukraine. “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel,” Trump told reporters. “We want the war to end, so we’re working with them and Russia on getting the war to end.”
Zelensky said Russia launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones overnight on Tuesday night, targeting energy facilities and critical infrastructure across Ukraine. According to the Ukrainian president, approximately 500,000 people were left without electricity following the attack.
Ukrainian negotiators traveled to the US on Friday and Saturday to urge US President Donald Trump to increase sanctions pressure on Russia.
Zelensky accuses US of inaction as Russian strikes kill over 70 in two days
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused the US of being unwilling to help Ukraine after a Russian bomb attack on Thursday killed at least 35 people in the east, sending the two-day death toll from Russian strikes to over 70.
Hours after the strike on the embattled city of Kramatorsk tore through two buses, Zelensky criticized Washington’s effort to pursue economic ties with Russia while also seeking to mediate the more than four-year war.
Speaking to reporters in Pryluky, the Ukrainian leader urged the US to accede to his requests to expand Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite service to help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers.
“Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I’ve said quite openly — give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table,” he said in an emotional statement.
Ukraine has in recent months aimed to wrest the battlefield initiative from Russia, whose gains have slowed this year, but is still suffering from Moscow’s increasingly brutal air war.
“So where’s the truth here, where’s the honesty? Where’s the stalemate? ... That’s called unwillingness,” he said, referring to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s assertion earlier on Thursday that the war is at a stalemate and that the United States would keep working toward a settlement.
“One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate,” Zelensky added.

articles.title: Houthis look to build ballistic missiles with Chinese supplies
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis look to build ballistic missiles with more Chinese supplies, report says
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are attempting to build a new advanced medium-range ballistic missile system with the help of Chinese parts, according to a new report released Wednesday by a group that tracks the use of weapons in conflict zones.
The report by the U.K.-based Conflict Armament Research group came as the Houthis, in their ongoing war with Saudi Arabia, are demonstrating remarkable ability to wreak havoc on one of the Middle East’s best equipped militaries.
The weaponry under development could help the group more precisely target the Saudis and Israel. By turning to China, it also appears to be a sign of increasing independence.
The rebels expand their ambition 
The Houthis have tried to acquire key parts from Chinese suppliers that could be used to make a version of Iran’s Kheibar Shekan precision-guided missile, according to the report. The Kheibar Shekan has a range of roughly 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers).
"The local ambition of the Houthis for manufacturing is beyond what was previously assumed," said Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at Conflict Armament Research, a research outfit specializing in tracing the flow of arms in war zones around the globe. "These types of parts are very specific, and producing them would have required design information related to the missile."
They're "not goods that can be used for a variety of civilian applications," Hinz said.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington didn't respond to a request for comment.
China is a major purchaser of both Iranian and Saudi oil and leveraged its ties with both countries to broker a rapprochement in 2023. It has condemned a series of attacks on Saudi airports by the Houthis and called for a de-escalation in the fighting.
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government launched a military campaign last month aimed at driving back the Houthis from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical Middle East trade route for oil and other goods.
Yemen interdicted key components to building missiles 
The Conflict Armament report was based on information released by Yemeni government authorities in July after officials interdicted two shipments that included suspicious equipment.
The shipments originated from China and were intended to be delivered to Hodeidah, a Yemeni port that Israeli officials say has been commonly used by the Iranians as a weapons transfer point. China accounts for the largest share of seized shipments destined for the Houthis, according to U.N. reports.
Components integral to the functioning of a missile were among the parts found in the cargo. They included stabilizing fin cores, rocket motor aft closures with nozzle attachments, and rocket motor igniters.
The cargo also contained phenolic resin, a material used in creating ablative heat shields. These shields protect ballistic missiles from the intense heat associated with atmospheric flight at high supersonic speeds, the report said.
Hinz said that the combination of materials made clear that the Houthis intended to assemble that specific type of Iranian-designed missile.
"This particular type of system is very difficult to smuggle. And you can’t just disassemble and reassemble them," he said.
Houthi weaponry has grown more sophisticated over time 
The Houthis rose to prominence more than 20 years ago as an insurgent group armed with Soviet-era and North Korean weapons seized from the Yemeni government's military.
But over the years, the group's access to advanced weaponry has expanded and so has its ability to menace neighbors.
In the current weekslong conflict with Saudi Arabia, the Houthis have fired ballistic missiles and utilized maneuverable warheads and long-range drones. They previously have fired scores of drones and missiles at Israel, more than 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) away.
