articles.title: U.S. moves leave Ukraine less able to defend itself
articles.body:
- Ukraine received no partner warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches for two straight nights, the Ukrainian Air Force said, detecting missiles only minutes before impact.
- Starlink also stopped working above 160 km/h for Ukraine’s military, hitting tactical drones used in defense, as Russia’s strike left 600,000 without power.
Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian strikes has been limited by two U.S. moves in a single night: the country went without early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches from its partners for a second time in a row, and Starlink, the U.S. satellite service its frontline units depend on, was cut back for the Ukrainian military just as Russia launched one of its heaviest missile attacks on Ukraine’s power grid.
The Ukrainian Air Force said Russia launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv at about 10:40 p.m. on Oct. 13, and that once again no information about the launches had come from Ukraine’s partners before the missiles were in the air. The Air Force said the reasons were being investigated.
“The situation is similar to yesterday’s. No information regarding launches from enemy territory had been received from our partners. The reasons are being investigated,” the Ukrainian Air Force said in an official statement.
Ukraine has relied heavily on early warning from the United States, whose satellites can spot the heat of a missile launch deep inside Russia within moments, giving Ukrainian air defense crews time to prepare and giving cities time to sound air raid sirens. Without those alerts, Ukrainian forces only detected the incoming ballistic missiles once they came within range of ground radars, a few minutes before impact, and tried to shoot some of them down. The lost minutes shorten the reaction time for interceptor crews and hit civilians hardest, leaving people in Kyiv and other cities less time to reach shelters and metro stations.
The attack that followed was massive. Zelenskyy said Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions overnight into Oct. 14 at energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and Kharkiv, damaging 26 facilities in the power system and four in the oil and gas sector and leaving at least 600,000 people without electricity. He said there were dead and injured and warned that outages could spread.
Zelenskyy said the missile salvo deliberately targeted the energy infrastructure covered by the ceasefire President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11, which Moscow never confirmed accepting.
“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” said Zelenskyy.
During the same night, Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military began losing their connection whenever they moved faster than 160 km/h (100 mph). Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy who is widely known by his call sign “Flash” and who has tracked Russian attempts to jam Starlink along the front, said the restriction hit the military StarShield package of the SpaceX service and that units received no notice before it took effect.
“Our defense forces did not receive any warning about this restriction, and it led to the disruption of a number of missions. It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation,” said Serhii Beskrestnov.
The restriction falls on Ukraine’s defense, not on its strikes inside Russia. SpaceX has never allowed Ukraine to use Starlink for strikes on Russian territory, and Zelenskyy said earlier this month that Kyiv was still asking for that permission, so Ukraine’s long-range drones and cruise missiles that hit targets in Russia do not rely on the service. Starlink has also been unavailable to Russian forces since February, when SpaceX and Ukraine’s Defense Ministry introduced a whitelist that cut off unregistered Russian terminals. Inside Ukraine, Starlink is used on tactical drones and uncrewed ground vehicles that operate over Ukrainian and Russian-occupied territory, so a speed cap above 160 km/h cuts the links of fast tactical strike and interceptor drones fighting Russian troops and drones along the front.
Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko, who first reported the change, said ordinary satellite terminals kept working and suggested SpaceX may have acted at the request of the Trump administration, while British analyst Jimmy Rushton noted that the limit does nothing to protect the Russian oil refineries Trump has criticized Ukraine for striking.
Ballistic missiles are the hardest part of Russia’s strike packages for Ukraine to stop, because they fly too fast and too high for most of its air defense systems, and Ukraine relies mainly on U.S.-made Patriot batteries to intercept them. Zelenskyy asked Washington and other partners for more Patriot interceptors and called on Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia under the law sponsored by Sen. Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed in September.
“We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine,” said Zelenskyy.
The Ukrainian Air Force warned that further Russian attacks cannot be ruled out. Neither the White House nor SpaceX has explained why the missile launch warnings stopped or why the Starlink speed limit was introduced, or said whether either change is temporary.

articles.title: Houthis turn to China for missile parts as threat to Israel and Saudi Arabia grows
articles.body:
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels are attempting to build a new advanced medium-range ballistic missile system with the help of Chinese parts, according to a new report released Wednesday by a group that tracks the use of weapons in conflict zones.
The report by the U.K.-based Conflict Armament Research group came as the Houthis, in their ongoing war with Saudi Arabia, are demonstrating remarkable ability to wreak havoc on one of the Middle East’s best equipped militaries.
The weaponry under development could help the group more precisely target the Saudis and Israel. By turning to China, it also appears to be a sign of increasing independence.
The rebels expand their ambition, an analyst says
The Houthis have tried to acquire key parts from Chinese suppliers that could be used to make a version of Iran’s Kheibar Shekan precision-guided missile, according to the report. The Kheibar Shekan has a range of roughly 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers).
“The local ambition of the Houthis for manufacturing is beyond what was previously assumed,” said Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at Conflict Armament Research, a research outfit specializing in tracing the flow of arms in war zones around the globe. “These types of parts are very specific, and producing them would have required design information related to the missile.”
They’re “not goods that can be used for a variety of civilian applications,” Hinz said.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington didn’t respond to a request for comment.
China is a major purchaser of both Iranian and Saudi oil and leveraged its ties with both countries to broker a rapprochement in 2023. It has condemned a series of attacks on Saudi airports by the Houthis and called for a de-escalation in the fighting.
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government launched a military campaign last month aimed at driving back the Houthis from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical Middle East trade route for oil and other goods.
Yemen interdicted key components to building missiles
The Conflict Armament report was based on information released by Yemeni government authorities in July after officials interdicted two shipments that included suspicious equipment.
The shipments originated from China and were intended to be delivered to Hodeidah, a Yemeni port that Israeli officials say has been commonly used by the Iranians as a weapons transfer point. China accounts for the largest share of seized shipments destined for the Houthis, according to U.N. reports.
Components integral to the functioning of a missile were among the parts found in the cargo. They included stabilizing fin cores, rocket motor aft closures with nozzle attachments, and rocket motor igniters.
The cargo also contained phenolic resin, a material used in creating ablative heat shields. These shields protect ballistic missiles from the intense heat associated with atmospheric flight at high supersonic speeds, the report said.
Hinz said that the combination of materials made clear that the Houthis intended to assemble that specific type of Iranian-designed missile.
“This particular type of system is very difficult to smuggle. And you can’t just disassemble and reassemble them,” he said.
Houthi weaponry has grown more sophisticated over time

articles.title: Ukrainian military’s access to Starlink satellite internet suddenly restricted
articles.body:
Ukraine’s military has suddenly had its access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry immediately.
The terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations and the sudden restrictions on the terminals travelling at high speeds on Tuesday evening led to the failure of several combat missions, said an adviser on military technology to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.
Donald Trump has denied that his administration has cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Zelenskyy also indicated that the US was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine in an interview with NPR aired on Wednesday, but confirmed that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited.
Ukraine did not receive any warning before Russia launched its first barrage of ballistic missiles on Tuesday evening, according to Col Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the air force. But it did receive warnings from “foreign partners” about three subsequent barrages, leaving further confusion about whether or not the US is intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine.
Musk said that Starlink is not licensed to clients who are using weapons, and that the Ukrainian military was linked to a separate network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government. “This is not under SpaceX control,” Musk wrote.
Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.
“With their actions our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.
But there have been no reports that access for static Starlink terminals has been cut, meaning critical battlefield communications for soldiers should remain unaffected. The detection of incoming Russian missiles and drones relies on other technologies.
Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukraine’s leader – an extraordinary act of political interference against a wartime ally – as a personal feud between the two presidents has burst into the open.
The reports that Starlink was being throttled on the frontlines were interpreted by some as further pressure on Ukraine to end the fighting and make a deal with Russia at any cost.
Serhii Sternenko, a political activist with close ties to the military, first reported the outage and later said that the speeds at which the loss of connectivity occurred had fallen even lower. “It is likely that the company ‘SpaceX’ resorted to such measures at the request of the Trump administration,” he said. “Ordinary satellite communication terminals are currently operational.”
Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say that the closure of the strait of Hormuz has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.
Zelenskyy had suggested, though not said, that the US was intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine about impending Russian missile strikes.
Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” Zelenskyy said. “Russia does not consider the American president’s statements strong.”
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become even more widespread.
Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed by either side. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”
Ukraine is observing a short-term moratorium on striking Russian refineries while Kyiv seeks to show that it is ready for talks with Russia. Zelenskyy arrived in London on Wednesday to meet Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister. He will also be received by King Charles.
Zelenskyy is seeking new negotiations with the US. He has sent proposals to the Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, saying Ukraine was ready to work towards a ceasefire and “Russia must also be part of this agreement”.

articles.title: North Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
articles.body:
North Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
North Korea test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday, state media KCNA reported Thursday, saying the launches posed no threat to neighbouring countries. The tests follow heightened tensions with South Korea after a September 21 landmine explosion in the Demilitarised Zone injured three South Korean soldiers.
North Korea has test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles, state news agency KCNA said Thursday.
The agency said the missiles were fired Wednesday into the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, without "any adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries".
The reported launch came after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between North and South Korea.
Three South Korean soldiers were injured in the September 21 blast in the Seoul-controlled area of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), with both countries testing upgraded missile technology in the aftermath.
The latest testing "aimed to examine the current mobilized posture of the underwater combat systems" and served as a Navy training exercise, KCNA said.
The tests showed the "high reliability, trustworthiness and ability of the war deterrents of the DPRK," the agency reported, referring to North Korea by the abbreviation of the country's official name.
Photos released by KCNA showed one missile blasting vertically out of the sea trailed by a thick plume of smoke. Another photo appeared to show a projectile erupting from the water at a 45-degree angle.
Read moreNorth Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts
Other images showed a missile flying horizontally over the sea, as well as a submarine traveling on the water's surface.
The North's ability to launch missiles from submarines at two different angles carries "tactical significance", Hong Min of the Korea Institute for National Unification told AFP, as the two launch methods serve different purposes.
"Vertical launches allow missiles to climb steeply before descending towards their targets, potentially extending their range," he said.
"Angled launches, on the other hand, allow missiles to fly at lower altitudes from the outset, making them harder for missile defence systems to detect and intercept."
North Korea has carried out several missile launches from submarines in recent years, although its sea-based launch capabilities remain unclear.
Cruise missiles tend to be jet-propelled and fly at a lower altitude than more sophisticated ballistic missiles, making them harder to detect and intercept.
Proven submarine-launched ballistic missile capability would take North Korea's arsenal to a new level, allowing deployment far beyond the Korean peninsula and a second-strike capability in the event of an attack.
North Korea has carried out multiple ballistic missile tests in October, most recently on Monday.
The two Koreas have engaged in a tit-for-tat series of missile tests this month, with both sides test-firing hypersonic weapons.
South Korea test-fired its first homegrown hypersonic missile last week, days after Pyongyang said it had launched an AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Are US, Israel racing to deploy space-based lasers or orbital weapons first? - analysis
articles.body:
In September, two consecutive top US military officials made public, for the first time, that America has offensive weapons already deployed in space.
That the US, China, and Russia have anti-satellite weapons available is no secret and has been assumed in recent years, with China unofficially demonstrating old space weapons in 2007, and Russia and China both demonstrating newer weapons since 2021.
But a public declaration by the US set off speculation about whether the deployed weapons are focused on the area of: either directed-energy weapons such as lasers; or kinetic anti-satellite weapons such as missiles; or platforms for disrupting or disabling satellites’ activity without actually destroying them, which is also known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs).
A fourth method could be nuclear, but it is assumed that this was not the focus of the US announcement since the terrible consequences in space would impact the attacker as much as the defender.
In April, Unit 9900 officer Lt. Col. “S” and space-war expert Tal Inbar discussed Israel's efforts to defend its space assets against adversaries.
Also, on June 24, with the Post noting that Russia, China, and Iran have all worked on ways to attack, damage, jam, or drag satellites in space, IDF Brig. Gen. Yael Grossman responded, “There are threats from space. We work with the Defense Ministry with a lot of power; with the broader defense establishment, we can all bring forward achievements.”
Developments in space vehicles
Regarding the US announcement, so far those space experts who are commenting are leaning toward category 3 of RPO.
This is especially true for deploying RPOs, which can fight off other RPOs.
The reason is that RPOs have existed in one form or another since the US used multiple space vehicles to repair one another in the 1960s. In that sense, the largest jump was developing the technology and tactics for sending one space vehicle or satellite to match the orbit of another.
Once a country makes that major scientific jump, adding on a robot arm to attack or an additional system to jam is just a matter of time and energy.
Another reason RPOs may be favored would be to avoid the debris problem caused by using kinetic anti-satellite weapons, such as missiles.
The US has said it is hoping to make major advancements in stationing anti-missile physical interceptors in space that can protect satellites by 2028.
Despite all this focus on RPOs for the US, China, and Russia, Israel has expressed keen interest regarding space weapons in relation to lasers.
On June 29, Defense Minister Israel Katz told a briefing of military reporters that Israel is developing space lasers to carry out attacks above the Earth.
This was an expansion and more specific version of a statement which Katz made earlier in June, when he committed Israel to becoming the leading player with space attack capabilities.
“One of the central goals which the prime minister and I set is that we are recruiting the best minds,” since “as of today, no country has the ability to mount attacks in space. We must be the leading country in the world with this capability,” said Katz.
The defense minister continued, “If we achieve this, it will ensure the advantage of deterrence, of the ability to attack, destroy, and all of the other matters, versus our enemies with large resources.”
Lasers to be used to defend Israeli assets
But Monday was the first time that Katz specifically mentioned space lasers.
Israel is already a leading country in developing Iron Beam as a land-based space laser, and during a visit to Elbit earlier in the summer, The Jerusalem Post saw and heard about work on presumed future fighter-jet-based lasers.
Overall, it seemed clear that Katz on June 29 was referring to Iran.
This is especially true since during the 2026 war, Israel struck multiple Iranian space war-related facilities, including facilities working on developing capabilities to attack satellites in space.
It was unclear if he indirectly also wanted to deter Russia and China from assisting Iran in this and other spheres.
According to foreign reports, lasers might be able to destroy enemy satellites and also burn up any debris that an attack in space by other means might cause.
Some have already speculated that Israel could destroy enemy space satellites using the Arrow 3 missile system, given that it already strikes ballistic missiles in space.
Yet, due to the same issue that Russia and China already fell into regarding debris, many countries are working on other techniques, such as paralyzing, damaging, jamming, dragging, or using lasers against satellites in space.
While some Israeli officials have hinted at such efforts, Katz’s public statements on June 29 were the clearest one to date by a senior Israeli official.
Why the US's first focus is on RPOs
In contrast, if Iran or other enemies advanced past Israel in space, they could attack Israeli satellites and reduce its surveillance capabilities.
After all of this, why then do most experts believe that the US's first and current focus is on RPOs, and not lasers?
It is not that the US and the other countries with space programs are not working on developing space lasers. They are.
Also, Israel’s success with developing the Iron Beam for actual deployments as a ground laser has spurred other countries forward in the more general laser defense area.
But lasers in space or on aircraft are still a distant solution, as they involve a series of more complex physics and engineering problems, which invariably will take longer to solve than RPOs.
RPOs are thereby an immediate answer to help deter enemies from attacking, since they can be used to attack enemy satellites, as well as providing defense against other countries’ potential RPO attacks.
If enemies have existing and immediate weapons to attack an object, such as a satellite, the US and other countries, potentially even including Israel, are likely to focus on immediate solutions, with the focus on space lasers being a longer-term goal.
In that sense, the US statement in September was about immediately deterring China and Russia from attacking American satellites.
In contrast, Katz’s June statement was less about immediate attack, defense, or deterrence.
Rather, it was more about either bragging to the Israeli public about a future distant achievement, or psychological warfare against Iran to the extent that the Islamic Republic might believe it can work with Moscow and Beijing to go after Israel’s satellite advantage.

articles.title: 1,125 Kyiv residents injured in Russian attacks since the start of 2026, more than a third of them in five weeks from late August, Kyiv health chief says
articles.body:
Russian attacks have injured 1,125 Kyiv residents since the start of 2026. Of these, 379 people, or nearly 34%, were injured in just five weeks, from 27 August to 7 October, Tetiana Mostepan, director of the Kyiv City State Administration’s Department of Health, said in an interview published on 13 October.
Russian air attacks on Kyiv have intensified since late August. Air attacks occur both day and night, and Russian drones target not only military facilities but also civilian buildings, including apartments. As a result, the number of casualties is also increasing. More than 40% of emergency medical responses to attacks this year occurred between late August and early October, Mostepan noted.
During this period, the capital’s emergency medical teams responded to 782 calls related to the attacks, the department director said. She also released data showing that 138 medical facilities in Kyiv have been damaged since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, including 47 this year.
“And when we talk about statistics, I always emphasize that behind every number is a human life. These are people who have been injured, as well as medical workers who respond to attack sites to save them,” Mostepan said.
Russian attacks on Kyiv have become more frequent
Russia attacked Kyiv with drones throughout the day, Suspilne Kyiv reported on 27 August. Air raid alerts were issued 12 times in the capital, drone debris was found in five districts, and at least four people were injured, the report said. Russian forces used about 140 attack drones against Ukraine throughout the day, more than 100 of them jet-powered, the Ukrainian Air Force reported at the time.
At least 38 people were killed and dozens injured in a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot in the Bucha district near Kyiv, triggering a massive fire and hours of explosions in a residential area, CNN reported. The attack in the Bucha district came amid near-constant Russian airstrikes, which continued into Sunday, the outlet reported.
Russian forces were likely seeking to exhaust Ukraine’s air defenses, disrupt civilians’ daily lives, and increase the scale of destruction, analysts at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said, citing CNN’s reporting.
On 8 September, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stressed the urgent need to strengthen support for Ukraine, particularly by providing air defense systems. Delays in delivering assistance cost human lives, he said.
On 1 October, a Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district while 104 children were inside, Suspilne reported. Students and school staff took shelter, so no one was injured, the report said.
Russian attacks continue after Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire
Following US President Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire, Russia continued striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, including in Kyiv. On 13 October, Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv, hitting a thermal power plant in the second attack in 24 hours without advance warning from Ukraine’s allies, Zelenskyy said. The evening and morning strikes killed four people in Kyiv, three of them women in a high-rise in Desnianskyi district, Kyiv prosecutors said.
Russia attacked energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv with 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 14 October. At least 600,000 people were left without electricity, he said. Later that day, an accident on the grid cut power to part of Kyiv’s right bank, energy company DTEK said.
Read also
- Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches
- US continues sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Trump says amid Russia deal backlash. Questions remain over missed warning for latest attack
- Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms

articles.title: Saudi Arabia trades strikes with Yemen, threatens Houthis
articles.body:
This live blog has now ended. Make sure to follow us for the latest news on Facebook, X, and Instagram.
Breadcrumb
Welcome to our continuing coverage of events in the Middle East and beyond.
Here are the updates of the day:
The former head of Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency on Wednesday sued Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for defamation weeks before elections in a row over responsibility for Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack.
Netanyahu, who polls show in a tight race to stay in power in the October 27 election, has been hammered by the opposition for failing to prevent the attack, the deadliest day in Israeli history.
Netanyahu, who has cast himself as a guarantor of Israel's security over his decades-long career, has insisted that he could have stopped the attack had the Shin Bet's then director, Ronen Bar, or military leaders called to wake him up the day of the early-morning attack.
In the 134-page court document, Bar accused Netanyahu of "lying to cover himself" and said it was slanderous to accuse him of "criminal failures" over the attack.
Netanyahu made accusations against Bar "that he knew to be false, with the aim of diverting the debate from his own responsibility for the events of October 7", the lawsuit said.
Instead it was Netanyahu's policies over several years that had "increased the dangers posed by terrorist organisations in Gaza", it said.
Bar resigned in June 2025, saying at the time that "all the systems collapsed" in the security agency and that Shin Bet "failed to sound the alarm".
New Zealand has issued new "Do Not Travel" warnings for the entirety of Saudi Arabia amid escalating regional tensions with Yemen's Houthis.
The NGO Human Rights Watch said Wednesday that military authorities in eastern Libya executed at least 31 people earlier this year, the first reported death sentences to be carried out in the country since 2010, according to the group.
Forces under the control of military leader Khalifa Haftar and his clan executed the people between late August and September 10 "following grossly unfair military trials", HRW said in a statement, adding another 50 people in detention were "at imminent risk of execution".
Read the full story here.
US tech firm Palantir and London mayor Sadiq Khan's office have settled Palantir's lawsuit over a decision to block a £50 million ($66 million) contract with London police, both parties said on Wednesday.
Palantir had agreed a two-year contract with the Metropolitan Police to use its artificial intelligence systems to automate certain tasks and for analysing evidence.
But the mayor's office refused to approve the deal, telling the Met Police it had failed to have an open competition for the contract, with reports also quoting a spokesperson for Khan citing concerns Palantir did not align with "London's values".
Federal authorities investigating Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar seized the Democratic lawmaker's phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the probe.
The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities probe potential fraud in Omar's immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar's Washington, D.C. home on Monday just weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are attempting to build a new advanced medium-range ballistic missile system with the help of Chinese parts, according to a new report released Wednesday by a group that tracks the use of weapons in conflict zones.
The report by the U.K.-based Conflict Armament Research group came as the Houthis, in their ongoing war with Saudi Arabia, are demonstrating remarkable ability to wreak havoc on one of the Middle East’s best equipped militaries.
The weaponry under development could help the group more precisely target the Saudis and Israel. By turning to China, it also appears to be a sign of increasing independence.
Palestinian officials said Israeli strikes killed four people in Gaza on Wednesday, days after the anniversary of the declaration of a US-mediated ceasefire.
Two young men died when Israeli forces struck a vehicle near Khan Yunis in the southern Gaza Strip, civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Bassal and Nasser Hospital said.
Two other people, including a woman, were killed when an Israeli aircraft struck an apartment building in Gaza City, according to Bassal and Al-Shifa hospital.
Israel's army chief said on Wednesday that the military was reinforcing troop levels "across all fronts", citing an increased risk of escalation as the country heads into elections this later month.
On a visit to the occupied West Bank, Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir said the potential for incidents on Israel's borders had grown because of the election period, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu facing a tight race to stay in power in the October 27 poll.
"In light of the increased number of alerts across all fronts and the sensitivity of this period, the potential for escalation has grown," he said, according to an Israeli military statement.
"We have reinforced our forces across all areas."
He added that the military had raised its level of readiness as it prepares "for scenarios in which attempts may be made to catch us by surprise".
Citing the need for "vigilance", Zamir said the military was "at a high level of readiness to launch extensive offensive operations against anyone who attempts to harm Israeli civilians".
A visiting senior United Nations official on Wednesday reaffirmed the body's commitment to stability in Lebanon as the mandate of its peacekeeping force in the country is set to expire this year.
Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations Jean-Pierre Lacroix met officials as well as representatives of countries contributing to the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), which counts some 7,500 personnel from nearly 50 countries.
"I thanked them for their critical support to UNIFIL and reiterated the UN's strong commitment to supporting peace and stability in Lebanon," Lacroix said.
The Istanbul governor’s office declared schools closed, placed some public sector workers on leave and urged people to stay at home after heavy rainfall caused floods across the city on Wednesday.
Media reports said that the downpour flooded homes and businesses and inundated roads and underpasses, stranding vehicles and causing traffic chaos in the city of around 16 million people. There were no reports of any serious injuries.
In one district, bystanders rescued a woman who was being swept down a street by the floodwaters, footage obtained by NTV television showed. Firefighters rescued another person who was trapped inside a flooded basement, the report said.
Images showed several parked cars being swept by the floods in another neighborhood.
The governor’s office said that education would be suspended for a day on Thursday, and state employees with disabilities and mothers with young children would be placed on leave. It advised residents to stay home unless travel was absolutely necessary and for people living in basement apartments to spend the night elsewhere.
Motorcycles, meanwhile, were barred from traffic.
Israeli forces are using tear gas during an incurrsion into al-Mughayyir near Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, according to Palestinian media.
Saudi Arabia plans to move ahead with a major investment conference in Riyadh despite Houthi attacks on the kingdom, offering on-site and virtual attendance as well as alternative air and land travel routes, diplomatic sources told AFP.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events, but it has recently seen escalating military tensions with the Iran-backed Yemeni group, which has intensified attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil facilities.
Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute hosts an annual forum dubbed "Davos in the desert", which usually draws foreign leaders and business titans, and this year it is scheduled to be held in Riyadh from October 26 to 29.
Diplomatic sources said that to prevent cancellation, organisers reached out to embassies and foreign companies to explore "hybrid" participation options, allowing officials and business executives to attend either in person or virtually.
They have even discussed arrangements for participants to fly by private jet to Dhahran airport in eastern Saudi Arabia before travelling by road to Riyadh.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said Wednesday that they targeted Riyadh's international airport with a ballistic missile, hours after the Saudi-led coalition reported an interception of one fired towards the capital.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces... were able to target King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi enemy's capital, Riyadh, with a ballistic missile, and the hit was accurate," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X.
French President Emmanuel Macron will travel to Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar to meet the leaders of these countries from October 19 to October 21, his office said on Wednesday.
He plans to discuss the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and its impact on energy prices, the statement said.
At least ten vessels have been attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz since Sunday, a high since war broke out between the United States, Israel and Iran, security data showed Wednesday.
Four vessels were struck on Tuesday and six on Sunday -- the highest number of attacks in a single day since the start of the conflict -- according to data from security firm Vanguard, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the British maritime agency UKMTO.
Two seafarers have been reported missing and a container ship reportedly sank as a result of recent attacks, according to the maritime sources.
Israel’s defence minister has threatened to seize more territory in southern Lebanon and forcibly displace residents of Beirut’s southern suburbs if Hezbollah joins Iran in an attack on Israel.
Israel Katz’s comments on Wednesday come amid reports that Hezbollah is preparing for a new round of fighting with Israel, while Israel is also reported to be considering an escalation of its offensive in Lebanon in the coming weeks.
Hezbollah and Israel began exchanging fire in October 2023, with the conflict dramatically escalating into a full-scale war in September 2024. Fighting resumed on 2 March this year, alongside the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Thousands of people have attended demonstrations across southern Yemen in response to a call from exiled separatist leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi for a "popular mobilisation" to halt the ongoing Houthi advance.
In his first address since fleeing the country in January, the head of the Southern Transitional Council on Tuesday called on southern Yemenis to join the Saudi-backed government's efforts to turn the tide of the war.
Videos published by pro-separatist media showed mass protests in several cities - including Aden, Mukalla, Seiyun and Al-Ghaydah - which coincided with the anniversary of the 14 October revolution, the South Yemeni rebellion against British rule in 1963.
The Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the Strait of Hormuz after being struck by a projectile on September 23, data from UN shipping agency the International Maritime Organization showed on Wednesday.
The loss was reported less than 24 hours after the sinking of the Singapore flagged GFS Pride, which was struck by a projectile in a separate incident, maritime security sources said earlier on Wednesday.
Israeli forces are using live ammunition and tear gas during a military raid in the West Bank town of Salfit, according to Palestinian media reports.
Spanish humanitarian rescue charity SMH has postponed its next mission in the central Mediterranean until 2027 due to soaring fuel costs, the group said on Wednesday, highlighting the financial pressures facing humanitarian efforts along one of the world's deadliest migration routes.
SMH, which operates the Aita Mari, a former fishing vessel converted into a rescue ship in 2017, said on X the doubling of fuel prices had forced it to suspend operations in the central Mediterranean and shift activities to waters around Spain's Valencia coast, and the islands of Mallorca and Menorca.
It also launched a crowdfunding campaign to cover the extra costs.
The central Mediterranean crossing from North Africa to Italy and southern France is one of the world's most dangerous migrant routes, used by migrants from Africa and the Middle East seeking to reach Europe, often in overcrowded or unseaworthy boats.
Spanish NGO Open Arms said it had also scaled back its central Mediterranean missions in recent years because of rising fuel costs and Italy's policy of assigning rescue vessels ports in northern Italy. The practice can require ships to sail for two or three days from their operating area, increasing costs and reducing time available for search-and-rescue work.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's right-wing, anti-immigration government has repeatedly argued that humanitarian rescue vessels encourage migrants to attempt the crossing.
Turkish Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek on Wednesday agreed to let prosecutors open an investigation into the former head of Turkey's capital markets regulator, state news agency Anadolu said.
Turkey has been grappling with the fallout from an investment fund scandal which erupted a month ago, prompting an investigation into allegations of widespread market manipulation.
Simsek's green light came two weeks after prosecutors requested authorisation to investigate Ibrahim Omer Gonul, who chaired Turkey's Capital Markets Board (SPK) for four years until his mandate ended in April.
In their letter to the ministry, prosecutors said there were "clear and sufficient indications" that Gonul had failed to fulfil his responsibilities during his tenure in office.
The scandal has put pressure on President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AKP, with one senior party official resigning after allegations about her investment activities.
The crisis erupted when several funds were unable to satisfy investor redemption demands.
The SPK quickly placed seven companies that manage 131 investment funds with assets reportedly worth some $17 billion into liquidation.
More than 455,000 individual investors have been affected, it has said.
The chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority on Wednesday said that the exhibition Six Kings Slam tennis tournament has been postponed for logistical reasons, after Yemen's Houthis carried out several deadly attacks on the kingdom.
"The Six Kings Slam tournament has been postponed due to logistical reasons and will now take place on December 27," wrote Turki Alalshikh on X, sharing a statement from the Riyadh Season entertainment programme.
Irish author Sally Rooney can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for the activist group Palestine Action, proscribed by London, her publisher Faber said Wednesday.
"Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work... As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," Faber said in a statement on its website.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) said on Wednesday that it now recommends airlines take potential risks into account when flying in Jordanian airspace, easing earlier guidance that advised carriers to avoid the airspace altogether.
The conflict zone information bulletin on Jordan was however extended until November 16, it said on its website.

articles.title: Former Ukrainian president Yushchenko writes open letter to Trump
articles.body:
Former Ukrainian president Yushchenko writes open letter to Trump
Viktor Yushchenko, Ukraine's third president, has written an open letter to US President Donald Trump over his agreement with Russian ruler Vladimir Putin on diesel fuel.
Source: Yushchenko on Facebook
Quote: "And against this reality, Ukrainians hear calls that Ukraine should stop. That Ukraine should restrain its strikes against the infrastructure that finances and sustains Russia's war. That trade in Russian energy can somehow be separated from the missiles and drones Russia sends against Ukrainian families. It cannot.
Money paid for Russian fuel is not an abstraction called 'commerce' It finances an economy geared toward total war."
Details: Yushchenko also reflected on events more than three decades ago, when the Soviet Union was breaking up.
He noted that Ukraine had then possessed the world's third-largest nuclear arsenal. "In negotiations with our allies, we agreed to give it up. We did so because we believed that a world governed by agreements was safer than a world governed by nuclear weapons."
Quote: "In 1994, the United States of America, along with its partners, signed the Budapest Memorandum, providing Ukraine with official assurances of security, sovereignty, and the inviolability of our borders.
They pledged not to threaten or use force against Ukraine. America assumed a moral responsibility toward Ukraine. So how can anyone today, when a treacherous enemy has attacked us, forget America's signature on this document?"
Background:
- On 9 October, Trump said he had spoken to Putin and reached an agreement with him on the supply of Russian diesel fuel to the US and global markets.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump's decision to unilaterally lift sanctions on Russia and allow it to export diesel fuel was unfair and dishonest.
Subscribe on Patreon to back our journalism long-term.

articles.title: Russian attacks on Ukraine leave 600,000 without power as Zelenskyy says Moscow ‘disrespecting’ US – Europe live
articles.body:
No indication intelligence sharing with Ukraine has stopped, EU says
The European Commission declined to comment on reported disruption to Starlink’s services in Ukraine, but said there are “no indication that [US] intelligence sharing has stopped.”
Repeatedly asked about the issue, the commission spokespeople said they were “aware of the report” on Starlink, but declined to comment “until we have more information.”
“[It is] important also to say that we have no indications that, intelligence sharing has stopped,” the chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, said.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
The European Commission and Nato’s Mark Rutte have said there were no sign that US intelligence sharing with Ukraine stopped, despite growing concerns after Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night (11:45, 12:44).
But it declined to comment on concerns about apparent restrictions on Ukraine’s Starlink terminals, which are critical for its military operations.
Zelenskyy is in Britain this afternoon, with talks with UK prime minister Andy Burnham this afternoon (15:01, 15:28), before going to Brussels to meet EU leaders later this week (16:29).
In other news,
Germany’s embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz warned German lawmakers about “the time of upheaval,” as he assured of his support for Ukraine and spoke of his government’s priorities in the face of surging support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (14:31).
A Ukrainian soldier led a team of divers that laid explosives on the bed of the Baltic Sea to blow up the Nord Stream gas pipelines, possibly on the order of state authorities, a court has heard as the much-awaited trial related to the incident got under way in Hamburg (10:43, 14:16).
Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte urged allies to “do more” in the face of “Russia’s aggression unrelenting,” as he insisted the alliance had “all the response options we need” to react to any Russian threat (11:42, 11:45)
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
Zelenskyy to attend European Council in Brussels, hold first talks with Hungary's Magyar
Back to Ukraine,Zelenskyy’s schedule for the coming days appears to be getting a bit clearer.
As reported earlier, he is in London today and meeting with UK’s Andy Burnham before joining EU leaders in Brussels later this week for talks on the margins of the European Council.
And Hungary’s Péter Magyar has just said he will also hold his first one-on-one talks with Zelenskyy on Friday, just days after Kyiv passed legislation addressing Budapest’s longstanding concerns over minority rights.
The move and the talks could unblock Ukraine’s EU accession talks after lengthy hold-ups under the previous Hungarian government of Viktor Orbán.
Excluding UK from ‘Made in Europe’ law will hurt entire EU car industry, Mercedes boss warns
Lisa O’Carroll
Senior correspondent
Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said.
Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”.
He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU.
The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU.
It is mainly aimed at China, which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland.
“It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry.
“We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added.
Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France.
French minister accuses Elon Musk of ‘online harassment campaigns’ against European leaders
Ashifa Kassam
European community affairs correspondent
Meanwhile, France’s foreign minister has accused Elon Musk of using his social media platform to orchestrate “massive online harassment campaigns” against European leaders as he took aim at foreign efforts to destabilise the country before next year’s presidential election.
Speaking at an Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development conference on Tuesday, Jean-Noël Barrot pointed to the role that social media had come to play in the global battle over democracy.
“The forces seeking to undermine democracy now dominate the information landscape, where they employ tactics designed to polarise public debate,” he said.
The result was that “political movements with authoritarian aims”, which “play right into the hands of democracy’s declared enemies”, had been gaining ground in Europe and North America, he said.
“They exacerbate the polarisation of our societies,” he added. “Their ultimate goal is clear: to seize power and then create the conditions to never relinquish it.”
Barrot cited the 2027 presidential election in France, where the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in the polls.
“The enemies of democracy are doing everything they can to destabilise us,” he said. “They exploit our divisions and use immigration, secularism and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to stoke hatred and tensions.”
Burnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ support
Peter Walker
Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump.
The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: “We are with you for as long as it takes.”
To coincide with the visit, the UK has said it will move more rapidly in providing Ukraine with British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect it from attacks by a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones.
In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyy visited a naval base in Portsmouth in the same month and when Burnham travelled to Kyiv in August.
Zelenskyy’s latest visit comes as Ukraine faces increased Russian missile and drone attacks, and after Donald Trump made a deal to buy Russian diesel, called for Ukraine to have a new leader, and announced a supposed ceasefire connected to energy infrastructure that the Ukrainian president said “was news to him”.
Burnham pledges to try to 'repair bridges' between Zelenskyy and Trump
UK prime minister Andy Burnham said he will seek to “repair bridges” between US president Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy amid strained ties between the pair, AFP reported.
Burnham made the comments before he was due to welcome Zelensky to his official Downing Street residence, in a show of support for Ukraine’s president after new criticism by Trump.
“What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back,” Burnham told the British parliament.
“Therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together. That is the role I intend to play.”
The pair is expected to meet this afternoon, and the Ukrainian president is also expected to meet King Charles III.
Interestingly, Zelenskyy departed for London from the Polish city in Rzeszów reverting to flying from Poland after months of flying from Moldova’s Chișinău during a period of strained relations with Poland over history.
Merz calls for 'creative efforts' to tame the rise of extremism
In pretty pointed remarks against the surging far-right Alternative fur Deutschland, Merz also recalls the opening line from the 1950 Schuman declaration, which said:
“World peace cannot be safeguarded without the making of creative efforts proportionate to the dangers which threaten it.”
Adapting it to today’s Germany and Europe, Merz urges parties to recommit to that “creative effort” and not “a scornful desire for disintegration, a delight in division, or exclusion or fear of others.”
“We must summon that effort and we will - not least in the face of the extremism that has always been a part of our society and is now surging with full force into this parliament, into state parliaments, and into the everyday life of our country.”
He acknowledges that “this extremism … has roots in legitimate dissatisfaction and legitimate feelings of injustices,” but insists it would not resolve any of the people’s problems.
Merz warns of 'time of upheaval' as he doubles down on support for Ukraine and proposes new trade measures to protect EU industries
Over in Berlin, Germany’s embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz is addressing the Bundestag, talking about his government’s plan of reforms, his plans for this week’s EU summit in Brussels and Ukraine.
He warns lawmakers that Germany faces “a time of upheaval, with crises and wars, some of which lie beyond our control.”
Merz repeats his key lines on the much-needed investment in Germany’s defence capabilities, and doubles down on his support for Ukraine.
He dismisses any suggestion that Germany’s support for Ukraine comes at an expense of social and welfare spending.
“This is simply not a case. Not a single euro flowing to Ukraine is being diverted from social or educational spending in our own country. Not a single euro,” he said.
Merz warns that “the danger is very real and concrete,” as Russia continues to show “willigness to escalate: against Ukraine, against our eastern European neighbours, and indeed against our own country.”
“Against this backdrop … it is incomprehensible to me how those on the far left and far right continue to play down the situation,” he said.
He says some comments were almost “deliberately driving the division … and disinformation” to “derivse partisan, political advantages from it.”
Turning to this week’s EU summit, Merz says the discussions will focus on the next EU budget with “negotiations now entering a decisive phase.”
He stresses Germany’s priorities of security and competitiveness, with a call to “further cut back EU bureaucracy and accelerate approval processes to boost and enable investment across Europe,” particularly in decarbonisation, AI and defence.
He also talks about the importance of a new legal regime for pan-European startups, advancing the EU’s capital markets union, and on developing new trade relationships with global partners while reducing “one-sided dependencies” with existing partners.
“We will no longer stand idly by while other states harm our economy through heavy subsidies, artificially devalued currencies, overcapacity, and aggressive pricing. We will not stand idly by any longer.”
(Yep, he probably means China.)
His comments come ahead of his planned trips to Japan, South Korea and Singapore.
He says the European Council will discuss creating “a new trade defence instrument” to respond “swiftly and forcefully to targeted attacks on our industries and supply chains.”
“These decisions would, among other things, provide the European Commission with a tool to react rapidly without needing to consult the European Council first. The European Council, for its part, would then have the power to reverse such a move by a qualified majority. This makes us faster and more effective, and gives the Commission a powerful tool.”
Nord Stream suspect's lawyers argue Nord Stream may have not been a crime, ask for case to be dismissed
Over in Germany, we have an update on the Nord Stream trial which began in Hamburg earlier today (10:43).
Defence lawyers for a former Ukrainian army officer charged with damaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines in blasts four years ago have called for the dismissal of charges in the first day of his trial.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Serhii Kuznetsov’s lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany’s imports of natural gas before Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a “Russian weapon” and therefore potentially a legitimate target, Reuters reported.
“Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor’s infrastructure without harming any human beings?”
Kuznietsov’s lawyers also argued that he was still an active duty solider an as such was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak about anything during his service for reasons of secrecy linked to national security, AP reported.
Protesters gathered outside the Hamburg court in support of the defendant, with a sign that read: “What are war crimes?”
“Russia is the only war criminal that belongs in the dock,” said one of the dozens of protesters.
Bulgaria says Russia likely behind Black Sea drone strikes but 'we cannot prove it'
In the Bulgarian parliament, prime minister Rumen Radev has said that Russia was most likely behind drone attacks in the Black Sea that sank two ships, but that “we cannot prove it”.
AP quotes Radev saying “There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favours Russia, and indeed, the logic points in that direction. The problem is that we cannot prove it.”
The Russian ambassador to Bulgaria was summoned yesterday over the issue, and Bulgarian president Iliana Yotova has called for an immediate halt to hostilities in the Black Sea and a moratorium on drone attacks against commercial and civilian infrastructure.
Bulgaria investigating report that Starlink antennas set on fire near Sofia
Bulgaria is investigating a report that several antennas used for communication with the Starlink satellite network were deliberately set on fire, prime minister Rumen Radev has said.
“The investigation is extremely intensive. We are working with partner services to successfully carry out this operation,” AFP reports Radev said in parliament, without confirming or denying the claim.
A Bulgarian opposition MP has claimed 11 telecommunications antennas linked to the Starlink network were set on fire over the weekend “at a secret facility near Sofia”.
A spokesperson for the Sofia prosecutor’s office confirmed to AFP that an investigation was under way but said no one has been charged.
A fire broke out at a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland in September, with the country’s digital affairs minister calling the blaze an act of “sabotage” and prime minister Donald Tusk describing it as an “act of hybrid warfare”.
Germany’s foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, has said his country has not observed a substantial reduction in US support for Ukraine, and does not expect to. The statement comes amid the US and Russia having secured a diesel supply deal, and reports that Elon Musk’s Starlink service has been reduced for Ukrainian forces.
Moscow has said that the US-Russia deal over diesel “will open other opportunities as well”.
Reuters reports Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Moscow would overcome any sanctions-related difficulties to ensure the diesel supplies were delivered, and that the deal could pave the way for further economic cooperation between the two nations.
Reuters, citing local media, reports that Bulgaria expects to join a Nato anti-drone initiative by the end of October. The news comes a day after a drone attack sank a cargo vessel off the country’s Black Sea coast for the second time in a week.
Defence minister Dimitar Stoyanov said “Bulgaria will be part of this project as soon as possible. Expectations are that by 30 October, we will already be part of the project.”

articles.title: Russian attacks on Ukraine leave 600,000 without power as Zelenskyy says Moscow ‘disrespecting’ US – Europe live
articles.body:
No indication intelligence sharing with Ukraine has stopped, EU says
The European Commission declined to comment on reported disruption to Starlink’s services in Ukraine, but said there are “no indication that [US] intelligence sharing has stopped.”
Repeatedly asked about the issue, the commission spokespeople said they were “aware of the report” on Starlink, but declined to comment “until we have more information.”
“[It is] important also to say that we have no indications that, intelligence sharing has stopped,” the chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, said.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
The European Commission and Nato’s Mark Rutte have said there were no sign that US intelligence sharing with Ukraine stopped, despite growing concerns after Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night (11:45, 12:44).
But it declined to comment on concerns about apparent restrictions on Ukraine’s Starlink terminals, which are critical for its military operations.
Zelenskyy is in Britain this afternoon, with talks with UK prime minister Andy Burnham this afternoon (15:01, 15:28), before going to Brussels to meet EU leaders later this week (16:29).
In other news,
Germany’s embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz warned German lawmakers about “the time of upheaval,” as he assured of his support for Ukraine and spoke of his government’s priorities in the face of surging support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (14:31).
A Ukrainian soldier led a team of divers that laid explosives on the bed of the Baltic Sea to blow up the Nord Stream gas pipelines, possibly on the order of state authorities, a court has heard as the much-awaited trial related to the incident got under way in Hamburg (10:43, 14:16).
Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte urged allies to “do more” in the face of “Russia’s aggression unrelenting,” as he insisted the alliance had “all the response options we need” to react to any Russian threat (11:42, 11:45)
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
Zelenskyy to attend European Council in Brussels, hold first talks with Hungary's Magyar
Back to Ukraine,Zelenskyy’s schedule for the coming days appears to be getting a bit clearer.
As reported earlier, he is in London today and meeting with UK’s Andy Burnham before joining EU leaders in Brussels later this week for talks on the margins of the European Council.
And Hungary’s Péter Magyar has just said he will also hold his first one-on-one talks with Zelenskyy on Friday, just days after Kyiv passed legislation addressing Budapest’s longstanding concerns over minority rights.
The move and the talks could unblock Ukraine’s EU accession talks after lengthy hold-ups under the previous Hungarian government of Viktor Orbán.
Excluding UK from ‘Made in Europe’ law will hurt entire EU car industry, Mercedes boss warns
Lisa O’Carroll
Senior correspondent
Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said.
Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”.
He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU.
The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU.
It is mainly aimed at China, which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland.
“It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry.
“We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added.
Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France.
French minister accuses Elon Musk of ‘online harassment campaigns’ against European leaders
Ashifa Kassam
European community affairs correspondent
Meanwhile, France’s foreign minister has accused Elon Musk of using his social media platform to orchestrate “massive online harassment campaigns” against European leaders as he took aim at foreign efforts to destabilise the country before next year’s presidential election.
Speaking at an Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development conference on Tuesday, Jean-Noël Barrot pointed to the role that social media had come to play in the global battle over democracy.
“The forces seeking to undermine democracy now dominate the information landscape, where they employ tactics designed to polarise public debate,” he said.
The result was that “political movements with authoritarian aims”, which “play right into the hands of democracy’s declared enemies”, had been gaining ground in Europe and North America, he said.
“They exacerbate the polarisation of our societies,” he added. “Their ultimate goal is clear: to seize power and then create the conditions to never relinquish it.”
Barrot cited the 2027 presidential election in France, where the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in the polls.
“The enemies of democracy are doing everything they can to destabilise us,” he said. “They exploit our divisions and use immigration, secularism and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to stoke hatred and tensions.”
Burnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ support
Peter Walker
Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump.
The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: “We are with you for as long as it takes.”
To coincide with the visit, the UK has said it will move more rapidly in providing Ukraine with British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect it from attacks by a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones.
In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyy visited a naval base in Portsmouth in the same month and when Burnham travelled to Kyiv in August.
Zelenskyy’s latest visit comes as Ukraine faces increased Russian missile and drone attacks, and after Donald Trump made a deal to buy Russian diesel, called for Ukraine to have a new leader, and announced a supposed ceasefire connected to energy infrastructure that the Ukrainian president said “was news to him”.

UK prime minister Andy Burnham said he will seek to “repair bridges” between US president Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy amid strained ties between the pair, AFP reported.
Burnham made the comments before he was due to welcome Zelensky to his official Downing Street residence, in a show of support for Ukraine’s president after new criticism by Trump.
“What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back,” Burnham told the British parliament.
“Therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together. That is the role I intend to play.”
The pair is expected to meet this afternoon, and the Ukrainian president is also expected to meet King Charles III.
Interestingly, Zelenskyy departed for London from the Polish city in Rzeszów reverting to flying from Poland after months of flying from Moldova’s Chișinău during a period of strained relations with Poland over history.
Merz calls for 'creative efforts' to tame the rise of extremism
In pretty pointed remarks against the surging far-right Alternative fur Deutschland, Merz also recalls the opening line from the 1950 Schuman declaration, which said:
“World peace cannot be safeguarded without the making of creative efforts proportionate to the dangers which threaten it.”
Adapting it to today’s Germany and Europe, Merz urges parties to recommit to that “creative effort” and not “a scornful desire for disintegration, a delight in division, or exclusion or fear of others.”
“We must summon that effort and we will - not least in the face of the extremism that has always been a part of our society and is now surging with full force into this parliament, into state parliaments, and into the everyday life of our country.”
He acknowledges that “this extremism … has roots in legitimate dissatisfaction and legitimate feelings of injustices,” but insists it would not resolve any of the people’s problems.

Over in Berlin, Germany’s embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz is addressing the Bundestag, talking about his government’s plan of reforms, his plans for this week’s EU summit in Brussels and Ukraine.
He warns lawmakers that Germany faces “a time of upheaval, with crises and wars, some of which lie beyond our control.”
Merz repeats his key lines on the much-needed investment in Germany’s defence capabilities, and doubles down on his support for Ukraine.
He dismisses any suggestion that Germany’s support for Ukraine comes at an expense of social and welfare spending.
“This is simply not a case. Not a single euro flowing to Ukraine is being diverted from social or educational spending in our own country. Not a single euro,” he said.
Merz warns that “the danger is very real and concrete,” as Russia continues to show “willigness to escalate: against Ukraine, against our eastern European neighbours, and indeed against our own country.”
“Against this backdrop … it is incomprehensible to me how those on the far left and far right continue to play down the situation,” he said.
He says some comments were almost “deliberately driving the division … and disinformation” to “derivse partisan, political advantages from it.”
Turning to this week’s EU summit, Merz says the discussions will focus on the next EU budget with “negotiations now entering a decisive phase.”
He stresses Germany’s priorities of security and competitiveness, with a call to “further cut back EU bureaucracy and accelerate approval processes to boost and enable investment across Europe,” particularly in decarbonisation, AI and defence.
He also talks about the importance of a new legal regime for pan-European startups, advancing the EU’s capital markets union, and on developing new trade relationships with global partners while reducing “one-sided dependencies” with existing partners.
“We will no longer stand idly by while other states harm our economy through heavy subsidies, artificially devalued currencies, overcapacity, and aggressive pricing. We will not stand idly by any longer.”
(Yep, he probably means China.)
His comments come ahead of his planned trips to Japan, South Korea and Singapore.
He says the European Council will discuss creating “a new trade defence instrument” to respond “swiftly and forcefully to targeted attacks on our industries and supply chains.”
“These decisions would, among other things, provide the European Commission with a tool to react rapidly without needing to consult the European Council first.
