articles.title: FACTBOX: SpaceX restricts access to Starlink for Ukrainian military
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. SpaceX limited the speed of Starlink satellite internet terminals used by the Ukrainian army overnight, Sergey Beskrestnov, Vladimir Zelensky’s external adviser and expert in communications and unmanned systems, said.
Below are the main facts on the subject.
Restriction of access
- SpaceX imposed restrictions on the operation of Starlink terminals for the Ukrainian army overnight, disrupting its operations, Sergey Sternenko, a former adviser to Ukraine’s defense minister, wrote on Telegram.
- Sternenko speculated that SpaceX had acted at the request of US President Donald Trump’s administration.
- Zelensky’s external adviser Beskrestnov later confirmed the reports on Telegram.
- According to him, the restrictions currently apply to the ‘military package’ of Starshield services, with the speed limit set at 100 miles per hour (about 160 kilometers per hour - TASS).
- This "disrupted a number of missions," Beskrestnov said.
- In his view, "this action cannot be a coincidence and has to do with the current political situation."
- Ukraine once again received no intelligence warning from its Western partners last night, Vladimir Zelensky said.
- The US warned Ukraine that it could suspend intelligence sharing, Zelensky said in an interview with NPR. According to him, Ukrainian generals reported that they had been notified of this possibility at the military level.
- Ukraine received no intelligence warnings regarding the first wave of Russian ballistic missile launches overnight into October 14, but warnings about subsequent attacks did come in, RBC Ukraine quoted Ukrainian Air Force Spokesman Yury Ignat as saying.
Consequences
- A slowdown in Starlink service is making it virtually impossible to launch medium-range drones, and some missions involving them have already been cancelled since the start of the day, the 7th Corps of the Ukrainian airborne assault troops reported on Telegram.
- The Ukrainian armed forces rely entirely on Starlink satellite internet, so the Kiev authorities must travel to the US to negotiate the lifting of access restrictions, Verkhovna Rada lawmaker Alexey Goncharenko (listed in Russia as a terrorist and extremist) said.
- The Ukrainian army will no longer be able to counter Russian jet-powered drones due to the reduced speed of the US Starlink satellite Internet service, Zelensky’s external adviser on communications and unmanned systems, Beskrestnov, said.
- As the adviser pointed out, Kiev uses Starlink to counter jet-powered drones, but restrictions on its operation will now prevent the Ukrainian military from doing so.
- Beskrestnov said that through their actions Ukraine’s partners "actually deprive" Kiev of one of the few chances to intercept such drones.
- The slowdown of Starlink terminals caught the Ukrainian military by surprise, occurring entirely without warning, the British newspaper Financial Times (FT) wrote citing sources.
- The report says that Ukrainian drones relying on Starlink terminals are experiencing signal disruptions at speeds above 160 kmph.
- The reduction in intelligence-sharing from the United States, combined with Starlink's operational restrictions, is seriously hampering the Ukrainian military, unmanned aviation expert and CEO of the Center for Integrated Unmanned Solutions Dmitry Kuzyakin told TASS.
- According to him, the Kiev regime’s unchecked actions are irritating both the US president himself and a segment of the American establishment that has heavily invested in Ukraine.
- A number of cyber operations by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) against Russia may be disrupted or delayed due to SpaceX restricting the speed of Starlink satellite Internet terminals used by Ukrainian security agencies, Sergey Trukhachev, a technical and digital security expert, told TASS.
- He also noted that the SpaceX restrictions would directly impact the Ukrainian armed forces as well.
- This would primarily affect Ukrainian operators of high-speed unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), the expert added.
Response
- Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned US entrepreneur and SpaceX owner Elon Musk on social media platform X, amid reports that connection speeds for Starlink satellite internet terminals used by the Ukrainian military have been throttled.

articles.title: ‘Massive’ Russian attack on Ukraine kills at least six, damages power sites
articles.body:
‘Massive’ Russian attack on Ukraine kills at least 9, damages power sites
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine’s partners failed to warn of Russian ballistic missiles attack on Kyiv.
Russian air attacks have killed at least nine people in Ukraine and left hundreds of thousands without power, days after United States President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” in the more-than four year war.
The Russian Defence Ministry said on Wednesday that its forces had carried out a “massive” strike against communications and energy infrastructure facilities in Ukraine, the Interfax news agency reported.
In a statement, it said Russian forces hit two plants supplying power and heating in the capital Kyiv, two other plants in the wider region and an electricity substation.
Other targets included a heating and power plant in Ukraine’s second-largest city Kharkiv, along with a thermal power facility which the ministry said supplied the Ukrainian military in the southeast of the Kharkiv region.
Moscow said its forces had also hit a data centre in Kyiv which it said was used to gather intelligence on Russia’s military.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to remain in shelters.
“Energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region have come under a massive ballistic missile strike. There are power disruptions in the capital,” he wrote on Telegram.
DTEK, Ukraine’s largest private energy provider, said the attack had caused emergency power cuts in several urban districts of Kyiv.
A Russian strike on a multistorey building in the capital’s Desnianskyi district killed two people, while another attack in Golosiivsky district killed one, Ukraine’s state emergency service said.
The Ukrainian military also reported that two people were killed and six wounded in Russian attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region. Another person was killed in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region.
In the Volyn region, a Russian attack on Ukraine’s western city of Lutsk killed three people and injured at least 12, governor Roman Romaniuk said on Telegram.
Further Russian missile attacks were reported in the Kharkiv and Zhytomyr regions, while other strikes hit Sumy and Chernihiv.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said a record number of hypersonic missiles were used in the attacks on the capital.
“Over half a million people in Ukraine are without power as a result of these strikes,” she said.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine received no warnings from its Western partners of a Russian ballistic missile attack on the capital, raising questions about intelligence sharing.
“A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners,” he wrote on Facebook. “This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches.”
The president said Ukraine detected the missiles only as they neared Kyiv.
He also accused Russia of violating the “energy ceasefire” Trump announced on Sunday.
“A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure – the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President,” he wrote on X.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect towards the United States.”
A technology adviser to the Ukrainian president said the operation of some Starlink internet terminals appeared to have been restricted overnight, preventing its military-grade version from operating above 160 kilometres per hour, disrupting combat missions.
“Tonight SpaceX introduced a speed limit for the Starlink terminals in motion,” Sergiy Beskrestnov said, referring to Elon Musk’s company, which owns Starlink.
“Our defence forces were not warned about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions. Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation.”
Russia also reported Ukrainian drone strikes overnight. The governor of Russia’s Saratov region, Roman Busargin, said a Ukrainian drone strike had killed one person in the city of Balakovo.
Busargin said all infrastructure facilities were operating as usual. Balakovo is home to a data centre of Russia’s top lender Sberbank, a nuclear power plant and a hydropower station, whose dam spans the Volga River, among other facilities.
Sberbank later said its data centre in the Saratov region had been attacked by drones, but that all systems were operating as normal.
Moscow mayor Sergey Sobyanin said air defence forces had downed nearly 500 drones flying towards the Russian capital overnight. Russian authorities said about 160 more were brought down over the Rostov region, while others targeted Moscow.
Russia’s military later put the number of downed Ukrainian drones overnight at 902, of which 180 were shot down near the capital, Moscow.

Moscow mayor Sergey Sobyanin said air defence forces had downed nearly 500 drones flying towards the Russian capital overnight. Russian authorities said about 160 more were brought down over the Rostov region, while others targeted Moscow.
Russia’s military later put the number of downed Ukrainian drones overnight at 902, of which 180 were shot down near the capital, Moscow.

articles.title: 'This cannot be a coincidence' — Ukraine's Starlink access restricted without warning, Zelensky adviser says
articles.body:
'This cannot be a coincidence' — Ukraine's Starlink access restricted without warning, Zelensky adviser says
Key developments:
- SpaceX implemented speed restrictions on Starlink systems for the Ukrainian military on Oct. 14 without warning, limiting speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour)
- The unexpected restriction disrupted active military operations, including the use of mid-range strike drones and interceptors
- Ukrainian officials said they believed the move was tied to the Trump administration's intensifying pressure on Kyiv to stop strikes on Russian oil assets
- Elon Musk said Trump holds ultimate authority over Starlink speed and usage limitations for Ukraine
- Starlink service has stabilized, but the speed cap remains in place, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said
Ukraine's Starlink access has been restricted without warning, severely disrupting "several" military missions, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Oct. 14.
The speed restrictions were accompanied by signal disruptions and instability, even at lower speeds. Military personnel from mulitple units reported serious issues with Starlink throughout the day.
"I confirm that (Starlink owner) SpaceX implemented speed restrictions on Starlink terminals while in motion last night. Currently, the restriction applies to the Starshield 'military service package' and limits speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour)," Beskrestnov said in a post on social media.
Ukraine's Defense Ministry later told journalists that the actual speeds available during the day were even lower than the 160 kph limit. By the end of the day, service was reportedly stabilized, but the restriction remained in place.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said only U.S. President Donald Trump had the power to determine the speed restrictions for Starshield systems.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action," he said.
Ukraine relies on Starlink for several military applications including operating its "middle strike" campaign in Russian-occupied Ukraine, as well as interceptor drones that defend against Russia's new jet-powered attack drones.
This mid-range strike campaign this year has allowed Ukraine to strangle Russian logistics, hampering its ability to fight on the front lines.
Sudden disruption on the front lines
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that speed limitations had been discovered and the cause was being investigated.
"This complicates drone missions —specifically those involving interceptors and mid-range strike drones — and hampers capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance, and signal relay," the source added.
A soldier working on mid-range strike drone operations, who requested anonymity, confirmed that "certain issues are being observed" but declined to elaborate, citing operational security.
Two other commanders — both from elite drone units working on the eastern and southern front lines — reported issues with Starlink terminals on "middle strike" drones flying at higher speeds over the last 24 hours.
Both likewise requested to remain anonymous, and declined to describe the problems in more detail, so as to not assist the enemy.
During the day, Ukraine's 7th Air Assault Corps said on social media that it was experiencing a "throttling" of its Starlink connectivity.
"The consequences are already being felt in the field. Since the start of the day alone, a drone unit operating within the 7th Corps' area of responsibility in the Huliaipole sector has had to cancel a number of missions due to these connectivity issues," the corps said.
Service restored — with a speed cap
Later in the evening of Oct. 14, ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov — who famously negotiated with Musk to cut off Russian forces from Starlink while in office — announced that service was being restored, with the speed limit in place.
"Attack drones and interceptor drones should be operational again," he wrote. "Now, the focus should be on completely removing the speed limit for Starshield."
Fedorov, who no longer holds a position in the Ukrainian government after being dismissed by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July, did not provide evidence for his claims or explain where he got his information, though he thanked Musk in his post on X.
The Defense Ministry confirmed that service had been stabilized at a speed of 160 kilometers per hour.
"SpaceX continues to maintain the 161 km/h limit. Throughout the day, the actual limits were significantly lower. However, as of now, we observe that connection quality has improved at speeds up to 160 km/h," the ministry said in a comment to reporters.
The Defense Ministry is currently negotiating with partners and with SpaceX "regarding stable service conditions and the prevention of sudden restrictions."
But Musk's response was not encouraging — particularly for Ukraine's middle-strike campaign.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government," he wrote in response to Fedorov.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."
Is Trump to blame? 
Musk comments point to a link between the Starlink disruption and Kyiv's deteriorating relationship with the White House — a fear voiced earlier in the day bey Beskrestnov.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," he said.
As reported by the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 12, U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened Ukraine with the withholding of intelligence and other assistance in a bid to protect Russian oil refineries.
Beskrestnov did not provide evidence that the Starlink restriction was connected to U.S. pressure on Ukraine, and the White House has not commented on the issue.
Serhii Sternenko, an activist and former advisor to Fedorov, also reported the restriction of access, saying "SpaceX likely took these measures at the request of the Trump administration."
The development comes after Ukraine worked with SpaceX earlier this year to deactivate unauthorized Starlink terminals being used by Russian forces. Starlink has played a critical role in Ukrainian military communications throughout the full-scale war.
The threats came after a confusing 48 hours during whichTrump announced a controversial "deal" with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, followed by repeated demands that Ukraine replace Zelensky as president, followed by Trump announcing a unilateral "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which blindsided both Moscow and Kyiv.
Ukraine has since refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries but Russia has continued its blitz on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, most recently overnight on Oct. 14 when "several" power plants in Kyiv were hit. Trump has refused to accuse Russia of breaking the ceasefire.
Consequences of US pivot
The reported Starlink restrictions come as questions have been raised about U.S. intelligence sharing in relation to Russian ballistic missile launches, following two straight nights of attack on Kyiv with little to no warning.
Five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, causing "massive explosions," Kyiv Independent journalists reported. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
Zelensky described the strike as "particularly vile," saying Kyiv "received no early warning from our partners about this strike." His remarks raised questions about whether Washington had suspended intelligence assistance to Ukraine.
Despite the failure of Kyiv's early warning system and threats to halt U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Washington made no such decision, Ukrainian and American sources told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 13.
But later that day, around 10:30 p.m. another wave of ballistic missiles hit Kyiv, again without the usual warning.
At least three women were killed, and another 24 people, including a 7-year-old girl, were injured as a result of a hit on a residential building in the Desnianskyi District. Three more waves of ballistic missiles struck Kyiv throughout the night.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat told Ukrainian TV that Ukraine received no warnings from its partners about the first wave, though it did for the following three.
"Ukraine did not attack Russian oil refineries, yet Trump has already begun imposing sanctions on my country. Meanwhile, sanctions against Russia have been eased," Sternenko said.

articles.title: Three days after Washington announced an energy ceasefire, Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid
articles.body:
Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at Ukraine’s energy system overnight into 14 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The barrage came three days after US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire, which the Kremlin never confirmed, saying on 12 October only that contacts were continuing.
Ukraine held off strikes on Russian energy for two days after the announcement, Zelenskyy wrote on 13 October. Russia’s barrage opened that evening with a ballistic strike on Kyiv. For the second time in two days, it came without a launch warning from partners.
How the night unfolded
The Air Force described one massive combined strike that began at 18:00 on 13 October. By 09:00 the next day, it had counted 39 missiles on ballistic trajectories and 128 drones, aimed mainly at Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv Oblast. Air defenses downed or suppressed four missiles and 115 drones, but missiles and drones hit 22 locations, the Air Force said.
Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches
The first wave hit Kyiv late on 13 October. Its primary target was CHP-4, a key power plant in the city, and there were hits, Zelenskyy said. Ukrainian systems spotted the missiles only on approach, with no warning from partners. After a call with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Zelenskyy wrote that Ukraine had not been warned for the second time. On 13 October, Trump said the US was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
A Russian strike also hit a high-rise in Desnianskyi district. Rescuers saved 16 residents, the State Emergency Service reported, and three women were killed there, the Kyiv City Prosecutor’s Office said. The prosecutor’s office counted 19 injured in the building, including a girl officials described as seven or eight, and five more hurt by shattered windows next door. Across Kyiv, the evening and morning attacks killed four people and injured 25, the prosecutor’s office said, while Suspilne counted 32 injured.
The second wave came early on 14 October and hit several of the capital’s energy facilities, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. It killed one person in Holosiivskyi district, he added. Russia attacked all three of Kyiv’s combined heat and power plants and key facilities in Kyiv Oblast that power the capital, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. Energy company DTEK reported emergency outages in five Kyiv districts.
Damage and demands
Zelenskyy reported damage to facilities and equipment at 26 elements of the power system and at four oil and gas facilities. At least 600,000 people lost electricity, he said, and outages could grow. He called the strike deliberate and said Russia had never before shown such demonstrative disrespect toward America.
He asked Trump for strong sanctions under the Lindsey Graham sanctions law, which he said was recently passed and signed. He also asked for additional Patriot interceptors.
Read also
- US continues sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Trump says amid Russia deal backlash. Questions remain over missed warning for latest attack
- Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms
- Hours after Trump declared an energy ceasefire, Russia hit Kharkiv power plant, one of 200-plus strikes on Ukraine’s grid this week, Zelenskyy says

articles.title: Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s power grid
articles.body:
- Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at Ukrainian energy sites overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power, Zelenskyy said.
- Zelenskyy asked Trump for strong sanctions under the Graham law and more Patriot interceptors after the strike hit infrastructure covered by Trump’s ceasefire.
Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions at Ukraine’s energy and critical infrastructure overnight into Oct. 14, knocking out power to at least 600,000 people days after President Donald Trump announced a halt to strikes on energy facilities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy said that the attack targeted Kyiv, the surrounding Kyiv region and Kharkiv, and damaged equipment at 26 facilities in Ukraine’s power system and four in the oil and gas sector. He warned that outages could spread further and said there were dead and injured, without giving numbers. Repair crews, power company staff and the State Emergency Service were working to restore supply on Wednesday morning.
Zelenskyy described the ballistic missile salvo as aimed specifically at the energy infrastructure covered by the ceasefire Trump announced on Truth Social on Oct. 11, and called the scale of the strike deliberate and demonstrative.
“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” said Zelenskyy.
Moscow never confirmed accepting Trump’s energy ceasefire, and its scope remained disputed after the announcement, with a White House official telling Axios that the proposal initially covered oil refineries, while power plants and electricity grids might follow later. Zelenskyy told Fox News on Oct. 12 that Ukraine had held off on striking Russian energy facilities after the announcement, while Russia kept hitting Ukrainian gas and power sites. Ukraine’s charge d’affaires in Washington, Denys Sienik, said Russia had struck electricity generation and transmission facilities more than 200 times in the week before the announcement.
“Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation,” said Zelenskyy.
Ballistic missiles are the hardest part of a Russian strike package for Ukraine to stop, because they fly too fast and too high for most of the country’s air defenses, and Ukraine relies mainly on U.S.-made Patriot systems to intercept them. Zelenskyy asked Washington and other partners for additional packages of Patriot interceptors, saying no country should be left alone against Russia.
He also called on Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia under the sanctions law sponsored by Sen. Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed on Sept. 18 and which gives the president authority to raise tariffs and restrict Russian energy trade, with key measures due to take effect by Oct. 18.
“We ask President Trump to impose STRONG sanctions on Russia, especially since the Lindsey Graham bill, which was recently passed and signed into law, authorizes and regulates such measures,” said Zelenskyy.
The strike followed Trump’s Oct. 9 announcement of a deal to release Russian diesel onto U.S. and world markets, starting with 300,000 tons immediately and 500,000 tons in November, after the Treasury waived diesel sanctions until April 2027. Critics in Congress have said the arrangement gives Moscow additional revenue for the war. The White House had not responded publicly to the overnight strike by Wednesday morning, and Russia’s Defense Ministry had not commented on its targets.

articles.title: “It finances an economy geared toward total war”—Ukraine’s third president on the Russian diesel Washington just cleared
articles.body:
Viktor Yushchenko, Ukraine’s president from 2005 to 2010, has written an open letter to US President Donald Trump and posted it on Facebook on 14 October. Without naming it, the letter takes aim at the green light Washington gave Russian diesel trade five days earlier, after a call between Trump and Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin.
Russia banned its diesel exports in July amid a fuel crisis at home, after Ukrainian strikes on refineries had already cut those exports, and last week’s US waiver and the supply deal Trump announced with Moscow would put that fuel back on world markets while Russian strikes still kill Ukrainian civilians.
What Yushchenko says Russian fuel buys
Yushchenko wrote that Russian ballistic missiles, Iranian Shahed drones, and aerial bombs strike homes every day and night in Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, Dnipro, and Kharkiv. Whenever there is talk of “concessions” or deals with Putin, he wrote, the Kremlin answers with more missiles, more drones, and more bloodshed.
Trump’s Russian diesel deal, which drew fury in Ukraine, is unlikely to lower prices, experts say
Yushchenko rejected calls for Ukraine to “restrain its strikes against the infrastructure that finances and sustains Russia’s war.”
“Money paid for Russian fuel is not an abstraction called ‘commerce.’ It finances an economy geared toward total war,” he wrote.
Nuclear arms, Pearl Harbor, and Iwo Jima
Yushchenko wrote that Ukraine inherited “one of the largest nuclear arsenals in the world” and agreed to give it up, trusting the words and signatures of great powers. In his view, by signing the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, America took on a moral responsibility toward Ukraine.
He compared trade in Russian energy to America’s trade with Imperial Japan, which included strategically important materials, before the US entered World War II. Washington hoped for years to avoid a wider war in the Pacific, he wrote, but economic pressure and diplomacy could not prevent catastrophe.
Ukraine warns of “a new type of humanitarian crisis” as Russia aims at its biggest cities
Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941. America knows how dangerous it is to believe that trade can tame an aggressor, Yushchenko wrote, adding: “History taught us that lesson at a terrible price.”
He also named two men he called Ukrainian. One was Sergeant Michael Strank, whose family, Yushchenko wrote, came from Lemkivshchyna. The son of immigrants from Czechoslovakia, Strank took part in the famous raising of the US flag on Iwo Jima, according to the Marine Corps. The other was Oleksandr Silvashko, “a Ukrainian boy from the Cherkasy region,” who, Yushchenko wrote, was the first to embrace US Lieutenant William Robertson when American and Soviet forces met at the Elbe in April 1945.
“One does not negotiate with tyrants—one stops them,” Yushchenko concluded.
Read also
- Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms
- Bipartisan US senators say Trump’s Russian diesel deal conflicts with 2022 ban, as he presses Kyiv to spare Russian refineries
- Deals with dictators lead to hell: Estonia’s PM urges Europe to help Ukraine destroy Russia’s refineries after Washington eased sanctions on diesel

articles.title: In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll
articles.body:
In Ukraine the situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns.
Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued.
Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph).
Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate.
The immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal with Russia.
However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental.
Even Serhii Beskrestnov, Zelenskyy’s high-profile military technology adviser, has expressed public doubts about whether the US had paused the sharing of missile detection. “Friends, this is not the first time that the launch of an S-400 has not been detected,” he posted on Monday. “We should not jump to conclusions.”
However, there has now been an absence of incoming warnings for two days in a row. The second of these was in tandem with the unexpected throttling of Starlink, a system supplied by Musk with the approval of the US military.
So it is hardly reassuring against the backdrop of White House threats, which have emerged every time a flailing Trump has tried to end the war in Ukraine.
The last time Trump paused intelligence-sharing – which is, in effect, valuable information about Russian positions and movements – was in March 2025, shortly after Zelenskyy’s infamous dusting down in the Oval Office.
“You don’t have the cards,” Trump said, as he took another away. Ukraine rapidly lost a chunk of territory it had occupied in Russia’s Kursk region before sharing was restored.
A confirmed pause this time would mark a serious breach when Ukraine is more than holding off its larger neighbour on the frontline, even as the situation on the home front is worsening.
Russia has bombed two bridges in Kyiv, gas stations, city centre buildings and out-of-town warehouses, showing little restraint as it aims to harm Ukrainian civilians while it struggles to win the conventional war.
The effect of a more permanent halt to Starlink for Ukrainian drones or anything military that moves faster than 50mph is a little more complex. Starlink is how Ukraine directs many of its mid-strike (or mid-range) drones accurately towards their targets into occupied areas behind enemy lines, critical for helping the defenders maintain the rough balance on the front.
Yet, ironically, Starlink is not used for the long-range missions that target the Russian oil refineries about which Trump is so concerned, because it has long been disabled by the company inside Russia’s internationally recognised borders.
“There’s no meaningful effect on deep-strike operations,” one Ukrainian soldier said, while conceding there could be as much as a 30-fold drop in mid-strike operations because the alternatives are 30 times more expensive. Commanders are “replanning everything”, the soldier added, and aiming to find ways to carry on missions using different technologies and techniques.
Starlink is also, more importantly – as Beskrestnov emphasised on Wednesday – used by air-defence interceptors in the most effective system to down Russia’s deadly new jet-powered Shahed drones. These are at least twice as fast as traditional piston-engined Shaheds, and Ukraine’s rate of interception had dropped to 60% in September, before recovering to 75% according to the country’s air force.
The reality, then, is that the Starlink manoeuvre may not have much impact on oil prices, and only a limited effect on Ukraine’s frontline position, while putting the country’s civilians in greater danger.
As the Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk put it: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.”
Meanwhile, diplomatically, the situation is more finely poised. It was already the case that the Trump White House had proved to be a difficult and unreliable partner. What Zelenskyy, on a visit to London on Wednesday, needs from the likes of the UK prime minster, Andy Burnham, is pressure on the US to ensure the Starlink pause and whatever is happening with intelligence-sharing does not metastasise into a deeper crisis.

articles.title: Record Zircon Barrage Targets Kyiv as Russia Fires 39 Ballistic Missiles at Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Record Zircon Barrage Targets Kyiv as Russia Fires 39 Ballistic Missiles at Ukraine
Russia launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at Ukraine overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power, while monitoring channels reported a record barrage of roughly 25 Zircon missiles aimed at Kyiv and the surrounding region.
Russian strikes on energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and Kharkiv left at least 600,000 people without electricity, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on October 14.
The Ukrainian President described the barrage as a deliberate strike on energy infrastructure that he said was specifically covered by a ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump. Zelenskyy argued that the scale of the operation represented an unusually open challenge to Washington.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Overnight, the Russians used 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and Kharkiv. A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure—the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine’s Air Force said air defenses neutralized 115 UAVs and four ballistic missiles during the barrage. The strikes nevertheless caused extensive damage, with Zelenskyy saying 26 facilities in Ukraine’s power system and four oil and gas facilities were affected.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale—Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States. Russia does not consider the American President’s statements strong,” Zelenskyy added.
Ukrainian monitoring channels also reported that Russia used a record number of Zircon missiles during the attack, with roughly 25 reportedly launched against targets in Kyiv and the Kyiv region. Ukraine’s Air Force has not yet officially confirmed the figure.
“Unfortunately, at least 600,000 people are now without power. Outages could become even more widespread. Unfortunately, there is significant damage to facilities and equipment—at 26 facilities of our power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector,” Zelenskyy stated.
He thanked repair crews, energy workers, and emergency personnel responding across the affected regions, adding that the strikes had caused deaths and injuries.
In Kyiv, the number of injured rose to 25. Among them was a 7-year-old girl in the Desnianskyi district who suffered cuts and burns to her hand.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, two people were killed and six others injured, while a business in Dnipro was damaged. Two more people were wounded in the Khmelnytskyi region, where a gas station was hit and a fire broke out at an industrial facility.
That brings the confirmed toll from the locations reported so far to at least two dead and 33 injured.
Zelenskyy called for a forceful international response, arguing that Moscow had rejected an opportunity for de-escalation.
“We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond—and to respond forcefully. Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation,” he said.
The Ukrainian leader specifically appealed to Trump to impose stronger sanctions on Russia, pointing to recently enacted legislation backed by US Sen. Lindsey Graham.
“We ask President Trump to impose STRONG sanctions on Russia, especially since the Lindsey Graham bill, which was recently passed and signed into law, authorizes and regulates such measures. The American President has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor,” the Ukrainian President wrote.
He also renewed Ukraine’s request for additional Patriot interceptor missiles as Russia expands its use of ballistic weapons, which are among the most difficult threats for Ukrainian air defenses to stop.
“We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine. It is entirely fair for us to tell the United States, Europe, and all our partners that no country in the world should be left alone to face such a deranged and pro-war actor as Russia,” Zelenskyy concluded.
Earlier, the Ukrainian President stated that Ukraine has refrained from striking Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities for two consecutive days following US President Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire, while Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Russia launches 39 missiles, 128 UAVs at Ukraine; 4 missiles, 115 drones downed or suppressed – Air Force
articles.body:
Russian forces on Wednesday overnight deployed 39 missiles and 128 drones of various types against Ukraine, of which air defense forces shot down or suppressed four missiles and 115 UAVs, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"On the night of October 14 (from 18:00 on October 13), the enemy launched a massive combined strike against Ukraine using strike UAVs and 39 missiles of various types approaching targets on a ballistic trajectory," the Air Force said in a message on Telegram.
In total, the radio-technical troops of the Air Force recorded 167 air attack weapons – 39 missiles and 128 drones of various types.
According to preliminary data as of 09:00, air defense shot down or suppressed four missiles and 115 enemy UAVs, including 59 jet-powered drones. According to the Air Force, this accounts for 90% of the total number of strike UAVs.
Russian forces used Iskander-M, KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Oniks missiles, as well as Shahed strike drones, including jet-powered ones, Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera, Italmas, and Parodiya-type decoy drones.
The main directions of the strike were Kyiv, Kyiv region, and Kharkiv region. According to the Air Force, a key feature of the attack was the simultaneous deployment of various air attack weapons from multiple directions, along with a large number of ballistic missiles targeting energy infrastructure facilities.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
According to preliminary information as of 09:00, impacts of missiles and strike UAVs were recorded at 22 locations, with falling debris from intercepted targets recorded at eight locations. Some Russian missiles failed to reach their targets.
As of the time of publication, the attack was ongoing, with Russian strike drones remaining in Ukrainian airspace.

articles.title: Iran and US on brink of war as Russian mediation falters
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran and US on brink of all-out war as Russia fails to break diplomatic deadlock
Diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between Iran and the United States remain deadlocked despite continued exchanges of messages and mediation attempts, raising fears of a renewed military confrontation as both sides step up their threats and preparations.
Qatar and Pakistan have continued efforts to bring Tehran and Washington back to the negotiating table, but little progress has been made as tensions escalate in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks on vessels attempting to use non-Iranian shipping routes have increased.
The diplomatic stalemate comes amid growing US threats and reports of a possible Israeli attack on Iran ahead of Israel's parliamentary elections on 27 October.
Iran, meanwhile, has placed its military on heightened alert, conducting new missile tests in recent days and threatening to unveil additional weapons.
Tehran has also warned Washington and regional governments that another round of war could trigger retaliation across a wider geographical area, including potential ground incursions.
The renewed fighting between Yemen's Houthi movement and Saudi Arabia has further complicated the regional situation, with observers linking the escalation to the wider confrontation between Iran and the US and Israel.
Russia's mediation efforts falter
Russia entered the diplomatic efforts around a week ago, with the Kremlin announcing that President Vladimir Putin had conveyed Tehran's proposals for ending the war with the United States to US President Donald Trump.
According to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, Putin discussed his forthcoming telephone conversation with Trump during a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan last week, on the sidelines of a summit of Commonwealth of Independent States leaders.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said on Monday that Pezeshkian had clearly outlined Tehran's position to Putin, including its seven-day proposal for resolving the conflict and other issues surrounding the negotiations.
However, Baghaei stopped short of describing Russia as a formal mediator.
"Technically speaking, in the strict sense of the word, Pakistan and Qatar are still playing the role of actual mediators between Iran and the United States," he said.
He added that Tehran welcomed diplomatic efforts by friendly countries, noting that consultations with Moscow on the nuclear issue and other matters were longstanding.
Iranian analyst Ali Gholhaki told The New Arab that Russian diplomacy was proceeding with "weak and lacklustre steps".
He argued that Moscow was attempting to link efforts to resolve the Iran-US conflict with negotiations over the Russia-Ukraine war, hoping that both disputes could be addressed simultaneously.
This, he suggested, explained Russia's more active diplomatic involvement.
Gholhaki said Iran had demonstrated flexibility, but warned that the current regional military positioning suggested another war was considerably more likely than a diplomatic settlement.
He said a new wave of military escalation could erupt at any moment, although Washington appeared reluctant to become embroiled in a full-scale war before the US congressional midterm elections in November.
According to Gholhaki, the Trump administration would prefer to postpone any expansion of the military confrontation until after the vote.
What could another Iran-US war look like?
Iranian military analyst Mehdi Bakhtiari told TNA that another war was a strong possibility, although he expected any confrontation to be relatively short and extremely intense.
He argued that Washington might attempt another military campaign to secure concessions from Tehran and overcome the strategic difficulties it had encountered in its confrontation with Iran.
Bakhtiari said the US and Israel had already fought two wars against Iran, inflicting substantial damage and losses but failing, in his assessment, to achieve their strategic objectives.
Instead, he argued, they had encountered new challenges, particularly the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz and the resulting rise in global energy and fuel prices.
He suggested that another military campaign could differ significantly from previous confrontations, with attacks potentially concentrating on Iranian nuclear facilities and the country's southern regions.
A central objective, he said, would likely be securing the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Bakhtiari also warned that Iran had prepared new military strategies for such a scenario.
These could include intensified attacks on US naval vessels, particularly destroyers, following incidents in recent weeks in which Iranian forces had fired towards American warships.
He also raised the possibility of Iranian attacks against a larger number of US military bases across the region, particularly in the United Arab Emirates.
According to Bakhtiari, Iranian military planners believe that targeting US interests in the UAE could significantly increase the costs of further escalation for Washington.
He said Iran's military establishment had spent recent weeks rebuilding its missile and air defence capabilities in preparation for a potential confrontation at sea.
Bakhtiari added that both Iran's political elite and wider public increasingly regarded another round of fighting as likely.
Deep divisions over terms for peace
Masoud Foroughi, former editor-in-chief of the conservative Iranian newspaper Farhikhtegan, said the approaching US and Israeli elections were closely connected to calculations about the military confrontation with Iran.
Speaking to TNA, he argued that the war had not ended in the conventional sense but had instead changed its form and geographical scope.
From Tehran's perspective, he said, the conflict would end only when Washington accepted that military force could not fundamentally alter Iran's political system or its behaviour.
Washington, by contrast, was seeking what he described as Iran's complete surrender, whether through military pressure or diplomacy.
Foroughi said the gap between the two sides' demands was so wide that negotiations under current conditions were unlikely to bridge it.
He compared the situation to two parties standing 50 kilometres apart without any means of communication, arguing that even a distance of one kilometre would be too great for them to hear one another.
As a result, he said, the outcome would continue to depend largely on developments on the ground and each side's political, economic and social ability to withstand pressure.
Foroughi argued that the increasingly aggressive rhetoric from Washington and Tehran was intended to influence each other's strategic calculations.
Regardless of whether Trump intended to launch another direct military campaign before the November elections, he said, the administration was seeking to maintain sufficient pressure to force Iran to reconsider its position.
He concluded that diplomacy would only become effective when the costs of continuing the war became sufficiently high to compel Washington to halt its military campaign.

articles.title: “Trump and Musk must be held accountable”: US senator warns Starlink network failing over Ukraine could cripple its shield against Russian missiles and drones
articles.body:
US Senator Richard Blumenthal, a co-author of the Russia sanctions law named after Lindsey Graham, has issued a sharp statement on the latest developments in Ukraine. He says that President Donald Trump and SpaceX chief Elon Musk should be held accountable for reported Starlink failures that could cripple Ukraine’s defense.
On 14 October, Ukraine’s military reported a Starlink disruption that halted its operations. It happened at the same time the country’s air defense stopped receiving intelligence on a Russian ballistic strike that killed three people in Kyiv. Both failures came right after the US struck a diesel deal with Russia, letting low volumes of fuel into global markets and America while pressure grew on Ukraine to stop hitting the Russian oil refineries that raise the cost of the war.
"Reports of Starlink failing in Ukraine are deeply alarming— potentially crippling air defense against Russia’s murderous missiles & drones. Trump & Musk must be held accountable," he says.
When the network falters, the war feels it
The alarm rests on how completely Ukraine leans on the system. SpaceX has reportedly throttled the StarShield military package Ukrainian drones use, with connections dropping once the drones move at speed, and breaking a series of missions.
Ukraine neither owns nor controls Starlink, and the latest limits revived long-running fears that its battlefield lifeline can be dialed down from outside the country.
Blumenthal’s demand sits inside a broader revolt in Congress. A bipartisan group of 12 senators wrote Trump on 13 October urging him to rescind his deal letting Russian diesel back to market, calling the Treasury’s General License No. 135 a gift to Moscow that should be withdrawn.
They pressed him instead to use the Graham-Leach-Bliley Act he signed in September to squeeze Russia and its enablers, above all, China.
"If there's one lesson from Trump's mindless warmongering, it's that we need to break our dependence on foreign imports of fossil fuels & embrace alternate sources of energy," he said.
Read also
- Ukraine’s anti-corruption bodies, whose independence EU made condition for membership, have clawed back $5.1 million for state budget
- Ukraine blocks Russia from outflanking its fortress cities in Donbas, retaking 277 square kilometers and hitting 8,000 Russian troops
- “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government”: Musk says Trump, not SpaceX, is behind cut hitting Ukraine

articles.title: What is Starshield, SpaceX's military version of Starlink?
articles.body:
What is Starshield, SpaceX's military version of Starlink?
Elon Musk’s SpaceX restricted “military-grade” Starlink services overnight into Wednesday, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses, Ukraine reported. In response, Musk said that the US government was behind any slowdown in Ukraine's Starshield system.
The claims drew renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink – SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service – and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon. While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.
“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
What is starlink?
Starlink is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines. It is the main profit engine of SpaceX.
Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.
While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
Watch moreStarlink restriction 'no surprise' after Musk condemned Ukraine strikes on Russian data centres
Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarised version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.
The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.
Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programmes has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.
Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about $25,000 per terminal.
Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s defence ministry has told Reuters.
Other US partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

articles.title: ‘Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government.’ Musk responds to Ukraine’s complaints about restrictions on the military version of Starlink.
articles.body:
‘Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government.’ Musk responds to Ukraine’s complaints about restrictions on the military version of Starlink.
SpaceX has restored service in Ukraine for Starlink satellite terminals moving at high speeds, former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said on the evening of October 14.
“Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h [about 100 mph] is being restored. Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense. Thank you, Elon Musk. We hope for your continued support,” Fedorov said on social media.
In response, Musk said Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said. He said Starlink is a commercial service whose use is “limited to civilian or defensive activities.”
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry told journalists that SpaceX still imposes a speed limit of 161 kilometers per hour (about 100 mph) on the terminals. “However, we’re currently seeing improved connection quality at speeds of up to 160 [km],” officials said.
Ukrainian military personnel and officials said on the morning of October 14 that SpaceX had restricted service without warning for Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s armed forces on the front lines. The restrictions affected Starshield, the military version of Starlink needed to launch drones. Some even compared the damage the Starlink slowdown caused Ukraine’s armed forces to a nuclear strike on Ukraine.
The restrictions on Starshield came amid a crisis in relations between U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky.

articles.title: Meink: Operational Prototypes for MMA Drones Coming in 2028
articles.body:
The Air Force will field operational prototypes for an autonomous drone to replace its MQ-9 Reaper in 2028, Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said Oct. 14.
“We’re going to be fielding operational prototypes by ’28, and we’re just awarding the contract now,” Meink said during a panel discussion with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, other service secretaries, and senior Pentagon officials at the annual AUSA conference in Washington. “That’s the speed of what we’re fielding capability, and into production—large-scale production—starting in ’29. That is the goal.”
An Air Force spokesperson confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine that Meink was referring to the Massed Modular Aircraft, the planned successor to the Reaper.
“The autonomous fighters are already in production,” Meink said, in reference to the Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft program. General Atomics’ FQ-42A Vengeance and Anduril Industries’ FQ-44A Fury have been selected for production and are undergoing testing with the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit at Creech Air Force Base, Nev.
“Now we’re looking at essentially the autonomous strike platform, the autonomous bomber,” Meink said, referring to MMA. The aircraft is envisioned as a multimission aircraft, like the MQ-9, that can conduct strike missions as well as intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. In contrast, CCAs are currently focused on an air-to-air role paired with crewed fighters.
Meink previously announced at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference that the Air Force would field 100 MMAs by 2029 and 500 by 2032.
Air & Space Forces Magazine reported Sept. 30 that the Air Force and Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit had narrowed the field for MMA down to seven companies. An Air Force spokesperson declined to confirm any selections, but Meink said Oct. 14 that “we just awarded those contracts … in collaboration with DIU.” He did not name the specific companies or say how many finalists there are.
Sources have told Air & Space Force Magazine the seven companies still in contention are Anduril, Chaos Industries, General Atomics, Grid Aero, Otto Aerospace, Shield AI, and Swarm Aero. They will develop their MMA candidates and submit a proposal to build a prototype.
The Air Force and DIU want each MMA drone to cost $10 million for the base aircraft, not counting the sensors, weapons, or other equipment it may carry. That’s half the $20 million target price the Air Force envisions for CCAs. MMAs will also use open architecture so they could be more easily upgraded with new sensor packages or weapons capabilities.
But while MMAs will have some autonomous capabilities, they won’t be built with all the latest cutting-edge technology in a bid to keep their price down below that of CCAs. They will likely be powered by turboprop engines, for example.
MMA drones are intended to be able to fly about 4,000 miles, twice the range of CCAs, and carry a heavier payload than CCAs. But they will be slower than CCAs.
The MMA effort is part of the broader push by the Pentagon and the Air Force to field more autonomous systems at a lower cost than crewed platforms, or even the drones that are in service today. The goal is to build “combat mass” to counter China’s growing military, which Meink said is going through “the largest weapons buildup probably in the history of the world,” and to respond to the proliferation of autonomous systems in conflicts of today, and the Pentagon’s view, tomorrow.
“There’s no question that there’s a shift coming,” Meink said. “It’s adaptability, scalability, and affordability. The only way we’re going to meet the threat is with autonomous systems.”
Meink said the Pentagon will work with Congress to secure the funding needed for MMA. The Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion fiscal 2027 budget request for the Department of Defense is currently stalled on Capitol Hill. With midterm elections approaching next month, Democrats could take control of one or both chambers, which could lead to congressional gridlock, particularly surrounding the Pentagon’s request for a massive budget increase—and plans to continue that—amid the war with Iran. The DOD plans to devote tens of billions to autonomous warfare just this fiscal year.
Meink acknowledged the uncertainty surrounding the Pentagon’s budget, but expressed confidence the Air Force would be able to hit its targets for MMA.
“It is heavily dependent upon the resources we get from the Hill, but I think we are not only going to deliver significant combat capability, but we’re going to deliver quickly and efficiently,” Meink said.
“We’ve got to make sure this stuff is affordable,” Meink added, referring to efforts across the Air Force and Space Force. “We’ve got to make sure we’re buying it efficiently. And depending on how you do the comparisons, we’re talking five to 10 times cheaper to field some combat power with these autonomous systems compared to not. So it’s critically important. The good news is, in my mind, there’s no question that the leadership we have in the Air Force, in the Space Force, both military and civilian, is ready to do that. And you see that with the results already. We are integrating autonomous fighters into experimental ops units out at Creech right now, from a year from when they first flew to when we were integrating them into experimental ops units. That’s unheard of. And it only took two years to build the first one.”
The goal for MMA is similarly ambitious.
“It’s in the scalability and the producibility,” Meink said. “In many ways, cost goes with schedule. If something is super expensive, there’s a reason for it, which means it’s probably going to take a long time to build, so we’re really focusing on rapid production and scalability, which means we have to get the cost down on these systems as well.”
Meink’s comments came during a panel focused on the Pentagon’s Project Agincourt, a drive to accelerate the fielding of autonomous systems and create a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command, or AUTOWARCOM, which Hegseth announced during a speech late last month.
“The folks who acquire it need to be right there up with the warfighter at the same time who understand how to iterate it and change on and innovate on it,” Hegseth said.
Adversaries such as Russia and Iran have fielded one-way drone attacks to wreak havoc in Ukraine and across the Middle East. Ukraine has used autonomous systems to great effect to defend against Russia’s invasion. Kyiv’s ongoing and thus far successful Operation Vivaldi offensive has relied heavily on the innovative use of drones, including dropping uncrewed ground vehicles behind enemy lines.
“That’s a different battlefield,” Hegseth said. “We’ve learned a lot from Ukraine, but you can’t use everything that’s in Ukraine because of all the Chinese components involved in it. So you’ve got to be able to ensure that we take the best of that and the lessons learned … and then push it through [with] an AUTOWARCOM commander with four stars who has the ability to drive that change. So we’ve done a lot with acquisitions and a lot with industry from day one to modernize, realizing this is the future of warfare.”

articles.title: North Korea Test-Fires KN-30 Missile 910 km, Having Previously Supplied Such Missiles to Russia
articles.body:
North Korea launched a KN-30 ballistic missile on October 12, flying more than 910 km. North Korea had previously supplied Russia with missiles of this model.
North Korea’s state news agency KCNA reported the launch and published photographs.
According to Yonhap, the secretary-general of the Korea Defense and Security Forum identified the missile in the photographs of the five-axle launchers as the Hwasong-11Da-2.5, also known by its Western designation, KN-30.
It is a North Korean solid-fuel, short-range ballistic missile with a reported warhead weight of 2.5 tonnes.
Militarnyi previously reported that North Korea launched at least two ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan on October 12. According to Japan’s Ministry of Defense, one missile flew approximately 220 km, while the other traveled more than 910 km and reached a maximum altitude of around 70 km.
KCNA reported that the test aimed to assess upgrades to key components of the missile systems.
However, Pyongyang did not disclose which components had been upgraded, nor did it officially identify the missile model tested or its flight range.
Russia has reportedly received KN-30 ballistic missiles from North Korea, which it could potentially use to strike Ukraine.
The transfer was reported on August 20, after the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine responded to a request from journalists at Ukrainska Pravda. According to the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine, as of July 2026, Russia had approximately 50 North Korean KN-23, KN-24, and KN-30 ballistic missiles combined.
Russian forces have previously used North Korean KN-23 and KN-24 missiles to strike Ukraine. However, there is currently no confirmed information that KN-30 missiles have been used in combat against Ukraine.
Read more details on the development of North Korea’s missile capabilities and Russia’s role in the process in Militarnyi’s article titled “North Korea’s Missile Program with Russian Support: A New Threat to the US and Its Allies.”
KN-30 is the Western designation for the North Korean Hwasong-11C ballistic missile, also known as the Hwasong-11Da. It is an enlarged version of the Hwasong-11 missile family. The missile is powered by a solid-propellant rocket motor and is launched from a mobile ground-based launcher mounted on a five-axle wheeled chassis.
North Korea first publicly presented the KN-30 at a military parade in Pyongyang on January 14, 2021. Its first known test launches took place on March 25 of the same year. At the time, North Korea claimed the missile had a range of 600 km, although Japanese and South Korean military authorities detected a flight distance of approximately 420–450 km.
North Korea has stated that the missile can be equipped with a warhead weighing 2.5 tonnes. However, this claim has not yet been independently confirmed.

articles.title: Zelenskyy on overnight attack: Russia has never shown such disrespect for America
articles.body:
Zelenskyy on overnight attack: Russia has never shown such disrespect for America
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Russia had shown unprecedented contempt for the United States by carrying out a ballistic missile strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure facilities overnight on 13-14 October.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy said that Russian forces had used 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions on Ukraine's energy and critical infrastructure facilities in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast and Kharkiv.
Quote: "A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure – the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President. The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States. Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong."
Details: Zelenskyy wrote that at least 600,000 people are currently without electricity and the number affected could be even higher.
"We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond – and to respond forcefully. Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation. We ask President Trump to impose STRONG sanctions on Russia, especially since the Lindsey Graham bill, which was recently passed and signed into law, authorises and regulates such measures," he said.
Zelenskyy added that US President Donald Trump has all the necessary powerful tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice and pressure on Russia.
He has also called for additional interceptor missiles for Patriot air defence systems.
"It is entirely fair for us to tell the United States, Europe, and all our partners that no country in the world should be left alone to face such a deranged and pro-war actor as Russia," Zelenskyy added.
Background:
- Trump claimed that the "energy ceasefire" he had announced between Ukraine and Russia is in effect and said reports of violations needed to be checked.
- On 11 October, Trump claimed on his social media platform Truth Social that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire.
- The Kremlin said it had nothing to say about the "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump.

articles.title: Kyiv Mayor Faces Questioning as Russian Attack Triggers Fresh Water Cuts
articles.body:
Kyiv is experiencing water supply issues once more on Wednesday after another Russian attack on Ukraine’s energy grid.
The attack, comprising ballistic missiles, hit Kyiv’s CHP-4 power plant and a nine-story residential building, killing at least three and injuring 26.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Kyiv City State Administration reported reduced water pressure in multiple districts as a result of the attack, with reduced voltage preventing the pumps from operating normally.
“Due to the power outage of some water supply facilities in the capital, the pumping equipment was stopped in an emergency,” it wrote in a statement, adding that restoration work is ongoing.
According to the agency, the upper half of the Pecherskyi district has no water, while the lower part has reduced pressure. The Solomyansky and Shevchenkivskyi districts also suffer from reduced pressure.
State media Ukrinform noted that Kyivvodfond, a municipal water-management firm, has developed an online map of available manual water pumps around Kyiv.
In October, the capital reported multiple water outages caused by Russian attacks, two months ahead of the cold spell. Most Ukrainians interviewed by Kyiv Post on Tuesday named water disruptions as their top concern for the upcoming winter, as signs of an energy truce touted by Washington remain elusive, with Ukraine’s energy grid not included.
Kyiv also said it was not warned by its allies for the first wave of ballistic missile strikes amid rumors of a US intelligence cutoff.
Ukraine’s Business Leaders to Tackle War Risks and Economic Resilience at 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum on Oct. 26
Kyiv authorities urged locals to stock up on food and water on Sunday, Oct. 11, after a Russian attack left over half of Kyiv’s households without running water.
Kyiv mayor summoned
On Wednesday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko was summoned to the Verkhovna Rada to answer questions about the city’s readiness for Russian attacks on power facilities.
The session is ongoing at the time of publication, and it was preceded by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s criticism of Kyiv’s response to the impending energy crisis, arguing that the capital trails behind other regions in preparedness.
However, Klitschko has defended the city’s preparedness, noting that progress is being made through backup systems despite limited funding, as facilities can’t be fully shielded without adequate air defense.
The standoff is also part of a longstanding animosity between the two that predates Russia’s full-scale invasion.

articles.title: Ukrainian military says SpaceX restricted Starlink terminals without warning
articles.body:
Ukrainian military says SpaceX restricted Starlink terminals without warning
SpaceX has restricted the Starlink satellite communication terminals used by Ukrainian troops at the front, slowing the drones that rely on them, according to Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president, and Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to the Ukrainian defense minister and a volunteer.
The news outlet Ukrainska Pravda, citing the military, reported that the restrictions targeted Starshield, the faster military version of Starlink used by drone operators. One commander sent the outlet a video showing two Ukrainian drones climbing into the sky with their connection “dropping out,” leaving them unable to continue their mission.
A source in the Ukrainian Armed Forces told Ukrainska Pravda that standard Starlink terminals installed on drones work at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (99 mph), but that speed is not enough for some missions, which is why drone operators use Starshield, the military version of Starlink.
“Our defense forces did not receive any warning about these restrictions, and it led to the failure of a number of missions. It’s obvious that this action can’t be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” Beskrestnov wrote.
Volodymyr Zelensky said over the past two days that Western partners did not warn Ukraine about missile strikes on Kyiv. The United States told Ukraine it had not shared intelligence because of poor weather conditions, according to Politico.
The United States threatened last week to halt intelligence sharing with Ukraine and block arms deliveries unless Kyiv agreed to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, according to reporting from the Financial Times.

articles.title: Ukraine-NATO AI built to forecast Russia’s front-line drone attacks from past data and weather is ready to plug into the army
articles.body:
Ukraine and NATO have unveiled two artificial intelligence (AI) tools in Vilnius, Lithuania, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported on 13 October. One forecasts Russian drone attacks near the front and is ready to join the Armed Forces’ situational awareness systems. The other helps plan artillery fire and is still in testing.
A forecast of where, when, and which drones will fly targets the main source of losses near the front. In March, Ukraine’s military put the share of front-line casualties caused by FPV drones at up to 80%. In May, Ukraine’s drone forces commander Robert Brovdi said Russia was copying Ukraine’s model to grow its drone forces. A month earlier, Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov wrote that adding more drones no longer fundamentally changes the battlefield. The next stage, he said, is full integration of AI.
Forecasting Russian drone attacks
The NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Center (JATEC) presented both at a three-day seminar in the Lithuanian capital. NATO’s Allied Command Transformation and Ukraine’s Armed Forces built the tools with JATEC’s support.
“The solution has already been validated using real-world datasets. It has been refined and is ready for integration into the Armed Forces of Ukraine's situational awareness systems,” the ministry said.
Model No. 13 works from past data, weather, and the current battlefield situation. The ministry said it can identify the intensity of attacks, the areas, the time windows, and the types of drones with a high probability.
Ranking artillery options
Model No. 32 is a decision-support module. It tests whether artillery plans can be generated automatically. It weighs the mission’s requirements and current operational data, including available weapons, ammunition, firing positions, and constraints.
Ukraine’s new military AI does more than watch the battlefield—it helps commanders plan what comes next
First, it applies logistics, ballistics, and impact-zone parameters to throw out unworkable options. Then it scores and ranks the rest. That means less hand-based comparison, faster decisions, and a more efficient fire loop, the ministry said. The prototype is now with the Ukrainian military for trials. If the trials succeed and it is validated, it could be expanded to other units that strike Russian forces.
