articles.title: Chinese company 'helping Houthis' improve missile capabilities
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Chinese company 'helping Houthis' improve missile capabilities as fears grow for civilians in Taiz
Yemen's Houthis are trying to manufacture their own ballistic missiles, reportedly using components delivered by a Chinese company, according to information obtained by Conflict Armament Research.
The Iran-backed group has bought a range of parts from a Chinese supplier and is attempting to locally produce Tehran's Kheibar Shekan missile, a cheap, precision-guided projectile that can evade air defences.
The Conflict Armament Research report says the missile would have a range of around 1,200 miles, enabling the group to launch strikes across the Gulf, Israel, Jordan and most of Egypt.
This is one of the first indications that the group is pursuing an advanced indigenous weapons programme independently of Iran.
The report was based on information given by Yemeni authorities in July after officials intercepted two shipments last year.
China has also emerged as one of Iran's biggest suppliers of dual-use components during its war with the US and Israel.
Customs data has shown hundreds of shipments have been delivered to Iran's defence ministry in recent months, providing it a vital lifeline to maintain military production during the war.
Advance on Taiz
The Houthis continued to advance towards Taiz on Tuesday, capturing the western entrance to the city.
The country's third-largest city is a major stronghold of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government's and has been a battleground since the long-running conflict was reignited in September amid the US-Iran war.
A Houthi offensive last week saw the group encircle the city, severing its last remaining supply lines.
Military sources told Reuters that clashes were ongoing in al-Dabab, 10 km from Taiz, and on Sabr Mountain, which overlooks the southern edge of the city.
Yemeni warplanes targeted Houthi forces in Dabab and Misrakh south of the city, government forces said in a statement on Tuesday.
Civilian casualties in the city are also mounting as the Houthis advance closer to the city. Yemen's internationally recognised government said Houthi shelling and drone attacks on Monday were responsible for the deaths of at least six people, including a child, and the wounding of another 17 in the city.
It accused the group of shelling residential areas of the city, damaging seven buildings.
Meanwhile, Houthi-affiliated media said one woman was killed and four others injured in an airstrike by the Saudi-led coalition outside the city.
Fears for civilians amid siege
Yemeni civilians in Taiz are facing a "devastating" humanitarian crisis as Houthi forces step up their attacks on the blockaded city, the UN has warned.
"We're alarmed by the intense hostilities across multiple front lines, particularly in Taiz, which is having devastating humanitarian consequences for civilians," UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said at a press briefing on Tuesday.
He warned that the blockade was beginning to cause shortages and drive up the prices of goods. Wheat and flour supplies could run out in less than three weeks, he said.
Dwindling fuel supplies are beginning to affect the water supply, risking water shortages for the estimated one million people who live in the city.
The World Health Organisation on Tuesday warned that the war is causing a resurgence in cholera. One quarter of the 8000 cases declared this year have occurred in the past four weeks alone, it said.
The resumption of the conflict last month has triggered a renewed humanitarian crisis across much of the country, displacing hundreds of thousands of people and putting millions at risk of famine.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes a Sberbank data center in Russia. Meanwhile, Kyiv isn’t getting crucial missile warnings from the U.S., and SpaceX is restricting Starlink.
articles.body:
Ukraine strikes a Sberbank data center in Russia. Meanwhile, Kyiv isn’t getting crucial missile warnings from the U.S., and SpaceX is restricting Starlink.
Russia
Ukrainian drones struck a data center operated by Sberbank in the city of Balakovo in the Saratov region overnight on October 14. Ukrainian monitoring channels were the first to report the attack. Saratov Governor Roman Busargin said the strike damaged residential buildings in Balakovo and killed one person. He said all infrastructure facilities in the city are “operating normally.”
A few hours later, Sberbank First Deputy Chairman Alexander Vedyakhin confirmed the attack on the data center, saying all the bank’s systems and services are “operating normally.” The bank’s press service said no employees were injured.
This is the first Ukrainian attack on Sberbank data centers. Last week, Ukrainian drones struck data centers belonging to Yandex in the Ryazan and Vladimir regions, as well as in Kaluga.
Sberbank announced plans to build a data center in the Saratov region in 2020 and began construction the following year. The facility is expected to cover almost 60,000 square meters (about 646,000 square feet). Authorities said it would be the largest data center in Europe, and one of Sberbank’s supercomputers is being built at the Balakovo site.
Ukraine
Ukraine’s Western partners once again failed to warn Kyiv that Russia was preparing a ballistic missile strike on the capital, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on the evening of October 13. He said the missiles were detected only as they approached Kyiv. The main target was the CHP-4 power plant, one of Kyiv’s major energy facilities.
Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said partners did not warn Ukraine ahead of the first ballistic missile strike during the overnight attack on October 14, but did send notifications ahead of the three subsequent waves of strikes.
A day earlier, Zelensky had said Ukraine had received no intelligence from Western partners about the Russian missile strike on Kyiv on October 12. “Intelligence about the launch of Russian ballistic missiles helps save people’s lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is exactly what helps prevent killings when there is a warning about ballistic missiles,” he said.
According to Politico, the United States told Ukraine it had withheld intelligence about the missile strike on Kyiv on the evening of October 12 because of poor weather conditions. Ukrainian authorities fear “this might not have been the case.”
U.S. President Donald Trump, asked directly by a journalist whether Washington had stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv, answered: “No.” Earlier, the Financial Times reported that the United States had threatened to cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian oil refineries.
On the morning of October 14, Ukrainian military personnel began reporting that SpaceX had restricted the operation of Starlink satellite terminals used by Ukrainian forces at the front. The restrictions affect Starshield, the military version of Starlink, and limit the speed of drones that rely on satellite communications.
Starshield is faster and necessary for drone operators, a source in the Ukrainian military told Ukrainska Pravda, a Ukrainian news outlet. Regular Starlink, installed on drones, supports speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (99 mph), which is not enough for some missions. One commander sent the outlet a video showing two Ukrainian drones climbing into the sky and then “lose” their connection, unable to continue the mission.
“Our defense forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and that led to the failure of a number of missions. It’s obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president.
SpaceX has not yet commented on the Ukrainian military’s statements.
The war in photos. The aftermath of the missile strike on Kyiv
Russian forces struck Kyiv overnight on October 14, killing three people and injuring 21, according to the latest data. A strike hit a multistory residential building in the Desnianskyi district. Among the injured is a child.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: The Kremlin’s faction in the European Parliament: Meet the MEPs still traveling to Russia to meet politicians, officials and even spies
articles.body:
On Oct. 8, in the wake of Russia’s nationwide legislative elections, the European Parliament overwhelmingly declared the resulting State Duma in Moscow to be illegitimate — the result of a stage-managed “vote” that was neither free nor fair. Nevertheless, 42 European lawmakers voted against what might have seemed to be an obvious resolution. Even after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the European Parliament’s faction of so-called Putinversteher — a German term meaning people who profess to “understand Putin” (and often rationalize Kremlin policies) — remains firmly in place. They continue to travel to Russia, repeat Kremlin narratives, and meet with Kremlin officials and intelligence officers involved in managing foreign influence networks.
The Insider found that one in 10 current members of the European Parliament has visited Russia since the annexation of Crimea in 2014, and at least two dozen of them can be described as openly pro-Kremlin.
“Che Guevara” visits the Foreign Intelligence Service
In April of 2026, Slovak member of the European Parliament Ľuboš Blaha walked through the Russian State Duma building to a song by the band Lyube and denounced what he called Western hypocrisy. Blaha knows something about political symbolism: while serving as deputy speaker of Slovakia’s parliament, he removed the EU flag from his office and hung a portrait of the Argentinean-born Cuban revolutionary leader Che Guevara. A year later, he was elected to the European Parliament, where he receives a salary of around 10,000 euros a month.
An ally of Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, Blaha visited the State Duma as part of a trip he officially reported as having been organized by the Russian Historical Society — which happens to be chaired by Sergei Naryshkin, the head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
Although there is no indication that Blaha and Naryshkin saw one another this time around, during a 2025 visit to Moscow the two did indeed meet. Notably, unlike in the case of Blaha’s other travels to Russia, that 2025 trip was not reported on the European Parliament’s website. The trip is nevertheless confirmed both by the politician’s own social media posts and by flight data obtained by The Insider.
During the 2025 excursion, the MEP also met with lawmaker Leonid Slutsky, who has been implicated in efforts to recruit foreigners, as well as with Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov. Blaha presents himself as a left-wing politician and makes a point of highlighting that identity during his trips to Russia — for example by sending a “heartfelt revolutionary greeting” from a Lenin monument in Sochi.
It is unclear what a self-described socialist finds so appealing about Russia, where economic inequality recently reached a record level. Nor did Blaha appear troubled by the fact that Naryshkin, at whose invitation he travels to Russia to criticize the West, is financially supported by oligarch God Nisanov.
Malofeev’s operative and a lobbyist for criminal oligarchs
French member of the European Parliament Thierry Mariani is a favorite of Kremlin propaganda. Russian state news agencies quote him almost as often as they do Russian officials. TASS, for example, obtains comments from Mariani directly. He has called a Ukrainian strike on the Panorama museum in Russian-occupied Sevastopol unacceptable, criticized financial aid to Ukraine, and called for ending the war on Russia’s terms. The French politician has long and consistently sided with Russian authorities. He even criticized Alexei Navalny while the opposition leader was still alive in prison.
Mariani’s wife is known to be originally from Russia. Publicly, the Yekaterinburg native has appeared either under her maiden name, Shaikhullina, or as Irina Mariani. In official documents, however, The Insider found that she uses the surname of her former husband, Ivanko.
Officially, Irina Ivanko did not work anywhere before meeting Mariani at a Moscow restaurant and moving to Paris in the 2000s. She is now 50 and is raising their son. Her brother, Sergei Presnetsov (formerly Shaikhullin) remained in Russia. From 2023 to 2025, he served as deputy head of the administration of Verkhnyaya Pyshma in Russia’s Sverdlovsk Region.
The brother of the French politician’s wife works for the Ural Mining and Metallurgical Company (UMMC), which is controlled by the oligarchs Andrei Bokarev and Iskander Makhmudov, both of whom have interests in France. Makhmudov has also appeared as a partner of the Franco-Russian Dialogue association, which is headed by Mariani. Former Russian Railways CEO Vladimir Yakunin is also closely linked to the group.
In 2021, French authorities opened two preliminary investigations into Mariani over his involvement with the Franco-Russian Dialogue. He was suspected of corruption, breach of trust, and money laundering, as well as influence peddling; questions were also raised over whether certain benefits, suspicious financial transactions, and trips may have been compensation for his maintenance of political positions favorable to the Kremlin.
French authorities investigated Mariani on suspicion of corruption, breach of trust, and money laundering
The Franco-Russian Dialogue was created in 2004 under the patronage of Vladimir Putin and then-French President Jacques Chirac. Despite allegations that the group was politically aligned with Moscow, Mariani continued making frequent trips to Russia through at least 2024.
Leaked documents also show that paperwork for Mariani’s visit to the 2018 World Cup in Russia was handled by Maria Reshetova, an aide to Konstantin Malofeev. Malofeev, often described in Russia as an “Orthodox oligarch” because of his ultraconservative religious politics, has long overseen foreign influence networks working on the Kremlin’s behalf.
Reshetova also handled World Cup paperwork for other foreign politicians, including French MEP Philippe Olivier, members of the Le Pen family, Austrian lawmaker Johannes Hübner, German far-right publicist Manuel Ochsenreiter, Bulgarian Russophile Nikolay Malinov, Italian political operative Gianluca Savoini, and Serbian lawmaker Boško Obradović.
The French Legion in Putin’s ranks
Former French military intelligence chief Christophe Gomart last visited Russia in 2016, but the effects of that trip appear to have lasted. In 2015, he drew attention for his controversial claim that Russia had supposedly never prepared a military invasion of Ukraine, and after entering the European Parliament, Gomart continued making statements favorable to the Kremlin.
The lawmaker has spoken of the impossibility of securing a Ukrainian victory in the current war and praised what he called Russia’s “deep strategy.” He also urged France not to supply tanks to Kyiv.
Two French members of the European Parliament, Virginie Joron and Catherine Griset, helped give legitimacy to Vladimir Putin’s 2020 vote on constitutional changes, which effectively reset his presidential term count and allowed him to remain in power until at least 2036. They were among the Kremlin-friendly Western politicians who traveled to observe the vote in Russian-annexed Crimea.
Virginie Joron and Catherine Griset helped legitimize Putin’s 2020 constitutional vote extending his path to remain in power
Joron called for avoiding steps that would “add fuel to the fire” in relations with Russia and argued that, instead of sanctions, Europe should seek ways to improve and expand cooperation. She also commented on Alexei Navalny: “If a Frenchman were arrested for such a violation, that would be considered normal.”
Griset, a former personal assistant to Marine Le Pen, was involved in the corruption scandal that saw Le Pen accused of misappropriating European Parliament funds. A few years later, Griset herself won a seat in the European Parliament.
Germany’s “Alternative”
Leaked border service records show that three German members of the European Parliament — Petr Bystron, Markus Buchheit, and Tomasz Froelich — have also traveled to Russia. Froelich continued making such trips through at least 2024.
All three represent the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), reinforcing the party’s reputation for pro-Kremlin positions. Buchheit, for example, opposes sanctions against Russia and is against arms deliveries to Ukraine.
German MEPs Ruth Firmenich and Michael von der Schulenburg also continued traveling to Moscow in 2026.
The Insider has previously reported on how AfD lawmakers received money and assignments from the FSB’s Fifth Service, the branch of Russia’s security service responsible for foreign intelligence operations in the former Soviet space and political influence work.
“Brothers” from Italy
When the European Parliament debated a resolution refusing to recognize Russian elections as free and fair, Italian lawmaker Danilo Della Valle was the first to speak up against it, arguing that Russia has an opposition while citing Yabloko and the Communist Party. He apparently did not know that Yabloko had not been allowed to take part in the election. Della Valle also said Europeans should look at themselves rather than criticize Russia.
Della Valle has long criticized EU policy toward the war in Ukraine. He also defended conductor Valery Gergiev, a longtime associate of Vladimir Putin, when his concerts were canceled. Della Valle traveled frequently to Russia from 2015 to 2019.
Another frequent visitor is Antonio Decaro, the former mayor of the Italian city of Bari. He traveled to Russia while serving as mayor and during that period took part in the opening of an honorary Russian consulate in Bari.
MEP Carlo Fidanza, who represents the Brothers of Italy party, traveled to Russia in 2017 at a time when when he was director-general of Liguria’s tourism promotion agency and worked on attracting Russian tourists. Later, while serving in the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, he argued for dialogue with Russia.
Pierfrancesco Maran visited Russia in 2014 and 2018 while serving on Milan’s city council.
Dario Nardella entered the European Parliament in 2024 after previously serving as mayor of Florence. He traveled to Russia in that capacity. At the time, he opposed sanctions against Russia.
Neighborly ties
Some members of the European Parliament from countries that directly border Russia not only continue traveling there, but also openly support narratives favorable to the Kremlin.
Polish MEP Grzegorz Braun recently disrupted a European Parliament appearance by Russian opposition figures. He has called for normalization of relations with Russia and has trampled an EU flag.
Lithuanian MEP Petras Gražulis traveled to Russia from 2015 to 2018 while serving in Lithuania’s national parliament. During those years, he said Lithuania and the European Union should follow Russia’s example in combating what he called “nontraditional” relationships, a phrase commonly used in Russia as a euphemism for LGBTQ relationships.
Gražulis was even accused of bribing Russian officials. He is no stranger to appearing in criminal proceedings, and last year he was stripped of parliamentary immunity.
Estonian MEP Yana Toom makes no secret of traveling to Russia, including during the war. More broadly, she has taken a relatively measured approach to defending the interests of Russian citizens in Estonia and criticizing the Estonian authorities, while also opposing Vladimir Putin and condemning Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Three Finnish MEPs have also visited Russia since sanctions were imposed. Eero Heinäluoma traveled there in 2015 and 2016 while serving in Finland’s parliament, where he chaired a “Russia friendship group.” Putin awarded him Russia’s Order of Friendship in 2017. In 2025, Heinäluoma called for dialogue with Russia.
Eero Heinäluoma chaired a Russia friendship group and received Russia’s Order of Friendship from Putin
Katri Kulmuni traveled to Russia from 2016 to 2019 while chairing the Finland-Russia Society. She developed an interest in Russia while still in school; she studied Russian and spent time studying in St. Petersburg. In 2022, however, Russia’s Foreign Ministry severed relations with the Finland-Russia Society, accusing it of taking an “openly anti-Russian position.”
MEP Maria Guzenina also has personal ties to Russia. She is of Russian descent, though she was born in Finland, so her visits to Russia can be explained by family connections.
An Orthodox-Slavic bloc
Among the “Russia enthusiasts,” a sizable group comes from countries generally considered predominantly Slavic, Orthodox Christian, or both.
Bulgarian MEP Petar Volgin has accused EU leaders of Russophobia, saying: “While the leaders of the United States and Russia are trying to stop the war, the European Union is doing everything possible to make sure the war does not end.”
Volgin calls Russia a great country and advocates the “normalization” of relations.
Greek MEP Elena Kountoura traveled to Russia while serving as culture minister in Athens. In the European Parliament, she refused to support the creation of a tribunal to prosecute Russia.
Another Greek lawmaker, Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos, voted against condemning Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. He criticized the European Commission for, in his words, lacking money for its own citizens while having billions for Ukraine.
Cypriot TikToker Fidias Panayiotou won a seat in the European Parliament after campaigning to make politics “fashionable, interesting, and closer to the people.” But he has turned out to be closer to Moscow than to Europe, as he traveled to Russia in 2023 and 2025, including for a meeting with State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin. His most recent visit was on May 9, 2025, for Russia's annual Victory Day military parade.
Panayiotou advocates friendly relations with the Russian authorities and has linked that position to his Orthodox Christian faith.
Antonín Staněk of the Czech Republic traveled to Russia while serving as mayor of Olomouc. During that period, he also attended the ceremonial unveiling of a monument to Red Army soldiers in the Czech Republic, appearing alongside Russian representatives. Another Czech MEP, Ondřej Dostál, attended the Victory Day parade in Moscow in 2025.
Branislav Ondruš of Slovakia declined to support a tribunal against Russia. Another Slovak MEP, Milan Uhrík, called in 2024 for the creation of an EU-Russia parliamentary cooperation committee.
To Russia — without love
The Insider also identified several dozen other members of the European Parliament who visited Russia after sanctions were imposed but were not known for openly expressing sympathy for the Kremlin. In some cases, they have indeed been harsh critics of Vladimir Putin. The following MEPs had an opportunity to form their own impressions of Russia from their personal visits there:
- Li Andersson of Finland
- Vytenis Andriukaitis of Lithuania
- François-Xavier Bellamy of France
- Olivier Chastel of Belgium
- Henrik Dahl of Denmark
- Michał Dworczyk of Poland
- Christian Ehler of Germany
- Alma Ezcurra of Spain
- Markus Ferber of Germany
- Borja Giménez Larraz of Spain
- Sunčana Glavak of Croatia
- Małgorzata Gosiewska of Poland
- Hannes Heide of Austria
- Romana Jerković of Croatia
- Reinhold Lopatka of Austria
- César Luena of Spain
- Marit Maij of the Netherlands
- Fulvio Martusciello of Italy
- Liudas Mažylis of Lithuania
- Sven Mikser of Estonia
- Ștefan Mușoiu of Romania
- Hannah Neumann of Germany
- Rasmus Nordqvist of Denmark
- Jüri Ratas of Estonia
- Karlo Ressler of Croatia
- Aura Salla of Finland
- Lena Schilling of Austria
- Raffaele Stancanelli of Italy
- Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann of Germany
- Nils Ušakovs of Latvia
- Brigitte van den Berg of the Netherlands
- Kristian Vigenin of Bulgaria
- Tomáš Zdechovský of the Czech Republic
The Insider sent questions to the lawmakers named above, asking them to disclose details of their trips to Russia. Several had responded by the time the article was published.
Fulvio Martusciello said he had never been to Russia — “I never went there. Never.” However, the Kordon border-crossing database contains a record matching his first and last name, date of birth, and citizenship; it shows that he crossed the Russian border in 2015. According to the record, he flew in from Brussels, spent three days in Moscow, and returned to the Belgian capital. At the time, he was already a member of the European Parliament. Martusciello has been seen supporting Ilan Shor, a pro-Russian Moldovan oligarch. The Italian MEP is now suspected of corrupt ties to Chinese telecommunications company Huawei, and the European Parliament has stripped him of immunity.
Reinhold Lopatka said he traveled to Russia in 2018 as an observer for the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) during the presidential election. He did not disclose another trip in 2021. The Insider confirmed it was the same person as the passport numbers recorded at the border checks in 2018 and 2021 matched.
The office of Nils Ušakovs responded that:
“Mr. N. Ušakovs has been a Member of the European Parliament since July 2019. Throughout his time as a Member, he has made no visits to the Russian Federation: none official, none private. Accordingly, there are no dates, purposes or organisers to report.”
However, according to The Insider’s data, the Latvian MEP’s trips did take place while he was mayor of Riga. Latvia suspects him of corruption offenses committed while in office, but he is protected by parliamentary immunity as an MEP.
Brigitte van den Berg said she traveled to Russia to take intensive language courses.
Markus Ferber offered substantive and informative responses explaining that his visits to Russia in 2016 and 2018 were made in his capacity as deputy chairman of the Hanns Seidel Foundation, not as a member of the European Parliament. Russia now designates the foundation an “undesirable organization,” a legal status used by Russian authorities to ban foreign organizations deemed threatening to the state and to open up opportunities to prosecute people associated with them.
Li Andersson said her trips to Russia were for tourism:
“Yes I have in fact, many years before I became an MEP, been on a few short weekend trips from Helsinki to Saint Petersburg with my friends. I must admit it is so far back that I don't remember the exact dates, but I think it was in 2016 and 2019.
It was nothing official, and was of course paid for by myself.
I haven't been to Russia since then. In recent years I have been on a few trips to Ukraine, to see the horrible damage from Russian attacks with my own eyes.”
Karlo Ressler traveled to Russia for the FIFA World Cup in 2018.
Tomáš Zdechovský — who has spoken out against Kremlin agents of influence operating inside the European Union — said he had never been to Russia, either before or after 2014. Michał Dworczyk — who condemns Russia’s invasion of Ukraine — gave the same answer. The Insider doubts those statements, even if in Dworczyk’s case, the border service records could be explained by another person having the same name and date of birth as the MEP.

articles.title: Russia Hits Kyiv Power Plant With Ballistic Missiles Two Days After Trump’s “Energy Ceasefire”
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Hits Kyiv Power Plant With Ballistic Missiles Two Days After Trump’s “Energy Ceasefire”
Russian forces struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles on October 13, hitting Combined Heat and Power Plant No. 4 (CHPP-4), one of the capital’s key sources of both electricity and heating, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He said Ukraine again received no advance warning of the launch from its partners.
Emergency services are currently working to extinguish a fire at a damaged residential building following impacts across the capital.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Domestic defense detection systems identified the incoming missiles only as they approached the city.
Intelligence sources indicate that additional ballistic launches are being prepared by Russian forces. The strike hits key infrastructure despite Ukraine supporting a pause in targeting energy facilities during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Local authorities noted that continued strikes on energy facilities without advance partner warnings create ongoing danger for civilians. Efforts remain focused on supplying air defense units with necessary interceptors to respond to threats.
The previous night, Russian forces launched over 100 aerial weapons, including drones and five ballistic missiles that struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv and destroyed a residential building in Kharkiv, killing four people and injuring 41 others.
Zelenskyy stated that Ukraine received no early warning from its international partners regarding that ballistic launch either, emphasizing that advance intelligence is critical to saving civilian lives given the extremely short flight time.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Sybiha: Putin must face consequences for rejecting peace, not incentives to continue war
articles.body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha called on international partners to increase pressure on Russia through sanctions and provide Ukraine with additional air defense systems, stressing that Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin must be held accountable for rejecting peace.
“Putin has delivered yet another negative “response” to the proposal of an energy ceasefire announced by President Trump and supported by President Zelenskyy. Instead of one “yes” to peace efforts — 39 missiles and more than 120 drones,” Sybiha said on X on Wednesday, commenting on Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities.
He said energy infrastructure facilities were the main targets of the strikes. At least three people were killed in Kyiv and more than 20 others were injured. Kyiv and Kharkiv came under massive attacks, while rescue and repair crews across Ukraine were dealing with the aftermath.
Sybiha said Russia was not only attacking Ukraine but was also openly challenging the United States and showing contempt for every effort to stop the war.
“There can be no economic rewards for aggression. No sanctions relief. No concessions that allow Russia to finance its next wave of terror,” Sybiha said.
He said every dollar flowing into Russia’s war budget becomes an additional resource for attacks on Ukrainian civilians and poses a threat to transatlantic security.
Sybiha called on partners to respond to the Russian attacks by tightening sanctions, strengthening enforcement and immediately providing Ukraine with additional air defense systems.
“Putin must face consequences for rejecting peace, not receive incentives to continue the war,” the minister said.

articles.title: Russian missile hits Kiev power plant as Zelenskyy flags lack of Western warning
articles.body:
A Russian ballistic missile has struck a power plant in Kiev without Ukraine receiving advance warning from its Western allies, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine relies heavily on Western, particularly US, intelligence to detect incoming Russian attacks and help identify targets of its own.
"A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kiev. Once again, no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy wrote on Facebook.
"The main target was energy infrastructure, specifically the CHP-4. Unfortunately, it was hit."
AFP journalists in the Ukrainian capital reported hearing several blasts.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine's systems detected the missiles only as they neared the city.
"This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches," he added.
At least two people were killed in the same attack, which also struck a residential building in the Desnianskyi district, said Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko.
Around 20 others were wounded, he said.
"Energy ceasefire"
Overnight from Monday to Tuesday, Kiev residents heard explosions from Russian strikes before air raid sirens sounded, something that has occurred only rarely in the past.
On Tuesday, Ukrainian officials attributed the situation to the Russian military's use of hard-to-detect missiles or potential technical issues.
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian drone attack killed one person and damaged houses in the town of Balakovo on the Volga River in Russia's Saratov region, Governor Roman Busargin said on Telegram, without providing further details.
Balakovo is home to a nuclear power plant and a hydropower station, whose dam spans the Volga River.
On Sunday, US President Trump made a surprise "energy ceasefire" announcement on his Truth Social network, saying Russia and Ukraine had agreed to end their punishing long-range strikes on power plants and oil refineries.
Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Zelenskyy for strikes on Russian oil refineries and on Saturday suggested it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".

Balakovo is home to a nuclear power plant and a hydropower station, whose dam spans the Volga River.
On Sunday, US President Trump made a surprise "energy ceasefire" announcement on his Truth Social network, saying Russia and Ukraine had agreed to end their punishing long-range strikes on power plants and oil refineries.
Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Zelenskyy for strikes on Russian oil refineries and on Saturday suggested it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".

articles.title: Russian authorities move to evict war refugees from temporary shelters south of Moscow. Many have nowhere else to go.
articles.body:
Russian authorities move to evict war refugees from temporary shelters south of Moscow. Many have nowhere else to go.
The Tula regional government has decided to evict residents from local temporary accommodation centers. Since 2022, the centers have housed refugees from Ukraine and Russia’s border communities. Many are single mothers with children, older people, or people who only recently escaped the fighting and have yet to find work and settle in. They cannot return home: The war continues where they lived, and many homes and even entire communities have been destroyed.
Journalists from the Bereg cooperative spoke with residents of one temporary accommodation center in the Tula region about how they became refugees and what they expect after eviction. Meduza is translating their report in full.
‘We’re all pleading with you not to throw us out on the street’
The parking lot outside a health resort in the Tula region is packed with cars bearing license plate codes rarely seen here. “180” and “181” designate the annexed Donetsk and Luhansk People’s Republics. The rarest code is “188.” Those plates were issued in the Kharkiv region during the six months in 2022 when Russia occupied part of the region.
Schoolchildren play on swings outside two buildings that were temporarily converted into a refugee accommodation center just two years ago. Pine trees surround the courtyard. Adults sit on benches under plastic canopies, smoking and talking.
These residents usually live in the neighboring complex, which has operated as a temporary accommodation center since 2022. In the summer, management moves them out and gives the better rooms to tourists and people attending forums held here. Those guests pay 8,000 rubles a night for the cheapest two-person cottage.
The refugees praise the accommodations. Their only complaint is the food: Cooking in the rooms is prohibited, and the cafeteria food is sometimes undercooked or spoiled.
In May 2026, the Tula regional government issued a decree requiring all refugees to leave temporary accommodation centers by September 1. Only a few categories of residents were exempt.
Residents say they were threatened with eviction by OMON riot police if they did not leave voluntarily. The refugees sought help from the regional Social Protection Ministry, the prosecutor’s office, and Tula Governor Dmitry Milyaev. Then they recorded a video appeal to Vladimir Putin.
Shortly after it was published, officers from Russia’s Federal Security Service came to the resort, residents told Bereg. “They searched all of us from top to bottom. They went through my entire phone. They asked: Who are the activists? Who are the traitors? Who do you support? How do you feel about the special military operation? What do you think of the president?” says one refugee, who asks not to be named.
Residents received perfunctory replies to their complaints about the eviction. But the deadline for leaving the resort was extended — first to October 1, then to October 15. In early October, the center’s management gathered the residents and told them there would be no further extensions.
The refugees have been unable to obtain any official documents explaining the grounds for their eviction. The prosecutor’s office had asked residents to supply those documents before it would look into the matter. Local officials said the residents were being evicted due to insufficient funding.
On October 4, the refugees recorded another video appeal to the president. About 70 people lined up in a clearing beneath the pines. The previous video had been filmed on the resort’s front steps, but this time, management asked them to ensure the center could not be identified in the footage.
Anna, 39, and Nataliya, who is about 50, address Putin on behalf of all the center’s residents. “Our communities are closed off and completely destroyed. We have nowhere to go back to,” Nataliya says. Her voice trembles slightly, and she breaks off midsentence. A dog barks nearby: Some residents managed to bring their pets out amid the shelling.
Nataliya continues the appeal. She says eviction will cost people both their housing and their temporary residence registration at the center. Without it, they will have trouble finding formal employment, enrolling their children in preschools and schools, and obtaining medical care.
Anna says refugees from the Kharkiv region will face particular hardship: They have neither official recognition as forcibly displaced people nor permanent residence registration in Russia. “We’re all pleading with you not to throw us out on the street,” she says as she finishes her appeal.
The participants disperse. Some recall that their previous video was mistaken for an AI-generated fake. I ask whether they believe the appeal will work. “We’ve already appealed to every authority there is!” one of them says in despair.
‘We supported the Russians so much — you wouldn’t believe it. But after living here for four years… It hurts that nobody wants us’
The resort currently houses 246 refugees. Roughly as many live in two neighboring temporary accommodation centers. All fled shelling in Russia’s border regions or destroyed towns and villages in the Donetsk, Luhansk, and Kharkiv regions. Some are still afraid to return home; many simply have no home to return to.
At the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Russian army captured part of the Kharkiv region, including Izium, Kupiansk, and Vovchansk. But by September 2022, during Ukraine’s counteroffensive, Russian forces had retreated — or, as the center’s residents cautiously put it, “redeployed.”
The number of cases in Ukraine involving collaboration with Russian forces is growing: Even residents of formerly occupied territories who worked as cleaners or building attendants and agreed to cooperate with Russian authorities are going on trial. Some refugees at the Tula center say they worked as teachers or distributed humanitarian aid, then found themselves on lists of “collaborators” in Ukrainian Telegram channels.
Tatyana worked on the railroad for many years. “I worked the switchboard: They moved railcars back and forth. And we were basically working with the Russian military,” she says. When Ukrainian forces entered Kupiansk, Tatyana and her husband were attending a funeral in another city. After learning that Kupiansk was back under Ukrainian control, they fled to Russia with just the clothes they were wearing and their passports.
“We supported the Russians so much — you wouldn’t believe it. But after living here for four years… It’s not exactly disappointment, but it hurts. It hurts that nobody wants us. Wherever you go, they tell you, ‘You’re one of us.’ And then it turns out we’re not,” Tatyana says with a sigh.
The Tula regional authorities are promising to reimburse rental expenses for families with three or more children and refugees receiving old-age pensions. People living alone will receive up to 20,000 rubles, and families up to 30,000.
But to apply for the payments, refugees need a rental agreement. Finding a landlord willing to sign a formal lease, pay taxes on the rental income, and then wait while local authorities review the tenants’ application is not easy.
Residents say they know of cases in which assistance was denied without justification: “There’s simply no money in the budget.” Many residents are also older people living alone who have never rented a home themselves.
Anyone who moved into a temporary accommodation center after July 1, 2025, is ineligible for the payments. The refugees estimate that one in five residents falls into that category. Some arrived as recently as September 2026. They are now being asked to sign an agreement to leave the center by April 1, 2027.
Marina, 50, fled the town of Yampil in the Donetsk region with her husband, Sergei, and their 15-year-old daughter, Daryna. They spent three and a half years living in a dugout Sergei had built under a shed. Daryna suffered a mild concussion when a drone struck the shelter.
Marina did not want to leave for Ukrainian-held territory. “Yes, I speak Ukrainian, and so does my daughter. But I’m Russian. I wasn’t going to live there looking over my shoulder and letting people push me around. [In a country] where they send men off as cannon fodder,” she says.
The family did not escape the combat zone until February 2026 and arrived at the temporary accommodation center in April. Sergei now works at the neighboring hotel complex, while Marina is currently unable to work because of health problems. In six months in Russia, the family has saved just 35,000 rubles — not enough to rent a home or move elsewhere. They do not even have warm clothes.
Marina is angry at indifferent officials who “sneer” when they see her Ukrainian documents. She emphasizes that she and her parents are Russian, and that she was desperate to get to Russia. But so far, she has been unable to obtain any compensation. “It hurts to spend all those years hiding from the Nazis, lose your health, have your daughter miss out on her childhood — and end up like this,” she says with a sigh.
Residents are certain it will be hard to find a landlord willing to arrange temporary residence registration for them. Without permanent registration in their passports, they believe it will be almost impossible.
The refugees insist that when they moved in, they were promised they could stay until the war ended. Still, those whose homes were destroyed would like to leave — if they received compensation to rebuild.
‘They came to our homes and destroyed everything’
Temporary accommodation centers in other regions remain open. Residents of the Tula centers have already learned that some even have vacancies. But they need authorization from the regional administrations to move in and have not received it.
Refugees who have received Russian passports do not understand why they face contempt from officials, bureaucratic hurdles, and scrutiny from the security services in their new homeland, which claimed the places they lived as its own.
“They [the officials] say: We want you to integrate into the Russian Federation. When did the DPR and LPR become part of the Russian Federation? When Putin signed the law in 2022. So we’re already integrated! I understand that every country has its own laws, and I accept that. But people were desperate to come here. They were desperate to come home,” says a refugee from the Donetsk region.
Balloons are taped to the walls of Anna’s room. She fled Kupiansk. The family recently celebrated her daughter Rita’s 12th birthday, then her mother Irina’s 62nd. For both, it was their fourth birthday away from home.
The Russian army entered Kupiansk without a fight in the first days of the invasion. Anna lived near a bridge that was repeatedly shelled. The family spent all of March in the basement.
During that time, Anna developed anemia and thyroid problems — she was later diagnosed with hypothyroidism. Rita also began getting sick. Rumors were circulating in Kupiansk that Russia would not hold the city and fierce fighting would soon break out. In April 2022, the family decided to leave.
Anna says she was in such a hurry that she did not even take her daughter’s birth certificate, and Rita was so nervous at border control that she forgot her mother’s name. But the border guards let them through: The photo gallery on Anna’s phone was full of pictures of Rita, so the guards believed them.
The family spent the next eight months in Belgorod. Without residence registration, Anna and Irina could not get passports, and schools would not enroll Rita. Eventually, Anna found a job and met a colleague who helped them arrange temporary registration. Other refugees had to pay for it: At the time, six months of temporary registration in Belgorod cost 9,000 rubles, Anna says.
The family’s life was starting to improve, but in late 2022, a Ukrainian missile hit a neighboring house. “It sliced the roof clean off, like a knife through butter,” Anna says. After that, the family decided to move to Voronezh.
In 2023, Irina was diagnosed with breast cancer, and the family was offered a place at a temporary accommodation center in the Tula region. Anna’s brother Andrei and his family were already living at another center in Tula.
Anna says he stayed in Kupiansk until September 2022 and “left the city in a tank.” Andrei was at work across the river when the bridge connecting the two parts of the city was destroyed. Ukrainian forces entered the area where his wife and their 1-year-old child were still at home. Andrei did not want to leave his family behind, but Anna says the Russian soldiers insisted: “Do you want to live? Then come on, [get in].” In November, Andrei’s wife and child managed to leave, traveling through Ukraine and Europe to reach Russia.
Before the war, Anna and Andrei’s family had two houses in a neighborhood of detached homes. Both are now destroyed.
In Russia, Irina underwent two operations and needed care. Meanwhile, Rita was bullied at school, so Anna switched her to a paid online school. Anna left her job to care for her mother and raise her daughter. The family now lives entirely on Irina’s pension and a child benefit — just 34,000 rubles. Anna says almost half goes toward schooling.
They were barely getting by on that money until the Tula regional authorities decided to evict the refugees. Only Irina can stay at the resort: She has a Group II disability classification.
To keep his family, which now has a second child, from ending up on the street, Anna’s brother Andrei bought an apartment with a mortgage. He used the government’s maternity capital benefit for the down payment. Anna says there was no money left for furniture, and the family is sleeping on the floor for now. The terms of his loan prevent Andrei from registering his mother and sister at his apartment.
Anna now uses the printer she bought for Rita’s schoolwork to print letters, complaints, and applications to help refugees from the Kharkiv region who have spent four years in Russia without official recognition as forcibly displaced people or compensation for their destroyed homes.
“Social services say, ‘You’ve been sitting here for four years. You should’ve saved up for an apartment.’ They also say, ‘We started from scratch too!’ But we didn’t choose to be in this situation, having to start over from scratch. They came to our homes and destroyed everything!” Anna says angrily.
‘We’ve been here all this time, and we’ll go home and get killed’
Vera Nikolayevna, 72, moved to the center from the Kursk region. She is shy about speaking to journalists: She feels others have it worse and that she should not complain.
Her village is about 60 kilometers (37 miles) from the border. She says the “incredibly loud explosions” began in the first days of the war. But Vera Nikolayevna did not consider leaving until the summer of 2023, when, she says, Ukrainian saboteurs shot up a column of Russian troops 20 kilometers (12 miles) from her home. Bereg could not confirm this account.
Her 48-year-old daughter, Olga, lived in a neighboring village and immediately drove over to her mother’s house. They packed in a hurry. Later, Olga and Vera Nikolayevna told neighbors they could take their stock of canned food — they no longer expected to return.
Vera Nikolayevna and Olga have lived at the center ever since. Vera Nikolayevna’s room is tidy, with few possessions. Photographs of relatives hang on the wall above her bed — she has three daughters and three grandchildren.
In one photograph, a young man in military dress uniform adjusts a young woman’s blond curls. Vera Nikolayevna’s grandson serves in Astrakhan. He was recently sent on a temporary assignment near Kaluga to “shoot down drones.” She speaks proudly of him and Olga. Her daughter received a “medal for supporting the special military operation”: While working at a kindergarten near the border, she spent her evenings mending soldiers’ uniforms.
Vera Nikolayevna’s house has not been destroyed, but she has been back only once since leaving, in 2025. She decided to stay, but on the very first night, an explosion woke her. “It wasn’t just a bang — I can’t even describe it. I thought the roof was gone, that everything had been blown away. We sat there and couldn’t tell whether we were alive or dead. We didn’t turn on the lights. We didn’t breathe,” she says.
In the morning, she learned that Ukrainian forces had attacked a place where Russian soldiers were sheltering. The missiles left craters and damaged neighboring houses, and Vera Nikolayevna changed her mind about staying in the village. “There are explosions and gunfire, and drones are flying around. We’ve been here all this time, and we’ll go home and get killed,” she says.
Vera Nikolayevna receives a pension of 20,000 rubles. Olga works every other day and is paying off a loan. Despite Olga’s disability, the family is not entitled to stay at the center: She has a Group III classification, while only people with Group I or II classifications are allowed to remain.
Vera Nikolayevna calculates that even with rental assistance, she and her daughter will not have enough money to live on. “The main thing is for them to let us stay here,” she says. “At least until spring. Surely the special military operation will be over by spring?”
‘We just believed in Russia, believed the words “We don’t abandon our own”’
Wagner fighters took Alina, her mother Olga, and her father Nikolai out of Soledar, a city in the Bakhmut district of the Donetsk region. The fighters forbade the refugees from looking out the windows of the combat vehicle, which was covered in camouflage netting, so they would not see anything they were not meant to see.
By early January 2023, when the private military company entered the city, Soledar had suffered extensive damage. Alina had already spent six months sleeping on the floor in the hallway; the family cooked over fires in the courtyard. Her grandmother died of cardiac arrest around that time, and they buried her amid the shelling.
Ukrainian forces repeatedly offered to evacuate the family, but they refused. Nikolai turned 58 in 2022 and was still eligible for conscription. He had worked as a miner for almost his entire life, Alina’s mother was a senior laboratory technician, and Alina managed facilities at a company. The family loved their city, lived comfortably, and did not want to lose everything they had built up.
Olga, Alina, and Nikolai were waiting for Russian forces to arrive. “We just believed in Russia, believed the words ‘We don’t abandon our own.’ Those exact words,” Alina says.
Alina and her parents did not want to leave Soledar with the Wagner fighters either. The family even offered to sign a statement accepting responsibility for their own lives, but the fighters would not listen and would not let them leave the basement to collect belongings from home. Fortunately, Alina always carried a backpack with their documents, and they were allowed to take their cat, Maruska.
Alina and Olga both recall the soldiers’ assurances: “Don’t worry, everything will be fine. Russia will welcome you there and give you everything. A shower, clothes, shoes, passports — they’ll take care of everything.” The family left Soledar confident they would be welcomed in Russia.
Disappointment came quickly. In Pervomaisk, a city 35 kilometers (22 miles) from Soledar, the evacuees were given a sack of sugar and flour for food. In Torez, 80 kilometers (50 miles) from Soledar, the local authorities did not welcome the displaced people either. “And that’s when we realized: Nobody wants us,” Olga says.
Despite his years of work as a miner, Nikolai was awarded a 10,000-ruble pension in Russia. Alina found work at a café in Torez, while her parents went to the Vladimir region to earn money. Her father died there of cardiac arrest in 2024. Olga returned to her daughter.
By June 2025, the temporary accommodation center in Torez had closed, and the women moved to the Tula region. Both started working and saving money. Alina developed rheumatoid arthritis. In the DPR, she was given expensive steroid medication, but her supply is running out. To receive the medication in Russia, she needs to have her disability officially recognized, which requires medical examinations she must pay for.
The women are upset that Russia has not welcomed people it claims as its own. Alina has changed jobs several times, and at every workplace, colleagues called her “khokhlushka,” an anti-Ukrainian slur. Sometimes people she spoke with blamed her and all of Donbas for starting the war.
Alina hopes they will be allowed to stay at the center at least until spring so they have time to save enough to rent a home in the Tula region. If that does not happen, Alina and Olga plan to move to Svitlodarsk, a city 35 kilometers (22 miles) from Soledar. Svitlodarsk is being shelled, but rent there is cheap.
Alina and Olga take turns showing a video from an unidentified Ukrainian Telegram channel. It shows part of a residential building in Soledar collapsing after a strike. Their apartment was in that very building.
Olga cries. She does not have a single photograph of her loved ones left. In a choked voice, she says: “We understand that nobody wants us. They took our lives away. Our bodies are still here, but our lives are gone.”
* * *
On October 5, regional officials visited the center. They offered to let the refugees continue living there if they paid. They did not give exact prices but said food would cost 300 rubles a day.
The residents who spoke with Bereg fear that staying at the center will cost about as much as renting a home in the Tula region. They do not have that kind of money.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Ukraine warns of “a new type of humanitarian crisis” as Russia aims at its biggest cities
articles.body:
Ukraine is drafting crisis scenarios for November to March as Russian strikes target the country’s biggest cities, Head of the Presidential Office Kyrylo Budanov said on 13 October after chairing a meeting with donor-country diplomats and humanitarian organizations. His deputy Iryna Vereshchuk warned the same day that this winter may bring a new type of humanitarian crisis. She asked donors to be ready with fast extra funding.
Russia has struck Ukraine’s grid deep into winter before: last February, it launched more than 500 missiles and drones as temperatures fell below −20°C. Strikes have continued despite a US-announced energy truce Moscow has not confirmed. Kyiv now wants donors ready to pay for the humanitarian fallout in advance.
Crisis scenarios for November to March
The core task is clear crisis scenarios and synchronized response plans for that period, Budanov wrote. The government is building a baseline threat scenario through the State Emergency Service, while the military and intelligence will provide a risk assessment.
“The available resource must be concentrated where people will have the hardest time,” Budanov wrote.
Ukraine, he added, must hold its rear as reliably as the Defense Forces hold the front line.
What officials mean by a new type of crisis
A war of rear areas is underway, Vereshchuk wrote. Russia is changing tactics in an attempt to deepen the humanitarian crisis, especially in Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa, and Dnipro, she added.
Vereshchuk did not define what makes the crisis new, but she tied her warning to the big cities.
“This winter, it is the big cities that may become the testing ground of our national resilience,” she wrote.
Humanitarian organizations must adapt their plans to protect and support civilians, Vereshchuk wrote. Donors, she said, must be ready to provide additional crisis-response funding quickly.
The capital lags behind
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on 13 October that even border and frontline oblasts were ahead of Kyiv on resilience plans as of mid-October. Even single hits by Shahed attack drones can cut power and water across much of the capital, he noted. He also began consultations on urgent security and management steps to fix the situation in the city.
Three days after Washington announced an energy ceasefire, Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid
Russia carried out more than 200 strikes on Ukraine’s power generation and transmission in the week to 11 October, Zelenskyy said. Overnight on 14 October, Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at energy and critical infrastructure. The barrage left at least 600,000 people without power, Zelenskyy said.
Read also
- Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches
- US continues sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Trump says amid Russia deal backlash. Questions remain over missed warning for latest attack
- Five Russian bombs kill 17 in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia next day after Trump lets Russia ship first 300,000 tonnes of its diesel

articles.title: Ex-President Yushchenko calls on Trump to abandon trade with Russia, concessions to Putin
articles.body:
Third President of Ukraine Viktor Yushchenko addressed an open letter to President of the U.S Donald Trump, criticizing the authorization of trade in Russian diesel fuel and calling for the fulfillment of security commitments under the Budapest Memorandum, the politician published the appeal on Facebook on Wednesday.
"It looks wild and painful when calls are heard for Ukraine to 'stop,' instructions on whom we should elect and how to live, or when a green light is given to trade in Russian diesel. Every dollar from this diesel is a purchased missile that will strike our homes tomorrow," Yushchenko stressed in his appeal.
According to the former president, trading with an aggressor country during wartime directly finances its war machine, while talks by the U.S about the possibility of concessions or agreements with Vladimir Putin immediately provoke the Kremlin into new strikes with ballistic missiles and guided aerial bombs against residential neighborhoods in Kyiv, Zaporizhia, Odesa, Dnipro, and Kharkiv region.
Yushchenko reminded the head of the White House that following the collapse of the USSR, Ukraine voluntarily surrendered the world's third-largest nuclear arsenal in exchange for official guarantees of security, sovereignty, and the inviolability of borders, sealed by the U.S signature on the Budapest Memorandum in 1994.
In addition, the former Ukrainian head of state drew a historical parallel with Washington's policy in the 1930s, when the U.S supplied oil to Imperial Japan for the sake of preserving stability, which ultimately led to the Japanese air attack on Pearl Harbor using American fuel. At the same time, the politician pointed to the joint struggle of Ukrainians and Americans in World War II, mentioning Ukrainian-born Sergeant Michael Strank, who raised the US flag over Iwo Jima, and Ukrainian Alexander Silvashko during the historic meeting of allies on the Elbe on April 25, 1945.
Concluding the appeal, Yushchenko emphasized that the Ukrainian people will never yield their territory and will not succumb to Russian missile blackmail, summarizing that "one does not negotiate with tyrants – one stops them."

articles.title: Mephedrone dealer with seven convictions kills six Russian drone recon troops during Kupiansk offensive, including a secret FSB operative
articles.body:
A court in Russian-occupied Donetsk is currently hearing a criminal case against Russian serviceman Alexei Korolev, who is charged with murdering two or more people, along with large-scale extortion. The Insider found that Korolev is a repeat offender who went to the front from prison, where he was serving an 11-year sentence in a case involving large quantities of mephedrone, a synthetic stimulant drug. The Ukrainian state project I Want to Live previously identified Korolev as the gunman who killed six fellow soldiers in the Kharkiv Region one year ago. The Insider confirmed that all six victims died on the same day — Oct. 25, 2025.
I Want to Live said the men served in a reconnaissance company, but The Insider was able to uncover an additional detail: Rodion Kravets, one of those killed by the former prisoner Korolev, had served in the highly secretive 16th Center of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), which conducts signals intelligence and organizes cyberattacks.
In February 2026, the Ukrainian project I Want to Live, citing a source in the Russian army’s 68th Motor Rifle Division, reported that a former prisoner sent to the front had shot and killed six service members from the reconnaissance company of the 27th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade. At the time, there was no independent confirmation of the incident. Another hearing in Korolev’s case was scheduled for Oct. 13 in Donetsk. According to the official file, the case reached the court on March 24, 2026, five months after the six soldiers died. Korolev’s lawyer, Yekaterina Kulik, confirmed to The Insider that the case involves a serviceman. “This is a case against a serviceman. All hearings are being held behind closed doors,” she said. Kulik declined to provide further details, citing attorney-client confidentiality, but she did not deny that the case involved the killing of Russian soldiers.
A shooting during the offensive on Kupiansk
According to I Want to Live, a conflict between soldiers of Russia’s 121st Motor Rifle Regiment of the 68th Division and reconnaissance troops from the 27th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade broke out Oct. 24-25, 2025 near the village of Lyman Pershyi in the Kupiansk District of Ukraine’s Kharkiv Region. The project said the dispute began after a Russian FPV drone mistakenly attacked an all-terrain vehicle carrying soldiers from the 121st Regiment.
On the evening of Oct. 24, several assault troops went to the reconnaissance company’s command post to confront the drone operators. According to the I Want to Live source, soldiers from the 121st Regiment were intoxicated, beat the reconnaissance troops who were there, took drone-control equipment, and left.
On the morning of Oct. 25, reconnaissance company commander Yuri Davydov assembled a group of soldiers in order to recover the equipment taken by the 121st Regiment. The dispute flared again at the unit’s position. According to the Ukrainian project, Sgt. Vadim Petukhov reminded grenade launcher operator Alexei Korolev of his prison past and threatened him with sexual violence. Korolev then grabbed a weapon and opened fire. Six soldiers were killed and two others were wounded.
The incident took place during Russia’s offensive on Kupiansk. In its Oct. 24, 2025, assessment, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) cited pro-war Russian bloggers while describing offensive operations in and around the city, referring to units of the 68th Motor Rifle Division and drone operators from the 27th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade.
Six killed on the same day
The Insider checked the list of alleged victims against a database of Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine that is maintained by the independent exiled Russian publication Mediazona and the BBC. All six service members named by I Want to Live appeared in the database with the same date of death — Oct. 25, 2025:
- Vadim Petukhov, 28, a sergeant from Cherepovets in the Vologda Region;
- Dmitry Galatov, 32, a sergeant from the Tambov Region;
- Rodion Kravets, 22, a corporal from the Krasnodar Region;
- Sergei Nizovtsev, 24, a junior sergeant from Kopeisk in the Chelyabinsk Region;
- Pavel Serov, 37, a junior sergeant from the Yaroslavl Region;
- Vyacheslav Kuznetsov, 24, a corporal from the Krasnodar Region.
According to I Want to Live, reconnaissance company commander Yuri Davydov and driver Alexander Velikanov were wounded.
Elite drone operator and specialist from the FSB’s 16th Center
According to I Want to Live, Vadim Petukhov headed an FPV crew in a UAV platoon at the Rubikon Advanced Unmanned Technologies Testing Center. The Insider was unable to independently confirm that detail, but it did find photos and videos on Petukhov’s social media that appear to show him among troops wearing expensive tactical gear. Petukhov concealed his face and personal details while alive, and photos showing his face were posted on VKontakte only after his death.
The most unusual pieces of information The Insider found concerned 22-year-old Rodion Kravets. Bank application records reviewed by the outlet list military unit 71330 as his workplace and his position as “specialist.” The forms also say he began working there in June 2023. Military unit 71330 is the FSB’s Center for Radio-Electronic Intelligence on Communications, known as the 16th Center, one of the security service’s most secretive units.
According to a British government report, the FSB’s 16th Center intercepts, decrypts, and processes electronic communications, conducts technical intrusions into foreign networks, and carries out cyber intelligence operations. The European Union has also attributed cyberattacks to the 16th Center.
Kravets was later listed as a private in military unit 61899, the 27th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade, which took part in the offensive on Kupiansk. It is unclear whether he had left the FSB’s 16th Center or was serving at the front on temporary assignment. During the same period, Kravets became a defendant in a petty theft case, suggesting the prosecution may have been suspended or closed because of his military service in the combat zone.
What else is known about those killed
Another one of those killed, 32-year-old Dmitry Galatov, commanded a reconnaissance squad in the 27th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade, according to I Want to Live. In other people’s contact lists, his number was saved under names including “Dima Tambov Commander” and “Dima Tambov Unit Commander.” The only two images on his VK profile showed him in military gear holding an anti-tank guided missile system, and a picture of a character dressed as an NKVD officer. Like Petukhov, Galatov concealed his face and personal information on social media.
37-year-old Pavel Serov served as a junior sergeant in military unit 61899, the 27th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade, according to records reviewed by The Insider. He was also facing a criminal case for “intentionally destroying or damaging military property during an armed conflict or combat operations.” The investigation was suspended due to the fact that Serov was serving in the military.
Vyacheslav Kuznetsov, from the Krasnodar Region, served as a reconnaissance combat engineer, according to I Want to Live. The Insider found his page on the social network VK under the name “Vyacheslav Aliyev,” where he posted photographs of armed troops in tactical gear. His final post was dated Oct. 21, 2025 — four days before Mediazona’s listed date of death. In November, a user named Sergei Ryabokon wrote on the page: “Rest in peace, brother.”
Seven convictions and six dead
Alexei Korolev, who is accused of killing the six reconnaissance and drone troops, began his criminal career in the early 2000s. An Aug. 14, 2024, appellate ruling by the Belgorod Regional Court lists six earlier convictions handed down by courts in Vladimir in 2003, 2007, and 2011. He had been convicted of robbery, armed robbery, theft, fraud and hooliganism.
Korolev was released from prison on June 17, 2016, after serving another sentence and, according to a 2023 judgment, later joined a group involved in trafficking large quantities of drugs. Fifteen other people were charged with him. Prosecutors said the group distributed drugs through online stores and dead drops. Investigative records referred to synthetic drugs including mephedrone and substances containing alpha-PVP.
Investigators said Korolev worked as a bulk drug courier, receiving the coordinates of hidden caches from handlers and transporting narcotics between regions. In October 2020, he picked up a shipment from a cache in the Tula Region for delivery to the Moscow Region. Police stopped the car he and his wife were traveling in and found 10 packages of drugs. Korolev later admitted in court that he had helped transport the narcotics.
On Nov. 16, 2023, he was sentenced to 11 years in a special-regime penal colony for attempted large-scale drug distribution by an organized group. On Aug. 14, 2024, the Belgorod Regional Court upheld Korolev’s sentence and rejected his request for a reduction. Yet a year later, he was out of prison and carrying a weapon.
Alexei Korolev is now back in pretrial detention awaiting a verdict on murder and extortion charges.

articles.title: Russian strike on Kyiv kills three, injures over 20; parts of city lose power
articles.body:
Russian strike on Kyiv kills three, injures over 20; parts of city lose power
Russian forces struck Kyiv overnight on October 14, killing three people and injuring 21, according to data from Ukraine’s State Emergency Service.
A strike hit a multistory apartment building in Kyiv’s Desnianskyi district late on October 13, sparking a fire. The bodies of two people killed in the blaze were found. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said an 8-year-old child was among those injured. Sixteen people were hospitalized, four of them in serious condition.
In Kyiv’s Holosiivskyi district, a strike on a non-residential building killed one person and injured another, the State Emergency Service said.
Klitschko also said a massive ballistic missile strike had hit energy facilities in Kyiv and the Kyiv region, triggering power outages in the capital.
Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine’s Western partners again failed to warn it that Russia would launch another ballistic missile strike on Kyiv on the evening of October 13. He said the main target was the city’s energy infrastructure, specifically the CHPP-4 power plant, one of Kyiv’s main energy facilities.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said on the morning of October 14 that the Russian Armed Forces had carried out a massive strike on communications and energy infrastructure facilities in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and the Kharkiv region, which it said served the military-industrial complex and the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
Donald Trump announced on October 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a ceasefire in the energy sector. Volodymyr Zelensky said the Ukrainian Armed Forces had “received all the relevant orders” in connection with this. The Kremlin said on October 13 that contacts on the energy ceasefire were continuing, but there had been no changes so far.
