articles.title: Russian attacks kill at least 10, injure 91 across Ukraine over past day as ballistic missiles strike Kyiv for second straight night
articles.body:
Russian attacks kill at least 10, injure 91 across Ukraine over past day as ballistic missiles strike Kyiv for second straight night
At least 10 people were killed and 91 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia struck Ukraine with 39 missiles and 128 Shahed-type drones, regional authorities said on Oct. 14.
In Kyiv, at least four people were killed and 25 others injured in overnight missile strikes on the capital, the Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office said. At least three women were killed, and another 24 people, including a 7-year-old girl, were injured as a result of a Russian strike on a nine-story residential building in the city's Desnianskyi District. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that at least one additional victim from Kyiv's Darnytskyi District was hospitalized, and another person killed in the city's Holosiivskyi District.
"Overnight, the Russians deployed 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 strike drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media, adding 600,000 people were without power.
In total, Zelensky said Russia struck Ukraine with 39 missiles including Iskander-M, KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles from Kursk, Bryansk, Voronezh, and Rostov regions in Russia, as well as with 128 Shahed-type UAVs, including 77 jet-powered ones.
Ukraine's Air Force said it neutralized four ballistic missiles and 115 Russian drones overnight.
In Kyiv Oblast, one person was injured over the past day by Russian strikes, regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said. Civilian facilities, energy infrastructure, homes, warehouses and production facilities, and commercial establishments were hit in Russia's attacks on the oblast.
In Rivne Oblast, a Russian drone strike on a university building in the northwestern city of Rivne, injuring 25 people over the past day, Rivne's National Police branch said. Of the 25 injured, two were in critical condition, while three others are under medical examination, the police said.
In Kharkiv Oblast, over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and settlements in the surrounding region, injuring nine people, including a child, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Russia targeted the region with eight ballistic missiles, as well as multiple drones, Syniehubov said.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, three people were killed and 17 injured in Russian attacks across the region over the past day, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin.
In northeastern Sumy Oblast, one person was injured by Russian mortar shelling, the Sumy military administration said. Russian forces attacked with a wide arsenal of artillery, mortars, glide bombs, and UAVs. In total, air alert in the oblast lasted 18 hours and 36 minutes during the day.
In southern Kherson Oblast, two people were injured by Russian attacks over the past day, said regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin. Russia attacked multiple settlements in the oblast with air, drone, and artillery fire, damaging critical and social infrastructure, as well as residential areas.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, one person was killed and three injured over the past day, according to regional governor Ivan Fedorov. In total, during the day, Russia launched 1,030 strikes on 56 settlements of Zaporizhia region using artillery, UAVs, and rocket launchers, he said.
In western Lviv Oblast, Russian drone attacks injured three people over the past day, said regional governor Maksym Kozytskyi.
Russian attacks in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast killed two people and injured five others, including a child, over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
Chernihiv Oblast suffered several Russian strikes on a school and administrative building, but no casualties were reported over the past day, regional governor Viacheslav Chaus said.

articles.title: Russian strikes hit key power plant in Kyiv, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Russian strikes hit key power plant in Kyiv, Zelensky says
- Published
A key energy facility supplying Kyiv with heating and electricity has been hit in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
Darnytska CHP-4, or CHPP-4, and a residential building were hit in a strike the president said came with "no early warning from our partners".
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people had been killed and 21 injured in the missile strike on the apartment block late on Tuesday. He said "several energy facilities" in Kyiv had been hit without giving more detail.
Kyiv has reported multiple Russian strikes since US President Donald Trump said an energy ceasefire had been agreed by Russia and Ukraine two days ago.
In the early hours of Wednesday, Klitschko said the "massive missile attacks" had knocked out power to parts of Kyiv.
Kyiv officials have urged residents to stay in shelters after declaring a red alert due to a "missile threat".
Following the strikes on Tuesday, Zelensky said: "Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire. Russia is targeting yet another power plant and the lives of our people.
"This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches," he added.
"It is important that the world does not stay silent about this. And it is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing."
It is the second night in a row Kyiv has been hit by Russian missiles, and comes as Zelensky prepares to meet UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday to discuss accelerating air defence supplies to Kyiv.
Following strikes on Monday night, there was speculation America had cut off access to key intelligence enabling Ukraine to track incoming threats.
Earlier on Tuesday, Trump denied that was the case.
"We are helping them and we are sharing intel," he said.
"We want the war to end. So we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end."
Asked about Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites, Trump said: "Ukraine hit many sites the day before."
But he demurred when asked if Russia had broken a ceasefire. He said both countries want the war to "come to an end" but "just don't know how to get there".
It comes after Zelensky said on Sunday that a 60-day ceasefire would allow his country to hold presidential elections, following comments from Trump that "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".
Following Trump's announcement on Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Ukraine doesn't deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
Lavrov added that under any ceasefire, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons" for it to continue the war.
CHPP-4, which provides heating and electricity to the Dniprovskyi district and parts of the Darnytskyi district, has been hit multiple times during the war.
It was severely damaged in a separate Russian missile attack in February this year, which forced it to shut down.
That strike left more than 1,000 residential buildings without heating and hot water, along with 47 schools, 72 kindergartens and 18 medical institutions, according to Reuters.

articles.title: It’s not all about strikes against Russia — why U.S. intelligence is important for Ukraine
articles.body:
It’s not all about strikes against Russia — why U.S. intelligence is important for Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. intelligence is critically important for Ukraine’s air defense and strikes. An expert called its provision and the sale of weapons levers of pressure on Trump.
American intelligence is needed by Ukraine both to defend against Russian missiles and to strike military targets on enemy territory. Over the past few days, Ukraine has not received warnings about the enemy preparing missile attacks. Will the United States put Ukraine in an intelligence “vice” and what other levers of pressure does Trump have — UNN journalists discussed these issues with Oleksii Buriachenko, president of the International Institute for Security Studies.
Why American intelligence is important for Ukraine
According to the expert, American satellite intelligence helps Ukraine detect missile threats and use weapons that operate according to U.S. communications standards. In the expert’s view, this concerns not only American systems but also some weapons supplied by other NATO countries. At the same time, European states have their own capabilities, particularly France and the United Kingdom, but they do not cover the full range of U.S. capabilities.
We use U.S. satellite intelligence in two areas: both for defense and for moving the war onto the territory of the aggressor state. That is why it is critical for us to be able to detect missile launches in time and accordingly configure air defense systems for our own protection
Oleksii Buriachenko also emphasized that European partners are already partially compensating for the need for intelligence, but there is currently no full replacement for American capabilities. Therefore, if the transfer of information to Ukraine is halted, it will have to adapt to new conditions.
The issue is not compensation, but the fact that we work simultaneously with American satellite intelligence and with our European partners. However, the specific nature of NATO and American weaponry is that it is primarily designed to work with American satellite intelligence. Therefore, as of now, Ukraine will not be able to emerge from this situation without losses if the United States really decides to stop providing us with satellite intelligence
Can Trump use intelligence as an instrument of pressure
The political scientist recalled that Donald Trump had previously restricted Ukraine’s access to American intelligence for several days. According to him, at that time it was more difficult for Ukrainian air defense systems to respond to massive Russian attacks. However, in his assessment, the current situation is different because Ukraine has partially diversified its sources of intelligence information.
If we are talking about the current situation, we have no confirmed information that Trump is doing this or will do so. At least in the public sphere, he clearly stated that the United States continues to provide intelligence to Ukraine. In other words, there is no delay. The military says that this delay may be related to the fact that Russia has modified its missiles for the S-400, which had already caused us problems
Oleksii Buriachenko also believes that the domestic political situation in the United States may influence the American president’s decisions regarding Ukraine. However, in the political scientist’s view, the possibility of restricting the transfer of intelligence and the sale of American weapons nevertheless remains one of Washington’s instruments of influence.
Elections are the main reason behind this entire story. The configuration may turn out completely differently. If major criticism of Trump in the public sphere over the diesel deal gains momentum, he may, on the contrary, do something else beneficial for Ukraine. But the opposite may also happen: if Trump decides to force through the terms he agreed on with the Russian Federation, he may resolve this issue by putting pressure on Ukraine. He has instruments of pressure — intelligence and the sale of American weapons
In addition, the expert noted that Ukraine’s dependence on U.S. permits for the sale of American weapons remains a separate problem, even if those weapons were purchased by third countries. He emphasized that without official authorization from Washington, Ukraine will not be able to buy such equipment from other states, and therefore called preserving access to intelligence and the ability to purchase American weapons important tactical objectives for Ukraine.
For Ukraine, it is important now that, under any circumstances, it retain access to intelligence and the ability to purchase American weapons. The United States and President Trump have their own political and economic goals. Sometimes they coincide with ours, and sometimes they do not

articles.title: Houthis threaten escalation after strike on Saudi oil giant Aramco
articles.body:
Houthis threaten escalation after strike on Saudi oil giant Aramco
Yemen's Houthi rebels said Wednesday they had targeted facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco after officials in Riyadh reported a strike on a building in an area housing the energy giant's headquarters. The Iran-back militia also claimed missile strikes on the capital Riyadh and vowed to continue attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities.

Yemen's Houthis vowed on Wednesday to press on with attacks on airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, a day after a strike that sources said caused extensive damage to the headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco.
The Houthis said the threatened locations were legitimate targets and described their attacks as retaliation for Saudi strikes on Yemen – threatening to escalate a conflict reignited by the US-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.
Saudi Arabia has faced widening Houthi strikes over the past week, including an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people.
Read moreSaudi Arabia threatens 'decisive' response after Riyadh airport strike kills at least 12
Tuesday night's attack on Saudi Aramco's base in the eastern city of Dhahran caused a fire that spread across several floors, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters. The Saudi energy ministry had said the strike caused a limited fire.
Operations at Aramco were continuing normally, with employees working from home, according to two of the sources. Aramco did not immediately reply to a Reuters request for comment.
Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said the Iran-backed group had conducted "a high-quality military operation targeting Aramco in Dhahran", as well as strikes targeting Riyadh airport and a refinery in the capital.
He added the attacks were carried out with missiles and drones, and that operations "will continue in the coming days, targeting Saudi enemy airports and oil facilities".
Saudi-led forces say they intercept missile
The escalating conflict has dealt a blow to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's ambitious plans to transform and diversify the Saudi economy and reduce its reliance on oil.
The Houthis say they have been retaliating for the kingdom's backing of Yemeni government forces in the Yemen war that restarted last month.
The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh on Wednesday, and several loud booms were heard in the Saudi capital.
Saudi authorities earlier issued an alert for a possible aerial threat in Riyadh on Wednesday before the warning was lifted, a witness said. It wasn't immediately clear what caused the booms and there was no immediate comment from the authorities on their source.
The Saudi government media office didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about the cause of the booms.
Read moreBlasts rock Riyadh as Houthis target Saudi airports, oil facilities
In their statement on Wednesday, the Houthis said they had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones at the Saudi Aramco facilities in Dhahran, Riyadh airport and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh.
In a broad threat, they urged "international shipping companies", civilians and workers to evacuate Saudi airports and oil facilities.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

The Dhahran complex hosts a major operations centre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.
Riyadh’s international airport has come under attack four times, including Saturday's attack which was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade.
Authorities have closed the airport until October 17, and airlines have canceled flights to Saudi Arabia.
Yemen hospitals overwhelmed, Red Cross warns
Fearing the rise of Iranian influence and the prospect of chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in support of the government in 2015 after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa.
The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace until this year.
Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The Red Cross said on Wednesday that hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties as fighting intensified along multiple front lines.
The UN World Food Programme warned that life-saving assistance had been cut off to the government-held city of Taiz, which was encircled by Houthi fighters earlier this month.
"WFP and its partners cannot access more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance, including more than 200,000 women and children," WFP said in a statement.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters, AFP)

articles.title: Ukraine accuses SpaceX of restricting Starlink access for military drones
articles.body:
Ukraine has accused SpaceX of disrupting military drone operations through restrictions on Starlink satellite communications, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticised Washington over its support for Kyiv. SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk denied responsibility for the restrictions, saying the US government controls the military satellite network and its operating limits.
Ukrainian military officials reported that terminals connected to Starshield, SpaceX's military communications service, began losing connectivity on Tuesday night when travelling above 160 kilometres per hour.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The restrictions affected Ukrainian attack drones and interceptors used to defend cities against Russian aerial assaults.
Presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said Ukrainian forces received no advance warning, resulting in disrupted missions.
"Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.
A Ukrainian Defence Ministry source told Reuters that some military units experienced connection failures at speeds below the reported threshold.
Musk responded on X that the restrictions were not SpaceX's decision.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.
Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov reported on Wednesday evening that services had been partially restored. He called for the removal of all speed restrictions.
The disruption coincided with Russian missile and drone strikes against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian authorities reported that approximately 600,000 people lost electricity following attacks on Kyiv, Kharkiv and surrounding areas.
Russia's Defence Ministry confirmed strikes against six power plants, while Zelenskyy said 30 energy facilities had suffered damage.
Six people were killed in Lutsk, western Ukraine, according to regional authorities. In Kyiv, officials reported two deaths and 21 injuries at a residential building struck during the bombardment.
Zelenskyy accused Russia of disregarding US President Donald Trump's proposed ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Speaking to Piers Morgan during a visit to London, Zelenskyy also expressed frustration with Washington's approach to the war.
"It's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side," he said.
Asked whether he felt betrayed by Trump, Zelenskyy replied: "Really, yes," adding that the situation involved more than his personal feelings.
The Ukrainian president warned that restrictions on satellite communications would result in further casualties.
"This decision will bring a lot of human losses," he said.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv have deteriorated following Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel purchases and his demands that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries.
The Financial Times reported, citing unnamed European officials, that Washington had threatened to restrict intelligence sharing unless Kyiv suspended those strikes.
Ukrainian officials also reported receiving no advance warnings from Western partners before Russian missile attacks for two consecutive days. Trump denied that Washington had stopped sharing intelligence.
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, whose government finances Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions, questioned Musk's involvement.
"Are you playing politics with your products again?" Sikorski wrote on X.
During Zelenskyy's visit to London, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged continued military assistance, including £45 million in surface-to-air missiles, with £10 million earmarked for accelerated delivery.
Britain also committed to examining further sanctions against Russia and measures to accelerate weapons supplies.
HT

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russian attack on energy grid leaves 600,000 without power, damages 30 facilities
articles.body:
A massive overnight Russian strike on critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv region, and Kharkiv damaged 26 electric power elements and four oil and gas facilities, leaving at least 600,000 consumers without electricity supply, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported on Wednesday.
"A targeted Russian ballistic strike specifically against energy infrastructure, regarding which the President of America defined a ceasefire. The strike was absolutely deliberate and demonstrative in scale – there has never been such a show of disrespect from Russia toward America," the head of state wrote on his Telegram channel.
According to the president, overnight Wednesday Russian forces deployed 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 strike drones and loitering munitions against Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure. The attack resulted in dead and wounded, and the scale of power outages may increase. Energy repair crews and units of the State Emergency Service are working at the impact sites.
Zelenskyy emphasized that with this attack Russia rejected the possibility of de-escalation and demonstrated contempt for U.S statements regarding an energy truce. In this regard, the Ukrainian head of state called on U.S President Donald Trump to introduce tough sanctions against the Russian Federation provided for in the recently passed and signed law by Senator Lindsey Graham, as well as to provide Ukraine with additional missile packages for Patriot air defense systems.

articles.title: Ihnat: Ukrainian air defense shoots down more than 100 Russian drones in one day
articles.body:
Ihnat: Ukrainian air defense shoots down more than 100 Russian drones in one day
According to Ukrinform, Yurii Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Ukrainian Air Force Command, reported this during a TV broadcast.
"From around 07:00 until 18:00, approximately 145 such drones were detected, about 70 of which were jet-powered — slightly less than half," Ihnat said.
According to him, as of 18:00, drones powered by internal combustion engines predominated in the skies.
"As a result of combat operations, more than 100 UAVs that attacked during the day had already been shot down by 18:00," the Air Force spokesperson noted.
Ihnat emphasized that despite the high interception rate, even a small number of drones reaching their targets could cause significant damage.
According to him, Russian forces combine different types of drones and missiles in an attempt to complicate air defense operations. To alter the capabilities and flight range of jet-powered UAVs, Russian forces may adjust their fuel supplies and warheads or install additional equipment.
"The enemy is already experimenting with different configurations: whether to put more fuel into the same jet-powered UAV or install a larger warhead. They may also add other payloads, such as cameras, network transmitters, modems, and so on," Ihnat said.
He added that Ukrainian specialists were examining recovered drones to determine how Russian forces were managing to deploy them over long distances.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Ukrainian air defense forces neutralized four ballistic missiles and 115 drones used by Russian forces in attacks on Ukraine beginning on the evening of October 13.
Photo: Ukrainian Air Force

articles.title: Musk blames Trump for throttling ‘military Starlink’ in Ukraine
articles.body:
Musk blames Trump for throttling ‘military Starlink’ in Ukraine
Elon Musk has denied instructing his company SpaceX to abruptly restrict Starlink and Starshield satellite communications services used by Ukrainian forces to operate drones.
Ukrainian officials and frontline commanders said terminals suddenly stopped working overnight Tuesday into Wednesday when drones flew faster than 100 mph, disrupting some combat missions. The problems with Starshield, the military-grade counterpart to SpaceX’s Starlink service, occurred as US President Donald Trump was pressuring Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he blamed for surging energy prices.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote on X on Wednesday in response to criticism from Ukraine. He had earlier suggested that the disruption might have been “a mistake” and said he was working to restore connectivity.
Musk also said that Starlink should be used only for civilian and defensive purposes, arguing that using it for offensive operations would be “inappropriate for a commercial company.”
Although Trump has not commented directly on the restrictions, a senior US official told Axios that his administration had nothing to do with the disruption of Starlink services.
In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky confirmed reports that the US had threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Kiev unless Ukraine halted attacks on Russian energy facilities.
Ukrainian officials also said they had received no advance warning from their Western partners before Russian missile strikes on Kiev on two consecutive nights, Monday and Tuesday. According to media reports, US officials attributed the failure to detect the missile launches to bad weather, an explanation their Ukrainian counterparts reportedly found hard to believe.
Asked by British talk show host Piers Morgan on Wednesday whether he had been “betrayed” by the Trump administration, Zelensky replied, “Yes.”
“It’s a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” he added.
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mikhail Fyodorov said Wednesday evening that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 100 mph was being restored, but urged the removal of speed restrictions on Starshield altogether.
Russia has argued that Ukraine would use a ceasefire without preconditions to regroup and replenish its forces. “We want not a ceasefire but a lasting peace, and we are ready to do everything possible to achieve it,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday.

articles.title: Russia strikes military-linked energy facilities across Ukraine (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Russia strikes military-linked energy facilities across Ukraine (VIDEOS)
Russian forces launched an overnight barrage against energy and communications infrastructure across Ukraine, targeting facilities that support the Ukrainian military, the Defense Ministry in Moscow has said.
In a statement on Wednesday, the ministry said high-precision ground-based weapons and long-range attack drones were used to attack facilities in Kiev, its suburbs, and Kharkov Region.
In Kiev, the ministry said the strikes hit the Darnytskaya combined heat and power plant (CHP-4) and Kiev CHP-5, which it said were supplying power to Ukrainian military installations and defense manufacturers. It also reported that it hit the ATM Ukrsibbank data center, which was used for collecting intelligence about Russian forces.
In the region of Kiev, the targets included Kiev CHP-6, the Trypilska thermal power plant, and the Kievskaya electricity substation. According to the ministry, the facilities supplied power to military logistics hubs, weapons storage sites, and defense enterprises.
In Kharkov and the surrounding region, Russian forces struck Kharkov CHP-5 and the Zmievskaya thermal power plant, which supplied electricity to military-industrial enterprises and Ukrainian defense installations.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky confirmed the attacks, saying Russia launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions overnight. “At least 600,000 people are currently, unfortunately, without electricity,” he said, warning that further outages are possible. He added that significant damage was done to 26 elements of Ukraine’s power system and four oil and gas facilities.
The Ukrainian Air Force reported that it shot down four missiles out of 39, amid reports of critically low stocks of US-made Patriot interceptors.
Kiev Mayor Vitaly Klitschko claimed that three people were killed and at least 22 were injured in the barrage, adding that the attacks caused extensive electricity outages.
The head of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway operator, Aleksandr Pertsovsky, also reported strikes on infrastructure in five regions – Kharkov, Kiev, Vinnitsa, Khmelnitsky, and Ternopol – with locomotive and carriage depots, maintenance facilities, railway stations, and rolling stock coming under attack. He described the material damage as substantial, adding that railway personnel did not suffer any casualties.
The attacks come amid growing tensions between Kiev and Washington over intelligence sharing. US President Donald Trump recently said “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” as Zelensky’s term expired more than two years ago. He also urged the Ukrainian leader to stop striking Russian oil refineries. Zelensky replied that he is ready to do so if Russia stops attacking Ukrainian energy facilities.
Following the strikes, Zelensky said Ukraine’s Western backers failed to provide advance warnings about Russian ballistic missile launches for the second time that week. He also claimed that the US threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stops attacking Russian refineries.
However, he stressed that cooperation has not been halted, echoing Trump’s earlier remarks in which he said the US is “helping [Ukraine], and we are sharing intel.”
The latest barrage came after the Russian Defense Ministry vowed earlier this month to intensify strikes on military-related facilities in Ukraine in response to Zelensky’s threat to step up attacks on Russian oil refineries.

articles.title: UK Allocates £45 Million for LMM Missiles for Ukraine’s Air Defense
articles.body:
The United Kingdom will accelerate deliveries of LMM missiles to Ukraine for air defense and is preparing additional packages of military, financial, and sanctions support.
The UK government announced this ahead of a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and UK Prime Minister Andrew Burnham.
One of the new measures is supplying air defense missiles to Ukraine worth £45 million. The UK plans to accelerate deliveries of Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMM), which Ukraine’s Defense Forces use for air defense.
The UK government specifically highlighted the use of LMM missiles against Russian jet-powered drones.
The prime minister has instructed ministers to prepare additional sanctions against Russia, along with military aid and financial support packages, to be presented in the coming weeks. The UK has also called on international partners to increase pressure on Moscow.
Under the new £45 million package, the UK will accelerate deliveries of £10 million worth of missiles to meet Ukraine’s most urgent air defense needs this winter.
Overall, the UK has already committed £1.6 billion to supply Ukraine with more than 5,000 LMM missiles over four years. The contract provides for their production at Thales’ facility in Belfast.
The UK continued to increase deliveries of these weapons in 2026. In June, Militarnyi reported on a new British package that included LMM missiles and 150,000 drones.
The increased military support comes with expanded British sanctions pressure on Russia. The government confirmed it intends to fully implement a ban on maritime services for exporting Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The restrictions cover, in particular, British companies’ involvement in the maritime transport of Russian LNG, as well as related financial and brokerage services.
They aim to restrict Russia’s access to British shipping, insurance, and financial services that support maritime transport.
In June, Militarnyi reported on new British sanctions targeting Russia’s defense industry and shadow fleet. The sanctions list also included LNG carriers involved in transporting Russian LNG.

articles.title: German air force fires IRIS-T SLM for first time in Crete
articles.body:
- The German Air Force completed operational certification of the IRIS-T SLM air defense system with its first live firing at NATO’s Crete range.
- Swedish and German Patriot units and German Stinger crews joined the tactical exercise that followed the certification shot, Diehl Defence said.
The German Air Force has fired its new IRIS-T SLM air defense system for the first time at the NATO Missile Firing Installation on Crete, completing the operational certification the system needed before it can be relied on in German service, manufacturer Diehl Defence said this week.
Air Defence Missile Group 61, the unit based at Todendorf on Germany’s Baltic coast that operates the system, trained at the NATO range in October on linking the full fire unit together: the TRML-4D radar, the Common Tactical Operations Center command post and the launcher with its IRIS-T SLM interceptors. After the certification shot, the IRIS-T SLM was folded into a wider tactical exercise alongside German and Swedish Patriot batteries and German Stinger short-range missiles on the LeFlaSys light air defense vehicle.
“Without the soldiers of Air Defence Missile Group 61, this first firing of the IRIS-T SLM in Crete would not have been possible,” said Lt. Col. Björn Klarl, the group’s commander.
Diehl did not disclose what targets were engaged, how many missiles were fired or the results of individual intercepts.
“The successful system certification firing confirms that IRIS-T SLM delivers reliable performance and a very high hit rate in operation,” said Helmut Rauch, CEO of Diehl Defence.
The system can engage targets out to 60 km (37 miles) and up to 20 km (12 miles) in altitude, according to Diehl, and is designed to protect cities and critical infrastructure against cruise missiles and drones as well as aircraft and helicopters. It sits below Patriot in Germany’s layered air defense, covering medium-range threats while Patriot handles ballistic missiles and longer-range targets.
Ukraine has used IRIS-T SLM in combat since October 2022, when Germany delivered the first fire unit to Kyiv, and the system has since become one of the main tools Ukrainian forces use against Russian cruise missiles and Shahed-type attack drones. Rauch said ten nations now rely on the system, and Sweden, whose Patriot crews took part in the Crete exercise, decided to buy IRIS-T SLM in 2025.
Germany was slower to field the system at home. Berlin ordered six fire units in 2023, and the first was delivered in August 2024, but its entry into service was held up because an ammunition loading crane had not been certified to German standards, Defence Industry Europe reported. The Bundeswehr says Air Defence Missile Group 61 formally put the system into service only in February 2026.
The NAMFI range near Chania was set up under a 1964 agreement among several NATO members and has hosted live missile firings by allied air defense units since 1968, with crews from Nike Hercules and HAWK through to Patriot training there over the decades.

articles.title: “He thinks Ukraine is a weak link and that it needs to be squeezed into giving in”: diplomat on why Trump pressures Kyiv, not Moscow
articles.body:
Washington is pressing the victim, not the aggressor, a Ukrainian diplomat says. President Donald Trump is using the threat of cutting military aid and intelligence as a tool to pressure Ukraine, while failing to apply enough pressure on Russia to stop the war, says Oleksandr Khara, executive director of the Center for Defense Strategies, Espreso reports.
Ukraine’s drones and air defense still lean on US satellite intelligence and weapons, which gives Trump room to squeeze Kyiv rather than Moscow. Khara argues Trump wants to end the war on Ukraine’s and Europe’s account to restore normal relations with Russian ruler Vladimir Putin, treating Ukraine as the weak link to be pushed.
“Trump wants to use restrictions, levers of influence on Ukraine to achieve his goal. To end or stop this war at any cost, at the expense of Ukraine and Europe, to restore normal relations with Putin,” Khara said.
Using American aid as leverage over Kyiv is not new for Trump, the diplomat noted, recalling earlier instances in which support was blocked or suspended.
The pressure points Trump picks, and the ones he leaves alone
Trump wants a visible success in ending the war, Khara says, partly against the backdrop of US domestic politics. He has economic tools to press Moscow but is in no hurry to use them, and his administration is instead gradually loosening sanctions on Russia.
“He doesn’t want to pressure Russia. He thinks Ukraine is the weak link and that it needs to be pushed,” Khara stressed.
Ukraine’s dependence on US support has fallen thanks to European partners, he added, so Kyiv has more room to keep fighting even as European states keep buying American weapons for it.
The one trade Kyiv might accept, and the pressure until then
An energy ceasefire is possible only on strict terms, Khara believes. Kyiv could agree to stop striking Russian refineries only if Moscow halts attacks on Ukraine’s power generation and transmission, heating, and the Black Sea ports and the ships heading to them.
Until such a deal exists, Ukraine must hit harder, he argued, because steadily draining Russia’s economic resources is what could force the Kremlin to reconsider.
“As long as there is no such agreement, and no desire from Russia, we must increase this pressure and destroy as much of their energy infrastructure as possible,” Khara said.

articles.title: The end of UNIFIL: What next for south Lebanon?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The end of UNIFIL: What next for south Lebanon?
Beirut, Lebanon - As the UN's longest-serving presence on the Blue Line between Lebanon and Israel counts down to its exit, a European replacement is being floated as the answer.
The real choice facing Beirut, however, is between a security arrangement written in Washington and one it builds itself.
For 48 years, the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) has been deployed across the country's southern border villages.
It never deterred the wars fought across the Blue Line - a 120-kilometre (75-mile) temporary demarcation boundary established by the United Nations on 7 June 2000 to confirm the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon.
What they did, consistently, was watch, record, and report, and in a region where every side contests every account, that act of witnessing carried weight of its own.
Few in Lebanon expect the UN body's exit to change the balance of force. “UNIFIL was merely an eyewitness,” retired Brigadier General Saeed Qazah, a military expert, told The New Arab.
Operating under Chapter VI of its mandate, it could only record violations and report them to the UN. Its absence, he argued, “will not change the military reality on the ground as much as it will leave a logistical and economic vacuum”.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun's push for an extension was blocked by a US-Israeli veto, and he had welcomed a French-Italian idea for a European Union force to take UNIFIL's place. On Monday, the contours of that EU role took a more concrete shape.
European Union foreign ministers agreed to establish a new support mission in Lebanon to advise and train the country's military and internal security forces. It would have an initial mandate of three years.
But the European option still lacks the mandate, consent, and the American backing it would need.
UNIFIL's real successor is being negotiated elsewhere, and what awaits Lebanon after December is less a handover than a test of whether the state can do alone what it has long outsourced.
A European force without a shape
The new European mission "will advise and assist the Lebanese Armed Forces and Internal Security Forces to strengthen territorial control, border security, and internal security," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a statement on Monday.
Over 10 EU members are reportedly willing to contribute people and resources to it, but more operational planning is required before it is launched. An EU official told Reuters this week that the mission hoped to deploy personnel in the coming months.
But retired Brigadier General Saeed Qazah sees a deeper flaw.
“UNIFIL could not prevent the Lebanese-Israeli conflict or control the land and the border, and European forces will have no effective role there either,” he said.
Enforcing peace would require a Chapter VII mandate, which a Russian and Chinese veto would block. “No country is willing to send its soldiers to fight or sacrifice their lives on behalf of the Lebanese army,” he added.
Consent is the other wall. Political analyst Ali Sbeiti says Israel refuses to give Paris any role, given their disputes over regional files and the Gaza war. Qazah agrees that no foreign force can deploy on the border without the approval of both Lebanon, Israel, and a UN resolution.
The one exception, he said, “is a mission limited to training and logistical support for the Lebanese army, away from the border. The only feasible European mission, in other words, is the one that does least of what UNIFIL did”.
UNIFIL's real successor is being negotiated elsewhere
Writer and political analyst Nader Hijaz points to the "third party" under discussion in talks between Beirut and Israel, a body that would verify implementation of the framework agreement.
“That is, in practice, the field replacement for UNIFIL,” he said. Whether it would merely monitor or hold broad powers, such as searching homes and seizing weapons, is unresolved, and a deal has been deferred until after Israel's elections.
On one point, Hijaz is categorical. “Washington will never accept any force that is not under direct American command,” he told The New Arab. The US and Israel, he said, are open to a specific Italian role but not a French one.
Sbeiti adds that the Europeans lack the nerve to act in the south without explicit American blessing. The successor, in short, is being decided in a US-brokered process, on a timetable set by Israeli politics.
Beirut and Hezbollah's calculations
The Lebanese state and army would welcome almost any arrangement that averts a vacuum, and President Joseph Aoun immediately expressed backing for the EU’s announcement this week of a security support mission.
Hijaz notes that military cooperation with France and Italy is already established, and Sbeiti describes an official welcome for any friendly presence, even as a mere eyewitness.
Hezbollah, however, is harder to read. Its secretary-general, Naim Qassem, has called the US-sponsored framework agreement a red line and a surrender of sovereignty, holding up instead the US-Iranian memorandum signed in Islamabad.
Qazah expects the party to reject any foreign force, since it does not want a witness to its breaches, “just as Israel does not want neutral forces bearing witness to its violations”.
Sbeiti, however, disagrees. “Hezbollah can no longer block a plan the state backs, and has no fundamental problem with France, given shared understandings between Paris, the party and Tehran,” he told The New Arab. “The main knot remains with the American and Israeli sides,” he noted.
Hijjaz, meanwhile, says the party's stance will hinge on whether a force operates south of the Litani or beyond it, and whether it pursues the group's weapons. Either way, the decisive veto lies outside Lebanon.
What south Lebanon loses
The mission is exiting in its worst hour. It has recorded a sharp escalation between Israel and Hezbollah, with hundreds of projectiles on some days. It still fields more than 7,400 troops from 46 countries, its backbone European, and seven peacekeepers have been killed in hostile attacks in 2026 alone.
Ceasefires have collapsed in succession, from April's arrangements to the US-sponsored Trilateral Framework in June, and Israeli forces still hold positions inside Lebanon that Beirut says block the army's full deployment.
Washington led the push to end the mission, favouring arrangements outside the Security Council, as in Gaza. Prime Minister Nawaf Salam warned of a vacuum, arguing the UN offers a neutrality no other actor can match, and more than two-thirds of parliament petitioned for UNIFIL to be strengthened, not withdrawn.
Since 1978, and especially after its reinforcement following the 2006 war, UNIFIL has been an economic engine for the border villages.
At its peak, Qazah said, more than 15,000 soldiers in a narrow area drove spending, services, and procurement. Their departure will cut “a vital economic artery” in a region already devastated by Israeli strikes.
Three roads after December
The first is direct military coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli armies, favoured by Washington and Israel and signalled by US envoys' talk of opening crossings once the weapons file is closed. Lebanon rejects it as security normalisation.
The second is a multinational force with European troops under American command, which depends on a wider regional deal and US-Iranian understandings and Israel's elections.
The third is self-reliance: Qazah argues the government can declare the border villages a military zone under National Defence Law No. 102 of 1938, placing all security forces under army command and allowing curfews, closures and searches.
A European coalition will remain ink on paper without a UN mandate, the consent of both parties and an American guarantee against escalation. None of these is in Beirut's gift. The world is not handing the south to a new guardian; it is handing it back to the Lebanese state. Lebanon can assert its sovereignty through its own army or risk a vacuum that turns the border strip into an open front once more.
For Qazah, the choice is already clear. Imposing security, he said, is the exclusive responsibility of Lebanon's political leadership, which must give the army firm orders “to impose security by military force, not by begging for it or imposing it by consensus”.
Alaa Sarhal is a Lebanese journalist
This article is published in collaboration with Egab
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Ukraine downs four ballistic missiles, 115 drones in massive Russian overnight attack
articles.body:
Ukraine downs four ballistic missiles, 115 drones in massive Russian overnight attack
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force reported this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on Tuesday, October 13, Russia launched a massive combined attack on Ukraine using attack drones and 39 missiles of various types following ballistic trajectories toward their targets.
The main targets were Kyiv, Kyiv region and Kharkiv region.
The attack was notable for the simultaneous use of different types of aerial weapons launched from multiple directions, as well as the large number of ballistic missiles aimed at energy facilities.
In total, the Air Force’s radio-technical troops detected 167 aerial attack assets: 39 missiles and 128 drones of various types:
39 Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400/Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missiles launched from Russia’s Kursk, Bryansk, Voronezh and Rostov regions;
128 attack drones, including Shahed drones (77 of them jet-powered), Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera and Italmas drones, as well as Parodiya decoy drones. They were launched from the directions of Millerovo, Oryol, temporarily occupied Donetsk, Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea, and the Sea of Azov.
The aerial attack was repelled by aircraft, surface-to-air missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 9:00 on Wednesday, October 14, air defense had shot down or suppressed 119 targets:
Four Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400/Zircon/Oniks ballistic missiles;
115 drones of various types, including 59 jet-powered drones, accounting for 90% of all attack drones deployed.
Preliminary reports indicate that missile and attack drone strikes were recorded at 22 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight locations as of 9:00. Some of the Russian missiles failed to reach their targets.
As Ukrinform reported, four people were killed in a combined Russian attack on Kyiv.

articles.title: Russian Overnight Strikes Target Kyiv CHP Plants and Kill Civilians Across Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian forces targeted all three of Kyiv’s municipal combined heat and power (CHP) plants in an overnight attack on Oct. 13-14, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi reported on Wednesday. Strikes across Ukraine killed civilians and damaged civilian infrastructure.
Russian ballistic missiles targeted energy infrastructure in Kyiv, Kharkiv and surrounding regions, Koretskyi said on Telegram. In the Kyiv region, Russian forces also struck critical infrastructure supplying electricity to the capital and central regions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Energy workers and emergency responders began working at the affected sites early in the morning, conducting firefighting and debris-clearing operations. Specialists have also started priority restoration work at the targeted facilities, according to the prime minister.
The attacks followed an evening strike on a high-rise residential building in Kyiv that killed two people and injured 25. Another person was killed and one injured in a separate morning attack on the capital, Koretskyi said.
Railway infrastructure was also targeted in five regions. No casualties were reported at the railway facilities, as timely evacuations helped protect workers and others at the sites. Restoration work is ongoing.
Industrial fires and residential damage reported across Ukraine
In the Khmelnytskyi region, Russian drone attacks sparked fires at industrial sites in the Khmelnytskyi and Shepetivka districts, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported on Telegram.
‘Blatant Disrespect Toward America’: Zelensky Slams Russia’s Strike on Ukraine’s Energy Sector
Falling drone debris also caused a fire at a gas station in Khmelnytskyi district, injuring two people. In the city of Khmelnytskyi, drone debris ignited fires at two private homes in a residential neighborhood. No casualties were reported there.
Emergency crews were repeatedly forced to leave their work sites because of renewed Russian attacks. Eighty rescuers and 22 pieces of equipment were deployed to extinguish a fire at one of the industrial facilities in Khmelnytskyi District.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian attacks killed two people and injured six others, including a child, according to the DSNS. In Pavlohrad, a strike on an open area killed one person and injured four others, including a child. In Nikopol district, attacks on the district center and the Myrivka community killed another person.
Russian forces also struck an enterprise in Dnipro overnight, injuring a man and triggering a large-scale fire. In Synelnykove district, attacks on the Yavornytske and Mykolaivka communities injured a woman and damaged a private house. Emergency responders extinguished all fires caused by the attacks, the DSNS said.
Strikes hit Sloviansk, Ternopil and railway infrastructure
In the Donetsk region, a Russian airstrike on a residential area in Sloviansk wounded seven people and damaged five apartment buildings. A fire broke out in a non-residential building and was later extinguished.
A car also caught fire following a Russian attack in Bylbasivka. Firefighters had to suspend their work because of the continuing threat posed by Russian drones.
In Ternopil, a Russian drone strike damaged an administrative building and sparked a fire on the second floor. Rescuers extinguished the blaze, and no casualties were reported.
Russian forces also attacked a railway infrastructure facility in the Vinnytsia region, causing a large fire. Emergency crews had to interrupt their work because of the threat of follow-up attacks involving drones and ballistic missiles. Responders eventually extinguished all remaining hotspots, and explosives experts inspected the site for unexploded ordnance. No fatalities or injuries were reported.
In the Kharkiv region, five people were injured in a Russian attack on the city of Derhachi, as per DSNS. A first person-view (FPV) drone struck a garage at a civilian enterprise, sparking a fire that spread across 200 square meters and engulfed trucks inside the building. Emergency crews extinguished the blaze.
Koretskyi thanked rescuers, police officers, medics, energy workers and others involved in responding to the attacks and helping affected residents.

articles.title: Canada’s Dominion Dynamics, Ukraine’s TENCORE Sign Deal to Build TerMIT Ground Vehicles in Canada
articles.body:
Canadian defense technology company Dominion Dynamics and Ukraine’s TENCORE signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to manufacture TerMIT unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) in Canada, with initial production targeted for 2027, according to the press release.
TENCORE is a leading Ukrainian developer and serial manufacturer of UGVs for military and dual-use applications. Since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the company has delivered over 4,000 robotic platforms to Ukraine’s Armed Forces (AFU), actively deployed across more than 50 combat brigades.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The biggest lesson from Ukraine is speed. Battlefield requirements change in weeks, so production, operational feedback, and engineering have to run as a loop: build, deploy, learn, change, scale. Canada gives us the manufacturing base, suppliers, and reliable power to run that loop alongside allies who need these vehicles,” the press release quoted TENCORE co-founder Roman Tkachenko.
The MOU, signed at the Canadian Pavilion during the AUSA 2026 defense conference in Washington, also provides for integrating AuraNet, Dominion’s autonomy stack for pan-domain command and control, as the onboard intelligence layer for TerMIT. Nadia Theodore, Canada’s deputy ambassador to the US, attended the signing ceremony.
“Canada has the workforce and the suppliers to build at scale. This agreement is how two companies start turning that commitment into vehicles, and we intend to move fast,” the press release quoted Eliot Pence, founder and CEO of Dominion Dynamics.
Shakhtar Dream of Champions League Return to Ukraine as London Keeps War in Spotlight
The deal follows a joint declaration on defense cooperation that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and President Volodymyr Zelensky signed in September. Both countries committed to manufacturing thousands of battle-tested drones and unmanned systems in the next two years, with one-third earmarked for Ukraine’s defense, the companies wrote.
The partnership will support the deployment and continued development of AuraNet for Ukraine’s front lines, according to the press release. It will also create high-skilled jobs in Canada and strengthen the country’s sovereign defense technology base.
Dominion plans to manufacture TerMIT in Canadian facilities. A TENCORE team will lead the initial technology transfer and train technicians in Canada to build the UGV, the companies wrote. Since 2024, TENCORE has delivered more than 5,000 UGVs to Ukrainian military units, the press release says.
Dominion also aims to develop an Arctic-hardened TerMIT for Canadian operations and for export to NATO allies. The companies will continue to work toward definitive agreements.
Dominion Dynamics was founded in 2025 and builds autonomy, sensing, and command-and-control systems. According to them, it has deployed its technology with the Canadian Armed Forces across the High North.

articles.title: SpaceX limits StarShield speeds on Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian drones
articles.body:
Elon Musk’s SpaceX has imposed new speed restrictions on the StarShield service used by Starlink terminals installed on Ukrainian drones. On Oct. 14, Ukrainian military communications and electronic warfare specialist Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov reported on his Telegram channel that the terminals now work only at speeds of up to 100 mph (about 160 kph).
He said the restrictions have affected StarShield’s “military package”:
“Our Defense Forces received no warning about these restrictions, and this led to the disruption of a number of missions. It is obvious that this decision cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
The new limit means the service can no longer be used on jet-powered drones or other high-speed unmanned aircraft.
Georgy Trishkin, a missile-launch analyst and commentator on spaceflight and rocketry, told The Insider that standard Starlink service on drones traveling faster than 160 kph had stopped working in 2025, while StarShield continued to function until Oct. 13.
“Military StarShield is physically a different system and a different service. It is available only to defense and government customers. Starlink stopped working under these conditions last year and never worked on Russian territory in the first place. Drones using it would lose their connection when crossing zones near the border and switch to other methods, including mobile networks using Russian SIM cards.
The decision was not made by SpaceX, but by the customer in the United States [meaning the Pentagon — The Insider]. That does not absolve the company of responsibility, but it is important to understand who made the decision and which service it concerned.”
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski also commented on the move.
“Hey, Elon Musk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you,” he wrote on Musk’s X platform.
A day earlier, on Oct. 13, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with NPR that the Trump administration had threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Kyiv unless Ukrainian forces halted long-range drone strikes on oil refineries inside Russia.

articles.title: Russia is trying the Dobropillia road to the last big free cities of Donbas again, a year after it failed. This time it brought another army
articles.body:
- Russian reinforcements are surging toward Dobropillia in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast
- The Russians have a plan: to fight through Dobropillia and open a path toward the free city of Kramatorsk
- Ukrainian forces aren't powerless to resist, but many of their own best troops are busy attacking elsewhere
The Russians are pouring troops into a key sector just southeast of the town of Dobropillia in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast, threatening to overwhelm Ukrainian defenses and march one settlement closer to Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, the last two big free cities in Donetsk.
But the Russians' push toward Dobropillia isn't without cost. Russian losses in this sector are "colossal," according to the mapper Playfra. And every soldier the Kremlin deploys along the Dobropillia axis is a soldier it can't deploy elsewhere.
And that may help explain why the Russians are falling back in two other key sectors. The Dobropillia axis is the Russians' clear priority. For the Ukrainians, that's an opportunity to attack elsewhere.
Dobropillia, a former mining town with a pre-war population of around 28,000, is now a fortress. It anchors Ukrainian positions along the T0514 highway threading north to Kramatorsk, 40 km away.
Russia has tried this road before. In August 2025, Russian troops pushed a salient toward the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk highway, and Ukrainian counterattacks cut it apart. By October that year, President Volodymyr Zelensky put Russian losses on the Dobropillia front at about 13,000.
For the Russians, there are several possible paths to Kramatorsk. But the southwest path along the T0514 is the likeliest to actually lead Russian troops to the city. There's a route into Kramatorsk from the southeast, but it's blocked by stubborn Ukrainian forces still clinging to positions in the ruins of Kostiantynivka. There's a northern route, too, but starting this spring the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps rolled back 18 months of Russian gains along that route.
The Russian command clearly sees the road through Dobropillia for what it is: the best way forward for an army that's been struggling to complete its conquest of Donetsk, to say nothing of breaking through in other front-line oblasts.
And that's why the Russians are channeling fresh forces into the Dobropillia sector. Part of the 41st Combined Arms Army and units of its 90th Guards Tank Division are now fighting there, Ukrainian military analyst Kostiantyn Mashovets wrote on 9 October, and the Russian command keeps feeding fresh assault infantry into the sector through the village of Nove Shakhove despite heavy losses. The open-source account Unit Observer tracked the buildup as early as September.
Potentially tens of thousands of troops from those formations join the main forces of the 2nd and 51st Combined Arms Armies, according to Mashovets, as well as elements of the Russian naval infantry, facing the Ukrainian 1st Azov Corps and 19th Army Corps around Dobropillia.
The reinforcements give Russian commanders more options. Mashovets expects the 51st CAA to push south and southwest of Dobropillia and the 2nd CAA toward Raksha and Sviatohorivka, enveloping the town and cutting its supply routes from Bilozerske before any direct assault. The neighboring 8th CAA is fighting around Kostiantynivka. The Russians' immediate goal is "to maintain this offensive pressure from summer into the fall," Unit Observer wrote, setting conditions for a possible siege of Kramatorsk next year.
The outlook for the Ukrainian defenders of Dobropillia is "worsening," Playfra warned on 13 October.
The Russians have a seemingly infinite manpower pool here and a clear numerical advantage, which allows them to significantly increase the flow of infiltrators and, as such, the chance of some passing through Ukrainian defenses.
This leads to especially deep Russian infiltrations, which in turn slowly but surely destabilize the situation for the Ukrainians, which are progressively forced to abandon their most advanced positions.
Trending Now
The Ukrainians aren't without options, Playfra explained. They should double down on their current strategy of saturating the fields around Dobropillia with drones in a ring at least 2 to 3 km deep, forestalling large-scale Russian movements until the winter strips the leaves off the trees, depriving the Russians of their best cover from overhead surveillance. This could buy Dobropillia "much more time," Playfra predicted.
Mashovets sees the same deadline. If Dobropillia and neighboring Druzhkivka hold until mid-to-late December, he wrote, Russia's plan would have to be substantially rebuilt.
Help isn't coming
Just don't expect a lot of Ukrainian reinforcements along the Dobropillia axis. Many of Ukraine's best troops are busy attacking.
Taking advantage of the surge of Russian manpower in the direction of Dobropillia, Ukrainian forces have counterattacked where the Russians are weakest: in northern Donetsk Oblast and also in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, just south of Donetsk.
In months of carefully planned assaults supported by ground robots and intensive drone strikes, Ukrainian forces have liberated hundreds of square kilometers in northern Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk. The Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi in northern Donetsk largely removed the immediate northern threat to Sloviansk and neighboring Kramatorsk.
But it didn't do anything to help in the direction of Dobropillia, where the Russians have many more troops, much more firepower, and—equally importantly—a singular focus: to open a road to the last free cities in Donetsk.
Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps took the lessons of the failed 2023 counteroffensive into Operation Vivaldi. It fought small, and won.

articles.title: Ukrainian foreign minister: Putin is not simply attacking Ukraine, he is openly defying the US
articles.body:
Ukrainian foreign minister: Putin is not simply attacking Ukraine, he is openly defying the US
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, commenting on overnight Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities, has said Kremlin ruler Vladimir Putin has rejected the US-proposed "energy ceasefire".
Source: Sybiha on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Sybiha noted that Putin responded to peace efforts by launching 39 missiles and more than 120 drones. Ukraine's energy facilities were the main targets of the attack.
Quote: "Putin is not simply attacking Ukraine. He is openly defying the United States and treating every attempt to stop this war with contempt.
There can be no economic rewards for aggression. No sanctions relief. No concessions that allow Russia to finance its next wave of terror. Every dollar that reaches Moscow's war budget is another resource for attacks on Ukrainian civilians and threats to transatlantic security."
Details: Sybiha called on Ukraine's partners to tighten sanctions, enforce them more rigorously and provide additional air defence support to Ukraine immediately.
"Putin must face consequences for rejecting peace, not incentives to continue the war," he concluded.
Background:
- US President Donald Trump claimed that the "energy ceasefire" he had announced between Ukraine and Russia is in effect and said reports of violations needed to be checked.
- On 11 October, Trump claimed on his social media platform Truth Social that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire.
- The Kremlin said it had nothing to say about the energy ceasefire announced by Trump.

articles.title: Ukraine says Starlink restricted operations overnight, disrupting military missions
articles.body:
Ukraine says Starlink restricted operations overnight, disrupting military missions
Elon Musk's Starlink imposed restrictions on the operation of internet terminals in Ukraine overnight, disrupting military missions, an adviser to the Ukrainian president said on Wednesday. The official said Ukraine was given no prior warning about the restrictions to the satellite system it relies on for battlefield operations.
The operation of some Starlink internet terminals appeared to be restricted overnight, a technology adviser to Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday, disrupting Ukrainian military missions as Russia launched targeted strikes on the country's energy infrastructure.
Ukraine uses the satellite system controlled by SpaceX owner Elon Musk for its battlefield communications, but the tech titan has shifted his stance on Ukraine several times since Russia's invasion in 2022.
"Tonight SpaceX introduced a speed limit for the Starlink terminals in motion," said the adviser, Sergiy Beskrestnov.
"Our defence forces were not warned about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions," he added. "Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," he added.
US President Donald Trump called for a pause in attacks on energy infrastructure while moving to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.
Read moreTrump, Zelensky clash over diesel deal as Russian strikes on Ukraine kill at least 21
A senior Ukrainian official told AFP that the disruption "severely restricts logistics, first and foremost".
Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, added that units had been forced to cancel some missions.
"According to our observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10–20 seconds at speeds of just 110–120km/h. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," it said in a statement to Reuters.
Ukraine has been using Starlink terminals to provide satellite internet connections as an alternative to radio control for its drones.
"Some restrictions were already being reported yesterday evening. So, in effect, it is happening in sync with this morning's Russian ballistic attack," the official added.
Trump wrote in a social media post Sunday that "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
But there is no sign either side is ready for such a ceasefire, with Ukraine reporting that a Russian missile struck a power plant in Kyiv on Tuesday evening.
Zelensky said in August that Kyiv was seeking to develop an alternative to Starlink in partnership "with a European country" that he did not identify.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

articles.title: Allies warned Ukraine of three ballistic waves, but not the first – Air Force
articles.body:
Allies warned Ukraine of three ballistic waves, but not the first – Air Force
Colonel Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, has said that during Russia's attack on the night of 13-14 October, Ukraine's partners did not warn it about the first wave of ballistic missiles but did give advance notice of the three subsequent waves.
Source: Ihnat during the national joint 24/7 newscast
Details: Ihnat clarified whether Ukraine had received warnings from its partners, as the issue has prompted many questions.
Quote: "At around 22:40, we initially said we had received no warning from our partners about ballistic missiles. However, our partners did alert us to the ballistic threat ahead of the next three waves of attacks."
Background:
- On the night of 13-14 October, Russia attacked Ukraine with 39 ballistic missiles and 128 drones, mainly targeting Kyiv and Kyiv and Kharkiv oblasts. Ukrainian air defence forces shot down or jammed four missiles and 115 drones.
- Reports of a missile threat reached users immediately before or as the explosions occurred.
- The president's office said Kyiv had received no warning from its partners about the strike and that the military and relevant services were investigating the circumstances.
- A similar situation occurred at 22:10 on 12 October, when Russia launched five ballistic missiles on Kyiv. Ukraine's Air Force said it had received no information about missile launches from Russian territory, leaving insufficient time to issue an air-raid warning.
- Commenting on the strike, Ihnat noted that this was not the first time intelligence had arrived too late. He said he hoped Ukrainian intelligence would work with Kyiv's international partners to determine the cause of the delay.
- Meanwhile, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Kyiv continues to receive intelligence from the US.

articles.title: UK to speed up delivery of missiles to counter jet-powered drones in Ukraine
articles.body:
UK to speed up delivery of missiles to counter jet-powered drones in Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will arrive in the UK on 14 October as London plans to speed up deliveries of Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs) used to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones.
Source: the UK government, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The visit comes as the UK steps up its support for Ukraine, including by supplying £45 million worth of air defence missiles and pressing ahead with plans to fully implement a ban on maritime services for Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.
According to the government, the UK will accelerate deliveries of its British-made LMMs, which have proved highly effective against jet-powered drones.
The UK has already committed £1.6 billion to supply Ukraine with more than 5,000 LMMs over the next four years. From the £45 million missile package, London will bring forward £10 million worth of weapons to meet Ukraine's most urgent needs ahead of winter.
"Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the front lines have the equipment they need to push back Russia. My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said.
Burnham has also instructed ministers to prepare additional sanctions, military aid packages and financial support to provide Ukraine with urgent assistance over the coming weeks.
Meanwhile, John Healey, Chancellor of the Exchequer, will urge London's partners to fully implement a similar ban on Russian LNG, following the UK's example, during meetings on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund's gathering in Bangkok. The foreign secretary made the same address to the UK's partners at the Warsaw Security Forum on 13 October.
Background:
- On 10 October, Zelenskyy and Burnham agreed to hold a bilateral meeting in the coming days to discuss maintaining sanctions pressure on Russia.
- Meanwhile, the UK has acknowledged that US President Donald Trump's diesel deal has complicated relations with Ukraine's allies.
